A WOMAN'S "NO." She had a parcel, small and round, One lovely afternoon last summer. I offered, as in duty bound, To take it from her. She tha,nked me, with a gracious smile, As sweet as rosy lips could make it; It was so small, 'twas not worth while To let me take it. Again I offered, as before, Of that slight burden to relieve her] She'd rather not—" pray say no more !" 'Twould really grieve her. I ceased to plead—she seemed content— The thing was small, and neatly corded, : And so along our way we went, To where she boarded. But when upon the step she stood, And here our last adieus were uttered, She eyed me in a roguish mood, And softly muttered, As swung the door to let her through, And left me there all unresisting; "I don't think very much of you For not insisting." Ir-rhe Century.

BETWEEN THE LIGHTS. The sunset fires are fading o'er the heather, I The flames of gold and crimson burn away, ' lipon the lea the purple shadows gather, And silence soothes the pulses of the day. • Toll, curfew, toll! The day of toil is over, Recall the banished who aweary roam; Chime! bells of peace, and wanderer and rover Will fondly turn their eyes to rest and home. • The morning gave us songs and joy and laughter,: The day was feverish with toil ani care; The night is cool, we think of rest hereafter, And sing our twilight songs upon the air. • Toll, curfew, toll! And still our fitful fever, Cover the fires of anguish and of pain; Peace shall be ours for over and for ever, Sorrow shall never tell her tale again. Not yet the stars of heaven in their splendour Reveal infinity in glorious heights, Not vet their radiance meets us, pure and tender, Their rising we await, between the lights. Ring, curfew, ring! But not with voice ofLsorrow, Utter melodiously our soft farewell To all that gieves us, for our fair to-morrow Will fairer be than sweetest tone may tell. "Between the lights" we watch, we wait, we ponder, Till beck'ning gleams from far-off worlds arise; In hush of spirit we await with wonder The starry-revelations of the sloes. .-811.71 day Magazine. CLARA TRWAITES.

div.head: Taritties.
div.p: Taritties.

Be just to your enemies, generous to your friends, and independent of both. If there be more pleasure in abundance, there is more security in a mean estate. Nothing more clearly indicates the true gentleman than a desire evinced to oblige or accommodate. The sun shines for everybody, the flowers smell sweet for all noses; and the nightingale warbles for all ears. Pity and virtue are not only delightful for the present, but they leave peace and contentment behind them. It is an unfortunate fact that many of us put off our manners as we put off our boots—on the threshold of borne.

The knowledge drawn from experience is of quite I another kind from that which flows from speculation or discourse. The real price of everything, what everything really costs, to the man who wants it, is the toil and trouble of acquiring it. Yen may depend upon it that he is a good man whose intimate friends are all good, and whose enemies are chitracters decidedly bad. " The;way to sleep," says a scientist," is to think of nothing." But this is a mistake. The way to sleep is to think it is time to get up. " Grant me 0 Lord," said a humble soul, "that I may peess unnoticed through the world." This should be the wish, or rather the aim, of all true devotion. Many do with opportunities as children do at the sea- shore; they fill their little hands with sand, and let the graLes fall -through, one by one, till all are gone. A young man who was jilted by his girl, and subse- quently married her, says she treated him like a bottle of patent medicine. He was "shaken" before taken. Partiality in a parent is commonly unlucky, for fond- lines,, are in danger to be made fools, and the children that are the least humored may make the best and wisest men. Chivalry is not confined to the relation of the sexes. It is a sentiment which should rightly inspire all who are highly favoured in any respect towards those who are less fortunate. "Lectures on cooking," exclaimed Mrs. B.; "no, I'm not going to 'em. My husband lectures on cooking, and when he mentions his mother he looks round for some- body to applaud." Naturalists saw that the feet of the common working honey bee "exhibit the combination of a basket, a brush, and a pair of pincers." This may be true, but we never knew before that a basket, a brush, and a pair of pincers were so warm to the touch. Lady, in registry office: I am afraid that little girl won't do for a nurse; she is too small. I should hesitate to trust her with the baby.—Clerk: Her size, madam, we look upon as her greatest recommendation. You should remember that when she drops a baby it doesn't have very far to fall. tow very low, how very poor, how very unfruitful a man must be who lives upon so low a level that he never has a sight of anything higher than that which he every day does. He eats, and drinks, and sleeps, and eats, and drinks and sleeps; and he and the swine are on one common level. There is nothing more of him than of them. It is a great mistake to set up your own standard of right and wrong, and judge people accordingly. It is a great mistake to measure the enjoyment of others by our own, to expect uniformity of opinion in this world, to look for judgment and experience in youth, to endeavour to mould all dispositions alike, not to yield to immaterial trifles, to look for perfection in our own actions, to worry ourselves and others with what cannot be remedied, to be- lieve only what our infinite minds can grasp. Tux INFLUENCE OF CONVERSATION.—One snowflake is nothing; it melts away on the outstretched hand in a momenbt ; but, flake by flake, the snow accumulates till it is the only thing visible in the landscape, and even the boughs of the oak crack beneath its weight. And such is the cumulative influence of the conversation of a life- time. No man can speak for a lifetime words of sense, kindliness, and purity, without consciously or uncon- sciously doing much good; nor can a talker, who> im- pure and profane, go through the world without doing nnapeakable mischief.—" Good Words" for March. SHE PAID EXTIIA.—A widow, whose age might have been 40, went into business on Grand River Avenue a few weeks ago, and the first move was to get a sign painted. The services of a sign painter were secured, zed when he finished his work he put on his "imprint" by placing his initials, "W. A. H.," down on the left- hand corner of the sign. When the widow came to criticise the work she queried, "What does W. A. H.' stand for ?" "Why, • Wanted, A Husband,'" replied the painter. "Oh, yes—l see," she mused. "It was very thoughtful in you, and here is a dollar extra."--e I Deiriit Free Press. *'OIVIt TELLING IN BIIRMATE.—Story-telling is a great art among the Burmese, and the tales are often hung together on a slender thread, as in the "Arabian Nights," branching interminably from one to the other, taking up a secondary character out of one recital and making it the principat feature of the next, so that there is no rea- son why there should ever be an end. Somo of these stories are full of point and contain considerable humour, but as in the early literature of every nation, they all re- Lite to grea,t people, kings and queens, and ministers and chiefs; the common people have not yet begun to be ihteresting to themselves. I was asked to write a story for a periodical which was circulated among the Chris- tian Burmese converts, but was warned that my peasant tales would not do at ; and, as it would be hardly ac- curate to describe our Queen as walking about the gar- den, with her crown on her head and the Kob-i-noor round her neck, or the Prince of Wales shooting rabbits in a field-marshal's uniform with a cocked hat and feathers, which would have been necessary to give the gorgeous colouring required, I was obliged to decline. Lady Verney, in "Good Words," for March. CETEWAYO'S CONTEMPT.—A. correspondent writes: A few, years ago when the Zulu King Cetewayo was a prisoner in the vicinity of Cat” Town—at Oude Molen—l and a. ft-Cow-seri:Jo were "told off" to write an account of an ath- let:o neeeine got up byk the militiry garrisoned at the ine- trupolis of the Cape, which was hold at a pretty village a • few miles up the line, known as Rhondeb3sch. Qieta un- ex7ectedly Cetewayo, whose confinement was apparently made as light ac possible, came on the field in company With some of the British officers. He was fully dressed in Euro- pean clothes, with a military looking cap. and appetred re- markably well. The sports included running, walking, jumping, sword dancing, and other feats, all of which " His Royal Ilizhness" wreclied with keen interest. Wishing to know his opinion of the British soldiers' skill and agility, We !Alt the question throu4h the interpreter, and were not a little surprised at the intimation in reply that "in his country his people did not play like children." He evi- dently viewed the whole affair as a fiasco compared with the warlike pursuits of his own subjects, and I and my companion retired with our national susceptibilities rather wounded.

In the middle of the night, in a heavy snowstorm, they boarded one of the numerous little trading boats which ply o‘n the river while it was moored to the bank at a lonely spot about 70 miles above Memphis. They found the owner, a man named Youpc, in bed with his wife, and forcing them to leave the boat in their night-clothes, took possession. They built a fire in the store, prepared and detoured a good supper, and remained on board until morning, when they left the boat, carrying away with them all the property that could conve- niently be taken. "I reckon he gets middlin' o' wage?" th' chap said. "Ay, but what will it do amung eight ov us ?" th' woman said. "We're gooin' to send eaur Joe apiecin' next week, an' that'll mak' things a bit better for us." "Well," th' °cap said, "yo'st have yo'r potatoes if yo'n see me th' feurpence." So he weighed 'em eant, an' spit upo' th' brass, an' sheauted—"Sowd again an' th' money drawn, as th' quack doctor said when he drew a bad shillin' for a box o' putty pills. Pike th' road, Jinny." He drove on, an' sheauted till he thowt nob'dy wur for havire owt to do wi' him any moore. At last he left a pluck at his jacket laps; so he turned reaund for to see what wnr up. It wnr a little lad wi' a check napkin i' one hont, an' a quart o' fagberry (gooeeberry) in a can i'th' other.

"Well, what does theau want, my little appleface?" th' chap said. " My mother wants t' know if, yo' sellin' fayberry," th' lad said. " Nawe, I dunno', my lad!" th' chap said, "but what's hoo want t' know that for, when thean's getten some P" "Well," ill' lad says, "if yo'n let her ha' five peaund o' potatoes, hoo'll give yo' these fayberry for 'em, an' then yo' con start o' sellin'. They'n conan eant o' eaur garden. Hoo has no brass, nobbnt tuppence, an' that hoo'll want for bacon." "I &nano' know, lad, what I man do wi' th' fayberry," th' chap said. "A quart wonldno' be sich a good start." "Well, boo says if yo' danno' want th' fayberry, win yo' let her ha' th' potatoes o' trust? an' if my feyther doesno' pay for 'em when he's demon (finished work), yo' man tak it cant on him when yo' leeten an him at th' Owd Bell." An' th' lad looked at th' fayberry as if he could like to ha' etten 'em hissel.
"Let's see, whoa is thy feyther ?" th' chap said. Billy o' Tummy's," th' lad said. "Oh, ay, to be sure; he wayves to Owd Aaron, doesno' he ?"

" Yoi," th' lad said; "an' my mother wayves chep trip to Sloper's." "Does theau like fayberry ?" " Ay," th' lad said; "but they gi'en me th' bally-warcht if I ate too molly." "Could theau ate o ther is i' that can ?" "Baur Alick an' me could," th' lad said. " Howd thy napkin, then," an' th' chap weighed cant five peaund o' potatoes, an' towd th' lad he met tak' th' fay- berry back, an' let their Alick join him at 'em; an' if his mother wanted Ave peaund moore th' mornin' after, hoo met have 'em. Well, he began o' doin' his biznese o' this plan straight- I forrad, an' by th' time he'd getten to th' yate, he'd emptied ' a hamper, an' started or a fresh un Thor war some ova row when he're gon. Th' quality eend o' th' fowt war up i' arms again th' other, an' I thowt ther'd be noses Waisted, an' yare poo'd up by th' roots afore they'd settled ther bother. Th' day after things war quite as bad; an' when Seturday coom ther sich a hullaballoo as I never yerd afore, for booath men an' women wur in at it. My owd rib kept i'th' helms., like a woman ut's a bit o' decency abeaut her; an' I said hoo deserved a wooden medal for it. But when Seturday fleet CGOM, an' things had quietened deawn a bit, Shoiny Jim's wife coom for her, an' said hoo're wanted at their heause very partikilar. I didno' like th' tbowts on her gooin, but when Shoiny's wife said it war o I' friendship, I said boo met goo, an' if hoo coom cant wi' flyin colours, hoo should have a tin medal. Well, hoo went to Shoiny Jim's an' fund th' heause full o' quality folk—th' women to-in' cant wi' ther husbant's, an' ther haseants neaw an' than givin"em a word or two back at hit 'em as heavy as hommers. Hoo could see in a minute what hoo're wanted for; s hoo lapt her apron reaund her, an' put her yure cant o'th sect, lest what boo said would leead to a scrimmage. "Neaw, then, Sarah," Shoiny Jim's wife said (boo coed my owd rib Sarah) "I want to see what theau'd do if theau're i' my place. Here's eaur Jim on th' spree two days this week, an' he's nobbut browt me one peaund twelve for t' do everythin' with. I wan to know what theau'd do with it, Sarah." "Ay, I want to know that, too," eaur Sal said. "Yer thee neaw, thean wastrel!" Jim's wife said, turnin' to her husbant, who looked as sheepish i'th' nook as if he'd bin drinkin' a whul week, "hoe doesao' know what boo'd do with it, an' a wayver's wife, too." "Duet' meean t' say thean doesno' know what theau'd do wi' one peaund twelve a-week ?" Shoiny said to my wife. " Nawe," th' owd lass said; "but I happen met lam; but just neaw, if yo'd tak' th' twenty off, an' leeave me th' odd twelve, I should happen know what to do wi' that." " Twelve shillin' a-week!" Shoiny Jim's wife said. "Twelve shillin' a-week!" Smoot Dody's wife said. " Heaw- ever could hoo mak' that do ?" "I connno' tell," my owd rib said; "but I have to mak' it t' do mony a time, an' sometimes less, when we're waitin' o' wark." Os but they oonldno' see it. floo met give 'ern an inklin' heaw It war done. . "Well," boo said, "for a start, I dunno goo a tee drinkin' ov a Monday, an' goo again o' Tuesday a-talkin' absent it. Nor I dunno goo to th' Owd Bell bar five or six times a-day wipia' my lips, and lookin' what time it is. Baur table doesno' know what potted shrimps an' salmon steaks, an' marmalade, an' lobsters are. I believe if owt o'th' sort war put on it, it nd want o'er, same as if it war drunken. We ha' no lamb an' green peas every day to dinner; not ut workin' folk should be begrudged o' sich like, becose I think if anybody deserves good mayte an' drink, thoose at dun summat for it owt to have it; but twelve shillin' a week winno' afford it. I never cook moore than we con ate; so at ther's nowt wasted. I wesh for mysel', as every woman nt's able owt to do, whether hoo be gentle or simple. I believe our Ab would goo as ittert (dirty) as owd Will Nest, afore he'd wear a shirt o' anybody's weehin' beside mine. (True, owd wench; I itch wi' th' thowts on't just nsaw.) I do my own eleeanin' ; but that's no' so mich, becose eaur heaase is nobbat a little un. I der= goo strollopin' abeaut i' silk an' satin a day or two a-week, as if I're Lady Mary, an' then Ward Thursday goo an' borrow someb'dy's ring for t' tak' to my uncle's; an' I dunno"-- Hoo could get no farr, for o th' chaps jampt no as sadden as If they'd bein' scanden ; an' o th' women, obbnt my owd rib, pet ther hands under ther apperns, an' looked as if they'rn just bein' drawn up afore th' magistrates. Ther wurno' a ring i'th' beaus*, nobbut one, at I'd gen two canaries for to a chap ut used to come abeaut wi' a little box, an' that wur upo' eanr Sal's finger. Th' apperns war turned up in a snifter ; an' when ther nowt breeter than a finger-nail could be seen, ther wur a dooment. Fists flew abeaut, an' threeatenins wur made wi' sich ven- geance, ut it mane my wife wish hoo're at th' side o'th' owd yate again ; for hoo thowt ther'd be some black e'en 'livered cant. But it didno' come to that. Th' women promised they'd be everythin"at warr reet an' good, 11th' chaps nd be th' same, an' they'd start that nest a tryin' to mak' best o' thingß. Th' storm passed off, an' th' sunshoine coom cant again, an' Pre sent for just to have a word amung 'em. I backed my owd rib up same as if hoo'd bin a tip-top racehoss, an' a rare spree we had. We'd just an odd quart *o' spigot-milk, as a gradely settler. I sung 'em "Jone o' Grinfilt," an' eaur Sal tweedled th' "Jolly Angler," an' we'rn as merry as a lot o' gipsies till midneet, when we parted. Walmsley Fowt has bin different ever sin'. Booath men an' women, an' I believe childer too, are tryin' to mak' Cr best o' things, an' they're lookin' better every day. Th' owd potato chap stops neaw at every dur ; an his donkey has getten so fat ut I believe it's begun o' thinkin' it's a hoes, for it draws as soon as it's towd, an it's gan o'er singin' "another wayver deead" at th' side o' th' yate. Shoiny Jim wears his hat a bit straighter on his yead, an' does a bit o' gardenin' neaw, when FVe seen th' time he'd ha' bin faddlin'. Ther's no wipie o' lips nor no borrowin' o' rings neaw ; an' th' last Scotchman ut coom geet a good dnckin' Owd Thuston's pit, an' he's bin shy at th' fowt ever sin'. I noticed one day, as I're gooin' a bearin' whoam, ut "my uncle," as they coed him, ut had a shop, wi' three brass oranges o'er th' dam, deawn Hazelwo'th, had put th" shut- ters up, an' takken his three-legged sign deawn, an' ther an ettererop (spider) th' &lye or a starfish, wayvin" a bed-tick P one corner o' th' dam hole. It made me think my owd rib had bin talkin' somewheere else than eaur fowt. An' one neet when I went i'th' Owd Bell kitchen I hardly knew wheere I wur, summat looked so strange to me. / believe I should ne'er ha fund it cant, aoather, if th' landlady hadno' come in, an' said— " We'n managed it at last, Ab." "Managed what ?" I said. "Wean getten th' kitchen der painted." That war it at made th' place look so strange to me. • Well, one fleet after this, as I're dividin' a blackpaddin' amung eaur lads, ther a little wench coom to th' dam, an' said me an' my wife war wanted at Smoot Dody's. So we went, little thinkin' what we'rn wanted for; an' when we geet theere we fund a gradely heauseful o' neighbours, o on 'em lookin' as breet as if th' sun war tryin t' put th' fire cant. Shoiny Jim's wife war theere, an' afore we'd gradely sit deawn, boo poo'd a cap eant ov a napkin, an' held it up for th' tothers t' look at. While hoo're doin' that someb'dy I mope at th' back ov eaur Sal, an' nipt her cap off her yead in a snifter, an' this new an war put on i'th' place, an' a fine an it wur too; an' hoo're towd it war hers—as a token, or summat they coed it, o' what her neighbours thowt abeaut her. Th' owd lass war some gloppent, I con tell yo'; an' boo hardly knew whether t' cry or let it a-be. But at lfuet hoo made a speech—l hardly know what abeaut, nor I durum' think hoo did, nobbut hoo said some foolish things

ICE ACCIDENTS.—SIX LIVES LOST.--A lamentable scene was witnessed on the Serpentine in Hyde Park on Sunday afternoon. The water was covered with ice. Disregarding the warning notices, three gentlemen walked on to the frozen surface, which gave way. One escaped, but his two companions were drowned.--In Windsor Park, on Sun- day, four young men were eliding on the Round Pond, when the ice broke and three of the men lost their lives. --Another young man was drowned on Saturday by the giving way of ice on a sheet of water near Alsager,

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

ALLaritxxxs.—Lord Eldon has recently laid out a con- siderable portion of agricultural land on his estate in Doraetshire as allotment gardens for the working classes. At a small village called Herston several acres have been set apart for this purpose, and the allotments have been very rapidly taken up: The land is among the best in the estate, and has been tilled for several years by some of the largest farmers in the neighbourhood. Mr. G. Burt, another large landowner in the same neighbour- hood, has also laid out large plots of land as allotments at the ground rent of 255. per annum, or the freehold at £25 per acre.

Tris no:Tr GARDM7.—" Gardening World " draws attention this week to a useful plant for front gardens— Anemone Fulgues—which, in point of brilliancy, is sur- passed by none, and only equalled by some of the more intense forces of the Crown Anemone, A. Coronaria. It thrives well in most soils of a rich vegetable nature, and deteriorates but in few. When it is found to fall off after a season or two, it should be lifted when fully matured and dried off by placing in dry silver sand in any shed or outhouse, wherein an uniform temperature may be maintained. If preference may be given to soil where it may be allowed to remain undisturbed for several years, then that soil is light, rich, sandy loam, of fair depth; after the end of the first season its progress in such soil is very rapid, and the yield of its flowers in spring time increases in the same proportion. Those who wish for a succession of its fiery scarlet flowers should plant it at intervals of a month or six weeks; for spring effect, however, plant early in September, and for summer and autumn from March to May. It should be planted about 3in. deep, always avoiding cold, clayey soils.

THB WINDOW.--Attend to Hyacinths in glasses and re- plenish with water before it gets any distance from the base of the bulb, and if at any time it should smell offensive it should be emptied out and replaced by clean. But to effect this the bulb must on no account be dis- turbed, no more than slightly movinc, it to one side to allow the water to escape and the fresh to be put in. As the spikes will be in an advanced stage they must be exposed to full light and the sunniest window, in order to keep them dwarf and give full development to the flower and colour. Turn them round occasionally if they show a disposition to draw towards the light. In the absence of the wire supports which generally accompany the glasses, a wire may be thrust into the bulb and the spike tied to it.

div.head: "WARRINGTON BOARD OF GITARDIA.NS.
div.p: "WARRINGTON BOARD OF GITARDIA.NS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev.. G. F. Roberts (chairman), and Messrs. Gibson, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Jolley, Brown, Ratcliffe, Maokie, Blackherst, Humphries, Derbyshire, Ba'harry, Harrison, Grange, Greening, Forster; and S. Sutton (assistant clerk). ;

div.head: THB WORYIIOI7SB.
div.p: THB WORYIIOI7SB.

The House Committee reported that the water mains at the Workhouse lad been tried, the hydrant was put on and found satisfactory, delivering a good volume of water on the roof. The present number of inmates ws s 377, as compared with 330 in the corresponding week last year ; increase 47. —Mr. BROWN moved the confirmation of the minutes.—Mr. JOLLY, in seconding the proposal, said they had four hydrants at the Workhouse, one at each corner of the build- ing, and they could all be used at the same time.—The minutes were confirmed. • SCHOOL COMIII7TER. This committee recommended that be given to Mr. Williams as a gratuity for drilling lessons given to the chil- dren. The committee nomated Mr. Joseph Tickle for the post of foster father, shoe maker, and drill master, and his wife as foster mother. The medical officer reported that the children were in good health.—On the motion of the CHAIR- MAN the reinutel were confirmed..

div.head: SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE.

This committee reported that fees had been allowed in 64 now and 132 old cases, making a total of 196.—Mr. BLecz- asT, in moving tite confirmation, said that owing to the dis- tress in the town these cases were growing on them, but they dealt with them as they best could.—Mr. RATCLIFFB mentioned that while the cases in Warrington were increas- ing, in Newton they were reduced, although there had been a good deal said about the Newton cases.—Mr. BROWN said many of the fees had only been granted for one month.— The minutes were then confirmed.

div.head: VACCINATION RETURNS
div.p: VACCINATION RETURNS

Vaccination returns from the various districts of the Union were submitted and considered satisfactory. A short discussion took place as to the following persons who left one district for another without having had their children vaccinated.—Mr. DABEYSHIRB said be knew a person who moved from one district into another in order to avoid vaccination, and he had done this very successfully.—The ASSISTANT CLBuir said that if the vaccination officer did his duty in that case be would follow the case up..—Tbe matter then dropped.

div.head: OTIIRCROWDED WORKHOUSE.
div.p: THE OTIIRCROWDED WORKHOUSE.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanc- tioning as a temporary measure in view of the overcrowded state of the ordinary hospital wards the utilising of the in- fectious diseases hospital for the simpler cases of .infirmity and sickness occurring in the Workhouse.

CONTAGIOUS DISEASBS ACT. A communication was read from the Farnham Union asking the Board to pass a resolution in favour of the Con- tagious Diseases Act being again put in force.—Mr. HARRI- SON spoke in favour of the proposal, and said that the Act had been dropped through the action of certain strong- minded women, as he supposed they called them, wkio would have been batter engaged with their domestic duties. He gyre notice that he would propose at the next meeting that the resolution be passed by the Board.—Dr. Mecam hoped Mr. Harrison would come primed with stronger argu- manta than he had used that day.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

Mr. DARBYSHIRE suggested that the Board should peti- tion Par Lamest-in favour of the application of the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal for powers to pay interest eat of capital. When the Bill was first before Parliament that Board petitiouesi in its favour, and he thought they might well do so again. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. HARRISON observed that the Warrington Town Council had forwarded a petition in favour of the Ship Canal promoters, and he agreed that it was desirable that Board should also do so, as the canal when commenced would find employment for a good deal of idle labour.-11r. BLACAURST likewise spoke in favour of the suggestion, and Mr. DAREYSEIRE then proposed that such a petition be sent. It was, however, mentioned that it was contrary to the standing orders to pass such a reso- lution without notice.—Mr. HARRISON thereupon moved, and Mr. GREENING seconded, that the standing orders be suspended, and this was agreed to.—Mr. DAREYSHIRE then formally moved his proposal, which was seconded by Mr. BLACERIIRST, and eupported by Messrs. MAMIE and Fo SM.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said he should like to see the Ship Canal go on, but it looked bad on the face ot it. If it was going to be a paying concern there was ninatY of capital to be had In England.—Mr. HARRISON said it was not every- body who could afferd to invest their money without re- ceiving interest upon it for several years. (Hear, hear.)— Mr. GREENING said it was nothing new to pay dividends out of capital, and he could not think that permission to do so would be refused by Parliament in the case of the Ship Canal.—Messrs. Brown and Jolley, and the Chairman having also supported the proposal, nem, con. it was agreed to This was all the business of public interest.

240 CATTLE DHOW:CM—The Liverpool steamer Missouri, which is ashore off Holyhead, fell over on Monday night and sank. It is feared she will be a total wreck. Of her five stock 150 cattle were saved. Tha re- mainder, numbering 244, were drowned. The Missouri registered ever 5,000 tens. A Bia DIAMOND.—In August, 1884, the arrival of the celebrated 457-carat fine white diamond from South Africa was announced, and its subsequent purchase by a syndicate of London and Paris diamond merchants. The gem was entrusted to the care of one of the most skilful cutters, who has been engaged on the atone during the past eight months, and expects to complete the work in April next. As antici- pated, the stone will turn out the most wonderful " brilliant- cut " diamond on record, surpassing in weight, as also, it is believed, in colour, purity and lustre, all the Crown and histbrical brilliants of the world. The stone in its almost finished state weighs still 239 carats, but in order to give it the best passible shapl and lustre it is intended to reduce its weight to something like 200 carats. The Koh-i-noor weighs only 1011 carats, the Regent of Paris 1361 carats, the Star of the South 125 carats, and the Piggott 82± carats. The Great' Mogul weighs 279 carats. It is, however, a lumpy stone, only rose-cut, and if cut to a proper shaped brilliant, it would probably not weigh more than 140 carats. • FIGHTING IxrEcnort.--Dr. W. S. div.head: F'JREIGN NEWS.
div.p: F'JREIGN NEWS.

THE SOUDAN.—GATHERING OF THE REBELS. CAIRO, SITSPLY.—A battalion of bleak% with two bat- talions of Egyptians and a battery ot Artillery, are being got ready to join the garrison of Snakim. They are to be well officered by Englishmen. . The rebels are reported to be gathering in increasing numbers round Suakim, and it is be- lieved possible that General Warren, should he be able to Strike a heavy 'blow there, may break the power of the rebels as far as the Nile. THE EASTERN CRISIS. SOFIA, Stiviam.•.—The Servian Government has not ac- cepted the Bulgarian draft of the treaty of peace, and insists on adhering to its own wording. It is 'rumoured that, in view of this fact, and of the expiration of the armistice, Which ends to-morrow, all the Roumelian troops have been ordered to leave /or Sofia, where the Princeiis expected to- morrow on his way to the frontier. VIENNA, SUNWAS.—The confident expectations that peace ' between Servia and Bulgaria would be signed to-day at ' Bucharest have not been realised. Instead of the news that was anticipated we have tidings of new difficulties and of something like a Cabinet crisis at Belgrade. 'King Milan ' has taken fright at the tactics of the Radical party, which, •as often explained, 'is to a large extent moved by Russian , Inspiration. EincuAncsr, MONDLY.—In political circles 'here the pre- • sent situation continues to be regarded as unfavourable, owing to the silence of the Servian Government and the in- telligence from Sofia that Roumelian troops have been •crdered towards the Bulgarian frontier. CONCLUSION OF PEACE. A.•BUCHAREST, WElMEsin.Y.—The treaty of peace was • 'signed here at noon to-day by the Turkish, Servian, and Bulgarian delegates. BELGRADE. WEDNESDAY.—A telegram received by the ,Servian Government from M. Mijatovics announces the sig- nature ef the Peace Treaty by the Ottoman, c"ervian, and Bulgarian delegates. FIGHTING IN BURMAH. MANDALAY, FEBRUARY' 23.—The second column which was recently despatched from Mandalay to co-operate with the Tounghoo force has Attacked and routed at Tontbamye :a large body of rebels, followers of the Mingeen Prince. 'The rebels subsequently joined a band of daceits and re- treated into a walled pagoda, • from which, after a etubborn ' • resistance, they were dislodged. Three men were wounded -on the British side. 'RUSSIAN EMMY INTO PENJDEII. WREN', SUNDAY.—Intelligence has been received here lthat a detachment of Russian troops under General Alik- baroff made a formal entry into Penjdeh on the 13th inst., in the presence of a large concourse of people. The 'General announced to the Sarvks the union of the district with Russia, and the establishment of a Russian adnainistra- ,tion. THE HEALTH OF THE GERMAN EMPEROR. BERLIN, MONDAY.—Although the contusion of the left ,hip, from which the Emperor is suffering, follows a favour- able course, it-will be necessary ,for his Majesty to remain 'quiet ,for some time. The Emperor continues to transact business-and to receive, the daily verbal reports as usual.

FRANCE. DESTRUCTIVE FIRE IN PARIS. PAIIIS, MOND/LT.—A great fire occurred this morning oni the St.. Ouen border of Paris, causing immense destruction of property, and, it is feared, loas.of life. The alarm wasl given soon after midtlight that the premises .of a rag mer- chant were-in flameaeand before the :firemen.could get to , work wine houses adSoining were also on fire. Most of the 1 inmates of these dwelliags were able .to make their escape; bat one family is reported missing, and there-is reason to fear the members of it have lost their lives. The morning was bitterly -cold, and.tha sufferings of the people, many only partially.clothed, were interse. PROPOSED EXPIKASION OF TICE PRINVES. PARIS, T0rma0,t5.7.--M3 proposal of IC Duche for the expulsion of the Royalist and Bonapartist Princes from :France was to-day discussed in the Chamber of Deputies. et.fter several members had spoken for and against the pro- position, N. de Freyeinet (the Prime Mialister; addressed the House, condetnning, N. Duche's motion as needless and inopportune. The Premier's speech was applauded, and the Chamber finally rejected M. Dache's bill by .34;5,votee to 195. The alternative bill of N. Rivet, authorising the ex- pulsion by Presidential decree of any member of a former reigning family whose conduct shall have tended to jeopar- dise the safety of the State, was next discussed, and in the ,end rejected by 383 votes to-188. THE UNITED STATES.—GREAT STORM. Prmanty„rettl, SIINDAY.—A furious wind storm has prevailed throughout the eastern and middle States since -Thursday night. The velocity of the wind exceeded fifty miles an hour. The highest velocity attained was at New York, 6.1 miles an hour. The mercury fell in some places to zero. Many buildings have been unroofed, and telegraphic communication is generally interrupted. The steamer Idle- wild was wrecked in Long Island Sound, but the passengers were rescued. Several serious fires occurred, the worst being at Troy, New York, where seven firemen were injured by the falling in of some walls. The gale declined En violence to-day. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four TER LUNACY LAWS.—The LORD CHANC2iILOII, in mov- ing the second reading of the Lunacy Acts Amendment Bill stated that the lact that any person could have another in- carcerated as a lunatic on the 'certificate of two medical men had sunk deeply in the public mind. It was prepoeed to go no further in the Bill than to provide that there should beno new licenses issued for such establishments, and that there should be no addition to the number of patients in those now existing.—Lord SISLBORNB expressed his hope that the Bill would pass both Houses in the present session. —The 'Bill was then read a second time, as was also the Lunacy Consolidation Bill, which is merely a codifica- tion measure. Their Lordships rose at 6-20. HOUSE OF COMMONS..—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. Nave MRMEBRS.—Sir E. J. Reed (Cardiff), Mr. 0. V. Morgan (Battersea). and Mr. O'Brien (Monaghan) took the oath and their seats. BoYcorrnici IN answer to Captain Weal- mom, who referred to 'cases of boycotting at Bally farnan, Mr. J. MORLAY said, in regard to the first case, the person said to be boycotted had made no complaints to the police, and the other Protestant families in the neighbourhood were not interfered with. (Irish cheers.) 'Dm police patrol was considered to be sufficient'for the security of the neighbour- hood. A Buneoes Brot,.—Mr. CHILDHRS, in reply to Mr. Henry Richard, said Mr. 0. Morgan, on behalf of the Government, would introduce a Burials Bill similar to the one of last year. TRH buss LEAGUE.—+COIOneI WIRING asked the Chief Secretary for Ireland whether he was aware that the National League indirectly and directly projaibited the payment of rent P—Mr. MORLEY said certain words quoted were used, not at a meeting of the National League, but at a sheriff's sale. (Hear, keen) THB SPENDING DEPARTMEINTS.—Mr. RILANDS asked the Prime Minister whether it was the intention of'Government to appoint Select Committees to inquire into the admini- stration and expenditure of the great spending departmen t of the State P—Mr. GLADSTONB very much regretted th circumstances which made it impossible to secure the ape pointment of these Committees in the last Parliament, bue the Government had by no means dropped the idea of ap- pointing them. But he could not give a positive answer on the subject for a week or two.—Mr. RYLINDS said he would put his question on a later day. LORD R Ceruncieloo's ULSTER SPERCHIS.—Sir M. HICKS-. BEACH asked the Prima Minister to use his influence with the private members on his side to withdraw their motions next night, in order that Mr. Sexton's vote of censure on Lord R. Churchill's Belfast speech might come on first.— Mr. GLADETONB declined a give a definite answer at that moment, and Sir J. PSLASE, who had a motion down, said that he for one would not stand in the way. SIR H. DRUMMOND WOLFE'S 'MISSION.—The House hay- ing gone into Committee of Supply ean the vote of £25,000 for the Diplomatic Services, including £12,500 paid in re- spect of Sir H. D. Wolff's mission, Mr. BRADLAUGH moved the reduction of the vote by the latter sum. He charac- terhed the appointment of Sir H. Wolff as an improper one, and contended that, as he was a member of Parliament at the time he was appointed, the paymeot of his salary was illegal.—Sir J. GOLDSMID objected to the mission on the ground that it was opposed to the policy of this coun- try to recognise any interference by the Sultan in the in- ternal affairs of Egypt, and challenged the late Govern- ment to •justify it.—Sir G. CAMPEULL pointed out that England was paying four and a half millions annually for the government of .Etypt, and thought the sum paid for Sir H. Wolff's mission was too trivial to object to.—Mr. RYLARD6 asked the late Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs at what time it was decided that Sir Henry Wolff should receive a salary P—Mr. GLAD- growls, who said that it was the desire of the Government to maintain a continuous policy in Egypt if it was possible, contended that immense practical improve- ments had been effected in that country, although, he ad- mitted, at great cost.—Mr. Thum; advocated the with- drawal of British tro pa from Suakirn, and the motion to reduce the vote was negatived on a division by 185 to 98. BECIRCANALAND.—Mr. °sooner]; Mceseifier next explained the vote of •£69,210 for South Africa (including Becimana- land) and St. Helena, and stated in reply to Mr. Baden Powell that 'the sale of intoxicating liquor to natives in Bechuanaland was strictly prohibited.—fhe conversation was continued by Sir G. Campbell, Sir R. N. Fowler, and Mr. Wierthur ; and Mr. LABOECHBRE, who argued that all .annexations in South Africa had resulted in loss, moved the reduction of the vote by £6B,ooo.—Mr. BIETHRLL warmly supported the vote, and on a division it was carried by 229 to-85. The Supplementary Army Estimate was agreed to. The Land Registry Bill passed through committee with- out amendment, and was read a third time. On the motion by Mr. Laressos-Gowsz for the reading of the Hyde Park-corner (New Streets) Bill some dis- cussion ensued, but ultimately the bill was read a second time and referred to a select committeb. The Glebe Loans (Ireland) Acts Continuance Bill and the Land Tax Commissioners' Names Bill were read a second time; and the Sporting Lands Rating (Scotland) Bill passed through committee. After other business the House adjourned at 1-15. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIMSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat upon the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. MOI7NYED SOLDIERS.—.Td SANDHURST, in reply to Viscount Midleton, said that permission had been given in six instances to attach mounted men to certain companies of infantry volunteer corps, but in two instances the permis- sion was afterwards cancelled, and in the other cases it was doubtful whether the scheme could be carried out. It would net, therefore, be desirable to grant any more per- mission until the authorities had had an opportunity of see- ing further reports. The Howe adjourned at twenty minutes to five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS..—TT. The Speaker took the chair shortly before four o'clock. BELFAST DRAINAGE.—Mr. Ssrros desired that the Com- mittee on the Belfast Main Drainage Bill should be instructed to insert clauses assimilating the raunicieal and Parliamen- tary Franchise of Belfast and providing for anew corporation election there.—Mr. COURTNEY, by moving the previous question, incurred the wrath of Mrellealy and other Par- nellites, and there was a succession ot speeches devoted to protest against Mr. Courtney's course. At 20 minutes past 9 the Parnellite indignation had for the moment exhausted itself, and after a division, which occupied another quarter of an hour, the question was disposed of in accordance with Mr. Courtney's proposal by 200 votes to 84. Inesn Eseistooss.—The late Attorney-General for Ireland gave notice of a motion declaring the unwillingness of the House to consider the Irish Civil Service Estimates before being put in possession of the Government Irish policy. A demonstration of derisive laughter from the Farnellites greeted the announcement. I LABOUR STATISTICS.— Mr. BRADLATIGII brought before the House a motion in favour of the full and accurate col- lection of labour statistics. Socialism, he said, was not gaining ground amongst the people. The old English indi- vidual endeavour lived, but fair play was wanted for it; and if there were the means of getting a chance here or there, it was a duty to put the knowledge within the reach of the poorest.—Mr. BURT seconded the motion, which was met by an amendment by Mr. STANUOPE proposing the ap- pointment of a Select Committee to consider the best means of collecting and publishing labour statistics.—Mr. Muer- leiangc weinithmitthte otioeemuunnnaencd ecessdaerpyr,eaxtipnrgestsbecie pro- ceed at once with the 'collection of statistics.—After a die- ;aphPlimPL:sikenlftmaYacemnitPnaftoahfvour of the appointment of a staff to cussion the amendment was withdrawn, and the motion agreed to without a division. A motion for a Select Committee on Town Buildings, re- cently promised by the Prime Minister,was made by Colonel Nolan and agreed to. The House adjourned at ten minutes past one. HOUSE OF COMMONS."—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve elelOCk. LABOURERS (IRELAND) BILL.—Dr. Clark's Crofters Bill and Mr. Macfarlane's Highlands and Islands Bill, which were on the paper for discussion in the Rouse of Commons were deferred until Monday, in order that they may be taken with the Government bill. The second reading of the Labourers (Ireland) Acts Amendment Bill was moved by Mr. MAYNE.—On behalf of the Government, Mr. JOHN Mon.toy stated that there were some provisions in the bill which he would not accept, but as some points wanted clearing up he would assent to the second readiog.—The bill was read a second time without a division. UNCLAIMED Dorosrrs.—There was some discuesion on the Unclaimed Deposits Bill, the second reading of which was carried by 107 to 88. INsrocremi O MINES—Mr. A. O'Coneroo moved the second reading of a bill to provide for the more- frequent inspection of mines, and other precautions with 'respect to lamps, the qualifications of firemen, the definition of dan- places. and the regulation of advances ob- geaeiro9eds ng by rejection of the bill was moved by Mn. TOMLINSON, who contended that it would diminish the responsibilities of ownero, that it was not carefully framed, and that it was not calculated to carry out the objects its ' promoters had in view.—Colonel Bwrangri, suggested that it would be well to wait for the report of the Royal Commis- sion, when a comprehensive amendment of the Act of 1872 would become necessary.—Mr. J. Wrosos, speaking as a working miner, said great necessity existed for the amend- ment of the law. declared that no Mines Act would be com- plete which did not prohibit female labour in this obnoxious trade, and recommended the appointment of a minister of mines —Mr. B. div.p: THE IXAMINER._SATURDAY, MARCH 6, 1886.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. The monthly meeting of this Council was held in the Town Hall on Puesday evening. The Mayor (Aid. Harrison) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Crosfield, Burgess. Holmes, Davies, Webster; Councillors • Greening, Mackie, W. Pierpoint, Tinsley, Marsh, Ashton, Fleming, Bolton, Wright, Jolley, Brown, Greenall, Whittle, Hutchin- son, Dixon, Francomb, Taylor, Roberts • Messrs. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk),Longdin (borough surveyor), and Chorley (borough treasurer). APPOINTMENT OF AUDITORS. The Towle CLERK said that Mr. J. Harrison and Mr. J. L. Tunstall had been duly appointed elective auditors for the borough, and the Mayor had appointed Mr. John Brown as Mayor's auditor for the borough. THE PAVING OF STREETS. The Tows CLERK also reported that the Mayor had re- ceived a communication from the Association of Municipal Corporations with reference to the Public Health Act Im- provement extension Bill, which had been brought into Par- liament but had not succeeded in being passed. In the com- munication it was asked that some one should attend frets that Corporation to support the Bill. The Bill was a most im- portant one, and most beneficial. It was in order to enable the question to be decided as to whether a road was repair- able by the public at large or by the frontager prior to the expense being incurred. Hitherto the only way of dealing, with this matter has been to serve notice on the frontagers requiring them to make the road, and if they 'did not do so the Corporation made the road and sent the usual notice of cost to the frontager, and the matter then came before the magistrate as to who were liable to pay. In reply to Alderman Davies the Tows CLERK added that the Bill applied to new roads, for instance it would apply to Arpley-street, where there was i question as to payment of Wei. Alderman Davos asked if the Bill would give them any further powers than they had at present with a view to ma- king roads that were being developed iron semi-private roads, as the might call it, into public highways. The Tows CLERK: No, it does net. The subject then dropped. WATCK COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that the tender of Messrs. James Smith and Cs., of Derby, for clothing for police and other officers of the Corporation, be accepted. - - COLLISION AT SEL.—A collision occurred about eight ' miles off Porthieven early on Wednesday morning, between a Plymouth smack and a Mount's Bay fishing lugger. The latter sank Immediately, and the master (Edyvan), his son, his brother, and one seaman were drowned. THE PIMLICO MISTERT.—At Westminster Police Court, London, on Saturday afternoon, Mrs. Bartlett and the Rev. G Dyson were again charged, the former with murdering her husband, and the latter with being accessory before the fact.. Mr. Humble, chemist, Putney, deposed supplying Mr. Dyson with an ounce of chloroform on December 28th. He asked if it was good for taking out grease spots. Wit- ness said "Very good," and labelled the kottle " Chloro- form." It was an unusually large quantity to sell at once. —Thomas Penrose, manager to Messrs. Cadman, chemists, Wimbledon, said Mr. Dyson bought two ounces of chloro- form on December 28th. He said it was for cleaning. Wit- ness put it in two bottles.—Mr. B. Hicks, deputy coroner, produced the depositions of Mr. Dyson at the inquest, and it was arranged that they should be put in evidence on Fri- day.—Dr. Leach said he attended the deceased from Dec. 10th until his death. He was suffering from hypochon- driasia, sleeplessness, diarrhcea, and other symptoms. On the day before he died there were symptoms of mercurial poisoning. Witness saw him again some three hours after death. There was a wine glass on the table, and it smelt of brandy. On the mantelpiece was a small blue bottle labelled" Chlorodyne." Witness formed a positive opinion as to the cause of death, and said to Mrs. Bartlett there must be a post-mortem examination. mINNIGREY."— " ERN EST LINWOO D." Was it correct, he asked, that the Water- works gas, were paid for the water that supplied the fountain and required payment for the water, after it had gone through the fountain, that was used for washing the chapels. div.head: GAS COMMITTEE.-THE GIVING OF _GRATUITIES,
div.p: GAS COMMITTEE.-THE GIVING OF _GRATUITIES,

_ The minutes of the Gas Committee, the confirmation of which was proposed by Alderman HOLMES, and seconded by Alderman WEBSTER, recOmmended that a gratuily of £2O be voted to Mr. W. S. Haddock, assistant manager, who had made application for an increase of salary, for fees paid and services rendered in connection with the manufacture of sulphate. Councillor Bovrox took objection to the recommendation. He had understood, from the very elaborate explanation the mover gave recently as a reason for not raising Mr. Hunt's salary, that the present time of depression was not a suitable one for the raising of salaries. They could not raise Mr. Haddock's salary, and therefore proposed to give him a gratuity. It was all very well to say that it was for fees paid, but he thought that they should have some explana: tion how and why those fees had been incurred. He proposed an amendment that the sum be not allowed. Councillor FLEMING said that he also did not agree with the recommendation in its present form. If the fees were cash out of pocket, it should be so shown in the regular I expenditure accounts. If it really meant an excess of salary he thought it should not be granted:in view of the present distress. He seconded the amendment. Councillor ROBERTS asked what portion of the gratuity consisted of fees out of pocket, and under what circum- stances those fees came to be incurred by Mr. Haddock? Whether it was an express instruction that he should do so in order to qualify himself to make use of some production of the gas works for the benefit of the Corporation? If so, he said, it would help him to support the repayment of any expenses he might have incurred under such circum- stances. • Alderman HoLuus: It was entirely voluntary on his part, and by no instruction of ours. Alderman BURGESS did not think the mode of procedure a regular one, and he considered the Gas Committee should not ask for sanction to the recommendation. If Mr. Had- dock had been gaining knowledge of the manufacture of i sulphate for his own benefit, and on his own account, he did not see why the Council should pay for it. The know- ledge he had obtained was his own property. The Council, he thought, was kept too much in the dark about questions appertaining to the management of the gas works. (Hear, hear.) They had a second plant, staff, and sub-manager at Longford, and he could find no evidence of how much it was costing to manage that part of the gas department. He bad tried to ascertain what was accruing from the large outlay of from £40,000 to £50,000, and found that in 1882, the year preceding the opening of the northern gas works, they were in receipt of £26,797, and that in 1885 the amount was £27,589, being an increase of £792 a year. He supposed that in round numbers the amount required for sinking fund and interest would be nearly £3,000 a year,and then there was the working expense q of that portion of the gas works to be reckoned. He thought that the committee had carried them far enough in the wrong direction, and that they should resist being carried any further. Alderman WEBSTER said that it was quite true that they hact gone to considerable expense at Longford, and for the first year perhaps the increase was only £700; but it was certain they could not have supplied the quantity of gas required if the works had not been obtained. The reason they were not constructed in Mersey-street was because the people in that neighbourhood began to complain of a nuis- ance, and they could not with justice to the ratepayers ex- tend the works in the centre of the town. Unfortunately, the value of residuals had greatly decreased, which made a considerable difference in the profit. Mr. Haddock thought that he would make himself acquainted with the most modern—and best methods of—manufacturing sulphate and the most economical way, and in doing so incurred expense, which the committee, by not objecting, sanctioned. They thought it would be to their benefit as well as his when they proposed the gratuity. Councillor Warrrtz remarked to the effect that they ap- pear to pay Mr. Haddock a salary to do certain work, and then proposed to give him a gratuity for educating himself to that work.
Alderman WEBSTER : It was no part of his duty to maian- facture it.
Councillor MACKIE said that large consumers of as were charged at a rate that allowed of no profit, which was made out of the small consumers.

Alderman CROSFIEth was very sorry for the Gas Com- mittee. They had got a very difficult job. The eyes of the people were pretty well open to the fact that the Corporation made a great blunder when they bought the gas works, and he was very glad he raised his voice against that purchase at the time. He only wished the Corporation had bought the water works instead.

Alderman Horaats said that during the dates mentioned by Alderman Burgess-1882 and 1885—there bad been two reductions of 3d per 1,000 in the price of gas, which was a factor which should not be lost sight of. Had the price been maintained the profits would have been much more.
On a vote being taken the amendment was carried by 13 votes to eight, and the remainder of the minutes were passed.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. The General Purposes Committee recommended that .a Petition be presented to Parliament in favour of the Man- chester Ship Canal Additional Powers Bill, which recom- mendation was approved. Briefly, the grounds on which the petition was made were :—Your petitioners believe that the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal will greatly contribute to the general prosperity of Lancashire, and par- ticularly to the district of your petitioners by cheapening the mode of transit, and from their own knowledge, and the opinion of those connected with ,the construction of great works they believe that the payment of interest to share- helders during the construction of the work.; will greatly facilitate the raising of the capital which, as to five mil- lions, must be raised before the 6th day of August, 1887 ; your petitions believe that, having regard to the provisions made by the standing orders of yo-ar honourable House, provisions with which the bill strictly complies, no rea- sonable objection can be raised to the bill. Your petitioners therefore humbly pray your honourable House that the said bill may pass into law as it now stands.

div.head: PAVING OF THE STREETS.
div.p: THE PAVING OF THE STREETS.

Alderman WEBSTER proposed, "That it be an instruc- tion to the Paving and Sewerage Committee, as the neces- sity arises, to repave Bridge-street with wood, instead of the ordinary granite setts." A few months ago, the alder- man said, when he brought this question before the Coun- cil, a pledge was given that before anything was done with regard to the paving of Bridge-street, communication should be made to the Council with regard to it. That part of Bridge-street then especially referred to had been altogether repaved since then with macadam. That, he contended, was a breach of faith. He urged that wood paving would greatly facilitate the business of the town, and said that the gentry of the district objected to come into the town because of the unsafe nature of the streets; they objected to the pavement of the streets of the town and the ap- proaehea. Anything that would tend to increase the trade of the borough shoeld in these depressed times readily be sanctioned, whatever the expense, providing it was any- thing like reasonable. But he did not think wood paving would be any more costly, than setts, and it would be more convenient, comfortable, and noiseless. What complaint could be urged against the part that had been wood-paved in Sankey-street as an experiment. The whole of the shop- keepers of Bridge-street had signed a petition that was on a previous occasion presented to the Council in favour of that system, which was one that was greatly appreciated in Bir- mingham, whet e the last contract was laid with six inches of concrete at 9s &I per square yard. By that they would see that the laying of wood in the first instance would be no more expensive than setts. It was urged that other straets would want similar treatment, and he said that they should have it. The business part of the town should be paved in a manner most advantageous to the business people. Councillor W. PIERPOINT seconded the Proposition. Councillor FRAMOMB said that he and the borough sur- veyor 'went to Liverpool as a deputation, and the surveyor of Liverpool said that the wood and sett pavement cost about the same to put do am, but that the wood cost about three times more per annum to maintain ; the life of the wood paving was, also, little more than one-third that of the sett.

Alderman DiVIES said that the committee gave a pledge not to do anything with the portion of Bridge-street from the end of Friar's-gate to the end of Rylands-street. What the committee had asked the Council to do did not affect that part, except so far as repairs were concerned. Their estimate for wood paving was not as much as Mr. Webster's. It was 8s Bd per yard, is 21 less than the amount the mover of the resolution had mentioned. The estimate for setts at the present price, a low one, was 6s per square yard. They had laid down wood pavement in Sankey-street as an experi- ment, and he was sorry to have to siy that the narrow I street, where there were only two ruts for carriages to case each other, would not bear the traffic, and the life of the wood pavement there would not last so long as they had expected, and was now beginning to decay. He then read a statement prepared by the borough surveyor, giving the advantages and disadvantages of wood and granite pave- ment. The cost of concrete foundation, which was essential in Bridge-street, either for wood or granite pavement, would be £6OO. To pave with six-inch wood setts would cost £1,326, and with six-inch granite setts £936. The life of wood pavement might be taken at 10 years, and that of granite at 20 years. Having the interest and sinking fund to repay in 10 years for wood setts would require £166 8s 10d, the interest on foundation would be £24, and sand- ing and repairs £176, making an annual total of £366 Ss Od. On granite setts, taking the interest and sinking fund for 20 years, it would be £69 18s • 16, interest en foundation £24, repairs £25, total £llB 18e ld. The borough surveyor had gone further into the question. The mainten- ance and renewals would be as follows for the four principal streets, for wood paving and macadam :—Bridge-street, from Market-gate to Warrington Bridge, £366, as against £ll9 ; Sankey-street, from Market-gate to Bank Quay, £560, as against £lB6 ; Horsemarket-street. from Market- gate to Scotland-road, £l9B 19s, as against £66 as 4d; and Buttermarket-street. ditto' £l5B 2s 6d, as against £52 148 Zd ; total £1,283 8s 3d per annum, as against £424 16s 16.

Councillor Mecmg painted out that the resolution simply said that it be an instruction to the Paving and Sewerage Committee "as the necessity arises" to re-pave Bridge- street with wood. Alderman Webster did not propose that the four principal thoroughfares of the town should be dealt with.

Councillor ROBERTS referred to the speech of Councillor Mackie as full of illusions and fallacies. Councillor Mackie would have them believe that they were not likely to be asked immediately to pave Buttermarket and Horsemarket- streets, but he would remind him that one of the very things Alderman Webster said was that if wood pavement was granted to Bridge-street they would be very rightly asked to follow it up. When he found, according to an estimate that was in no way disputed, that in one street the difference be- tween the annual cost of wood and set paving was £248, he thought that it would be suicidal at the present moment to adopt such a policy. It was not an easy or economical matter to replace wood pavement; but it was easy to do so with sets. He thought it would be a very bad thing indeed at this time of trade depression to depart from a policy so well established.

Alderman BURGESS said that he could find a shopkeeper in Bridge-street who WAS making a great deal more money than any manufacturer in Warrington. (A voice; Glad to hear it.) He thought there was too much inclination on the part of members of the Council to give instructions to committees with which they had never had any experience. The Paving Committee was being constantly instructed by gentlemen who had never had anything to do with paving as to bow they should go about their work. If the gentle- men on the committee did not understand their work, for goodness sake remove them, and let some one else take their places. His view of the question was that the outside gentry whose interests Alderman Webster advocated, con- tributed very little indeed to the making of Warrington; the town depended a great deal more upon the tarry than the carriage. He thought that the life of a wood pavement in the narrow streets of the town would be much nearer five than ten years. The whole, of the people, however humble they might be, would have to pay towards the money ex- pended for making the business of the tradespeople more profitable. They would thus take money out of the pockets of the poor to put it in the pockets of the rich. He was told that in Liverpool the people who required wood paving had to contribute sixty per cent, of the cost. He believed that if that rule we made in this instance they would not find many people in Bridge-street willing to contribute to the extra cost. He contended that the proposed system was more costly, dangerous, and less healthy. Alderman CROSFLELD thought that the matter lay in a nutshell, and that the figures given by Alderman Davies settled the whole question. It was no use arguing against those figures. He heard that Bold-street, Liverpool, was paved with wood before the resolution referred to was passed, and since then not a single street had been paved with wood setts.
On the resolution being put to the meeting it was de. !eated, three voting in favour and seventeen against. The meeting then terminated.

STARVATION OR "NATURAL CAUSES." On Thursday week Mary Livesey, single woman, 74, years of age who lived at 14, Merton Bank-road, St. Helens, was found in a dying condition. A week previously she complained of being unwell, but being in poor circumstan- ces she declined to send for a doctor, and refused to have the parish doctor called in. When found she was lying groaning on the floor, and expired shortly after P.C. Rat- cliff arrived. A mug, containing a whitish liquid, appar- ently milk and beer, was on the table. She had drunk some of the contents, which had caused her to vomit. An inquest was held on the body of the deceased was held before Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner. on Friday.—Mrs. Sarah Buckley stated that she rented part of the house from de- ceased, who earned her livelihood by knitting and sewing, besides which she received two or three shillings a week from her nephew and niece at Ormskirk in payment of money lent during the "better days" of deceased. During the last few months she had complained of not baing well, and on Friday witness wanted to fetch the parish doctor, but she refused. On Thursday witness went into her room and found her lying face downwards on the floor. She had never said anything to lead witness to think she would take away her life. She was a "good living" woman, hut ' through poverty she was unable to go to church. She had applied to the relieving officer, but was told she could not have relief, as she had not been in the union three years.— Jane Fillingham, a neighbour, was of opinion that death was from want and starvation. On Sunday last deceased had cothing to eat, and witness took her a dinner of pota- toes.—Mrs. Woodier, another neighbour, stated that on Mon- day last deceased came to her and appeared to be very hui • gry.—The Coroner said it was quite clear that deceased had not had enough to keep her, and was starved. Being at an advanced age, the facts were consistent with death from natural causes.—A Juryman said it seemed hard that the relieving officer could not do something,—The Coroner said, judging from what they had heard, the relieving officer had a wrong impression of the operation of the poor law. When a destitute person asked for relief, no matter who he or she was, the relieving officer was bound to assist. If a wandering tramp he must give him an order for the tramp ward, and if an urgent cAse temporary relief must be given. It vrould then be for the Guardians to relieve or bring them to the workhouse. The relieving officer would then have to in- quire into the settlement, and if she had not lived in the union long enough, to arrange for her removal or charge- ability. No person ought to be allowed to starve.—The Foreman said many were relieved who did not want it so badly as deceased bad done.—The Coroner said this was a case in which the woman ought to have had 2s 61 or 3s a week. No doubt the relieving officer liked to keep down the outdoor relief.—A relative said deceased had always expressed a wish to be buried at Ormskirlz, and she had promised that it should be done, but she was not in a posi- tion to do it. Deceased had been in considerably better circumstances.—The Coroner remarked that it was a very hard case.—The jury returned a verdict of " Deatk from natural causes."

WHY HAS THE SALE OF "GORDON'S" EXTRACT

BECAUSE there was a demand for such a medicine Because there was a crying want for st remedy on which the people might depend in their hour of need, and "Gordon's Extract" has supplied that want, and is filling the aching void that existed before its advent. Because "Gordon's Extract" enables the sick person to regain health, and the well one to keep it. Because health to the people—to • hem who have to work with their brains or their hands to earn the bread they eat—is a vital neaessity. Because ill-health means to them inability to labour; inaptitude for work means lack of wages; want of money means the parting one by one of the possessions of the household, the ornaments from the mantel, the beat furniture from the parlour, the watch from the fob, the chain from the neck, and the rings from the finger. These and the Sunday clothes and the best boots, alike of man, wife, and children, are taken one by one to the sign of the. three brass balls, and are there mortgaged for the bread which ill-health prevents from being earned. They are fol- lowed by the blankets from the bed, the sheets from under the sick person, the tablecloth from the table; for even though sickness be in the house, bringer must be appeased. All the pages of this paper would be sadly insufficient to tell of the woes andsmisery, the gangs of hunger, the despondent minds, the broken hearts, and the p, enaature deaths which preventable sickness (preventable by the use of "Gordon's Extract") has caused. Because ill- health is the bane and poison of life, and "Gordon's Ersi- tract "is its antidote. Because "Gordon's Extract" ensures health, imparts health, regains health, and keeps health when gotten. And because health means strength; strength means work; work is synonymous with wages; with wages come the comforts and enjoyments of life, decent clothing for the children, and the ability to nay their school fees, likewise en- abling people to pay their way, "to look the whole world in the face," and to "owe not any man," thereby securing the respect and gaining the esteem of friends and neightours ; and because health secures all this, "G-ordon's Extract" owes its phenomenal success; because "Gordon's Extract" is a health keeper. mr.anAynd be- heaeausltehtigleivila a" laarlroni imparter, and an 1, cause it relieves sick headache, disperses biliousness, is a I curative for dyspepsia, a foe to liver complainls, and an I enemy to kidney diseases; because of these " Gordon's Extract" has a place high in the bead roll of the world's fame. , How can it be wondered at—the aching limbs, the pains in the ribs and under the shoulder blades, the loss of appetite or the loathing of food, the bilious vomit, the acidity and heartburn, the pain after meals, the weight at the stomach, the dragging down of the intestines, the deficient bile, the deranged bowels, the impaired digestion, the failure to assimilate food, the In- ability of the organs to extract nourishment, the wasting away of flesh, the decrepitude of confirmed ill-health, the despondent and despairing mind, the fierce fits of temper, the unnatural gloom, the fear of impending danger, and the sores of other psinful, ccnfusing, untoward, end disagreeable symptoms, have, one and all of them been found to be amenable to the curative power of "Gordon's Extract." Because" Gordon's Extract "disperses, relieves, and cures the strangest, the most , severe, and the most contradictory symptoms, and the worst I complications of disease.. And because "Gordon's Extract" does all this—and is a blessing to humanity and the natural enemy to disease—because of th se things the sale of *4 Gor- don's Extract" has grown snarvellously, and is still in- creasing, and in bottles at Two Shillings is sold at all chemists.
A REMARKABLE CURE OF EPILEPTIC FITS EFFECTED BY GORDON'S EXTRACT."

D. THONIS, 74, Hoxton-street, Bradford, writes July 24th, 1885.—G-entlemen,—Permit me to attest my unsolicited and . humble testimony to the healing and curative properties of your EXTRACT..not only in restoring the weak and debilitated but in the curing of Epilepsy in its most aggravated form; not only do I speak from information, but personal observation in one special case—Viz, that of a woman subjected to the above disease for upwards of twelve years; not so severe at ' first, but as tme went on the fits became more frequent, until the patient was seldom a week without the recurrence, until she was reduced to sheer helplessness, and almost to a state of idiocy; for over three years not able to do her own household work, and the family had tried anything and everything that doctors and patent medicines could do without effect; in fact, she gradually became worse, until the doctors said there was no cure, and the patient could not sur- vive long. They had tried many patent medicines. one preparatlon to the amount of £7 This for a time seemed to have a little effect, and the family had hopes of a cure, but so soon as the system became used to the medicine, the medi- cine became use:ess and all hopes egain blighted. The family, In fact, became seriously impoverished in expending mosey with hope of a cure, but all to no purpose; besides, the hus- band's health became enfeebled for want of rest for such a length of time that he was laid aside for long, until the family was reduced to a pitiful condition indeed. However, as the last effort your EXTRACT was resorted to, and with surpris- ing effect : six or seven bottles regularly taken successively until the fits became less frequent and the health became im- proved, until the woman was enabled to attend her household duties; and now, though she has not used the EX VRACT for many months, she h-s not had Ats for twelve months, and is now in her usual health. Any party writing me for proof, I will gladly ',tomer and give the full name and address of suf- ferer, and at my expense; they will most gladly reply to any inquiry, but for reasons which are justifiable, they would rather not have their name come before the public. Yet you are at perfect liberty to make what use of my statement you like, and, believe me, yours respestailly,
DAVID Timms.% Bookseller and Statilner.

div.head: EXAMINER • SATURDAY, MARCH 6, 1886:
div.p: THE EXAMINER • SATURDAY, MARCH 6, 1886:

THE Warrington Co-operative Society. con- fer a great benefit on the community when they make provision for such lectures as-those given by the Rev. W. TUCKWELL, rector of Stockton. Last year the rev. gentlemen at- tracted and delighted a large audience by•alls, eloquent discourse on the "New Utopia. On Monday night his subject was The Church of the future," and a charming and powerful lecture he gave. It was a lecture to set people thinking who are not in the habit of considering such matters, and to cause those who have come to a conclusion on the question of a State Church to take a fresh.look at the ground upon which they stand. Mr. JOHN CROSFIELD, who presided, set the ball, rolling by saying he "was not one of the extreme people who would have the churches put up to auction and sold to the- highest bidders, to be used as music halls, or pulleel down and the streets paved with the stones.' Seeing that Mr. CROSFIELD is a church-goerr although a leader of the Liberal party, such a- statement might be regarded as superfluous, so far as he is concerned; but it would be interesting to know who are the extreme people who have proposed such an extreme thing. Certainly not the Liberation Society, notwithstanding that they are justly credited with desiring to disestablish and disendow the Church. The Rev. W. TUCKWELL ex- plained that his object was to furnish materials for leisurely and dispassionate study; and he put the case fairly when he said the recent political crisis—which showed how much the Church and the People were at issue—had forced into prominence the al- ternative of reconstructing it, or abandoning as impracticable the idea of a State-controlled ecclesiastical system. Mr. TUCKWELL. seems to think the State Church can be so reformed as to become truly national; and he drew a beautiful picture of brethren dwelling together in harmony in a church so wide in its basis as to "suit all religious natures" and show respect for all religious peculiarities." If mankind were all Tuckw.-11s, this might be possible, but that, in other words, is to say that the millennium would be at hand. No, no, the Orange lion is not yet ready to lie down with the Catholic lambk except, once in a while, for a fa/ days at election time, and then he makes up for his temporary gentleness by a long-con- tinued exhibition of ferocity. Put it to the POPE, or CARDINAL MANNING, or, for that matter, to any Catholic priest in this district, whether he thinks it possible to reconstruct the English Church on such lines as those suggested by the reverend lecturer, and he will immediately give an emphatic no. He will urge that the true Church needs no re- constructing; that it is the same yesterday, to- day, and for ever; and that all that is needed is for such stray sheep as the Rev. W. Turcic, WELL and the Rev. R. FILCHER to return to the fold. Need it be said that the Church of the future which failed to include the members of the Roman Catholic Church could not be a truly National Church?: The idea of including members of every denom- ination in one State Church is pretty as a Conceit, bur, politically, it is impracticable. No Act of Uniformity that could possibly be framed would hold together such heterogen- ious bodies; it is an attempt to make a rope of sand. The true remedy for the "narrow- ness, incompetence, and tyranny" in the Church which Mr. TUCKWELL deplores is, not to be found in forging fresh fetters, but in setting the Church free. It is no part of the duty of the State to provide a Church for the people; and our colonies profiting by the blundering and plundering, blows and blood- shed which have weakened and discredited the mother country, have had the good sense- to &tart business without one. They let each tub stand on its own bottom, if it can; and,. if it cannot, it must go. to pieces; it is not required of the Legislature to provile fresh hoops. We have moved so far in this direc- tion on this side of the world as to dises- tablish the Church in Ireland. Are we to re' 0' tablish it on Mr. TUCKWELL'S new plan in OP,, position to the will of the people of Ireland r To put the question is to reveal the absurdity of the case. There must be ll° turning back; even standing stilt means being left behind; we must go. forward. Ti connection between Church and State is an, evil one; it is an unholy,alliance, and all goo.ci men both within and without the Churcn ought' to labour for separation. There has been enough and too much of State patronage; what is wanted is justice---.'•
