equality before the law; a fair field and no favour. The Rev. R. PILCHER says the Non- Conformist "damn" is as offensive to him as the Episcopalian " damn ; "but what of that? As one of our poets has it— Each one, damning, damns the other; They are damned by one another By none other are they damned. Why not proceed a step further, and insist that the Legislature shall say to the sects—" Go T.Our Way; bless or curse each other as you !Ike; but don't trouble us; we have other and better work to do than meddle with what is outside our sphere." The National Church the such is a failure; it no longer represents nation. It is in its relation to the State a I. round peg in a square hole, and can never auie made to fit. A Reformed Nltional Church there may be which may ultimately flourish, not in alliance with the State. The Church as a branch of the State must be dis- !stablished ; and having been disendowed in Ireland, it must be disendowed in Scotland, and Ent,land, and in Wales. Mr. MONKS Was ill advised in suggesting that the Church ' Owned its possessions "just as much as any 14. them own their property." He allowed betsttekindliness, for the moment, to get the r of his judgment; for the highest authorities are against him. Lord PALMERS- rI.°N knew something of the subject, and he rld---" The property of the Church belongs ~: the State, and the Legislature has the vower and the right to deal with that pro- -I:.ertY according to the circumstances of the 114 e." We have all, it may be admitted, a gued deal to learn as to the relations of ' Church and State. Meantime, let us welt' curae such lecturers as the Rev. W. TUCK- ,ELL ; he is a "magnificent dreamer ";; and, if b" :e does not solve the problem, he is doing `tiOnlething towards its solution by directing 64 b.,e att en ti on of the people to a question ' Zuich sooner or later will be the great ques- "lon of the day.

TRE Melbourne papers which have recently rlved are unanimous in congratulating Dr. z°oltHousE upon his appointment to the see Manchester, while deploring his loss to °outh Australia. Bishops are not now-a- (laYs in the best repute, and it is therefore the r,cire refreshing to find 'that the Bishop of lelbourne is regarded by all classes as worth !apt only his salt, but a great deal more. He looked upon amongst them as a citizen of riel.nown who has been helpful in every way to I,ls fellow men. Although a Bishop of the '•inglish Church, he has shown by precept and ttarnple what Voluntaryism can do on the e.ther side of the world, whtre a State Church 148, not tolerated. He has been a worker in tue church as well as an ' overseer," for it is said of him that he has visited every nook and corner. of his vast diocese. But what has tlii°st endeared him to the Australasians is his iialorough manliness, his broad views, his rge sympathies, and kindly toleration. They go-ahead in the colonies, and Dr. MOOR- pii-TSE has shown himself to be a go-ahead silop. Haying at times long distances to t`ravel, he has thought it better to use Sunday ns than to ride in a carriage of his own, then proceed to denounce Sunday travel- as Sabbath. breaking. He has seen and . acknuwledged the good side of the theatre; iand is so earnest an advocate for making the !est use of Public Libraries that he is in !arour, under certain circumstances, of their being open on a Sunday. When he has had tittle to breathe after his long journey, an 'ffort must be made to induce him to visit Parrington, where books instead of being larieely lent to the ratepayers are hoarded, at (ne expense of the ratepayers, with "miser •,al'e." In Melbourne Protection is popular; 'Jut Dr. MooßHousE did not pat Protection 11 the back on that account. Believing it to ue, an error, he spoke of it as such, and he *III do likewise, it is to be hoped, when he settles to his work in Lancashire. It will be leen from all this how likely it is that Bishop 1400RHousE will be a worthy successor of the ate BistiOD FRASER. It is to the credit of Lord A.LisnußY that he has made such an appoint- ent ; and it is deserving of note that, over Ivo years ago, Mr. GLADSTONE sounded him rto whether he would like to take an Eng- -18/1 bishopric. Bishop MOORHOUSE is the aPProved of two Prime Ministers, but, better IQ, he is the approved of the people, for a 44elbourne journal tell us that "he will leave 1/ithout a foe, and with a million friends."

A single woman, one MARY LIVESEY, an C)ld woman of seventy-four, residing at St. 4elens, has been allowed to die of starva- tion! We say allowed to dip, for it appears that the poor creature did in her extremity apply for relief; she asked for bread and told she might enter the Workhouse. &Nothing could be done for her, because, it was she had not been in that particular allion for three years. The Relieving Officer states that her case was fully reported to the ..t;ommittee of the Guardians, but "no order 10r out-door relief was made by them." It !eerns she had "seen better days," that she 'tied to earn a living by knitting and sewing, arid that she received two or three shillings a Nc'eek from her nephew and niece, who re- lided at Ormskirk. All this, which should 4ave been something in her favour, went against her; she was allowed to starve, and I‘.as at last found by a neighbour lying :Pri the floor of her house—ill and dy- LlIg• The CORONER remarked that it was "clear that deceased had not had ehough to keep her, and was starved ;" 80 the jury brought in a verdict of Death from natural causes." Natural Causes! Of course—what can be more natural than for an old woman of seventy-four to die

Then she cannot obtain sufficient food to keep body and soul together? The CORONER proceeded complaisantly to say that "the relieving officer had a wrong impression of the ,oPeration of the poor-law. The woman ought have had 2s 6d or 3s a week." This being 11,0, We submit that the verdict should have en something very different to the one "'en. A terrible wrong has been done ° the late MARY LIVESEY a. wrong 'Mich, in view of the provision made for the 13'or, becomes an outrage on society. The , 4`,4se is one which ought to be further inves- qated. If it is allowed to rest where it is— 'with that mockery of a verdict "Death from !latural causes" staring everybody in the face, It Will be a lasting discredit to the humanity °F St Helens.

VANGELISTIC SERVICES.—Mr. and Mrs. Henry 'thlggan, the well-known London evangelists, With h" Revs. J. Calvert, Seddon, Overton, Shuttlewor.th, tild others, are continuing their successful singing Vi;C:angelistic services in Ilutchinson-street Chapel, virldnes. On Sunday evening a large congregation TlBl.B present, and the meeting was a cheerful one. b 0 singing and playing of " Wiggan's Hymns" a large choir, and a greater number of instru- 40!italists than has ever been present at Mr. and .41'8. Wiggan's services in Widnes, and these, led by ..LeWis, added as before to the interest of the .B'rvlce. Mr. and Mrs. Wiggan will continue their wer. vices in Widnes on Sunday, closing on Monday 34.1_th a public tea meeting; and commence in War- -'4gton on Tuesday evening.

"TOUCH AND GO." The tug of war as to the payment of in • terest out of capital in connection with the Ship Canal scheme commences on Tuesday next; but the promoters have no fear as to the result. Having weathered so many storms, they believe they will weather this. "The Pall Mall gazette" has issued an " extra " giving the opinions of eminent men on "The best Hundred Books." It is ex- ceedingly readable, if not wholly edifying The poor student is likely to be bewildered with so many guides who point in opposite directions.

The St. Helens Town Council have re- solved to sign a petition in favour of extend- ing the Parliamentary Franchise to women. They evidently do not think that "women's rights mean men's wrongs." A similar pro- posal would set most Town Councils by the ears.

There are four Primitive Methodist Minis- ters in the present Parliament; and they were breakfasted on Thursday—for even ministers must have something besides spiritual food. It would be impossible to breakfast, under like conditions, four clergymen of the Church of England. As State servants, they are not allowed to sit in Parliament. They have many advantages, but that is one of their dis- advantages.

The Chinese Government are demanding compedsation from the United States Gov ernment for the recent massacres of Chinese in the Western States. Having had to grant compensation to Americans under somewhat similar circumstances, the " heathen Chinee " thinks that what is sauce for the goose should be sauce for the gander. President Cleve- land has referred the matter to Congress. "Tis sport to have the engineer hoist with his own petard."

In the House of Commons, on Monday. Mr. Mundella, in answer to Mr. Hickman, said the Customs authorities did their utmost to stop the importation into this country from abroad of cutlery marked with the brand of Sheffield, and had recently seized several cases. This is good, but something more might be done. Why not take steps to punish Sheffield merchants who themselves stamp German cutlery and tools in their Sheffield works? This is the sort of "pro- tection" that the Sheffield trade requires.

Writing to a Liverpool contemporary, the Rev. R. J. Ward, pastor of the St. Helens Con- gregational Church, says :—" The Battle of Life," by the late Rev. Hugh Stowell Brown, was an inspiration to him in his youth. He adds, "I was then a printer's devil ; ' I am now an angel of the Church.'" This is just a little hard, isn't it, on the " P.D. ?" Unhappy thought: If all the " P.D.'s " were to be converted into angels, the Rev. R. j. Ward would be unable to write to the papers —there would be no papers to write to.

The Bishop of Liverpool, in a brief speech which he made on Tuesday, at the re-open- ing of Wargrave Church, said they did not want a clergyman who neglected his duties and bought his sermons. It seems, then, that there are parsons who preach other people's sermons. Conduct like this is akin to that of the upstart editor who buys his leading articles_ The excuse in each case is the same; conscious of incapacity, they seek to purchase what they know, they cannot pro- duce. There is no such editor, and no such preacher, in this district; of course not.

The Runcorn Board of Commissioners had before them, on Thursday, a communication from the promoters of the Colonial and Indian Exhibition suggesting that they should en- courage working-men to visit the exhibition. The matter was referred to the committee, who'. will do no harm if they do nothing. This unusual mode of advertising an exhibition is one which local authorities ought to resent ; it is not their business to lecture working- men as to how they shall spend their earnings. The Runcorn Board of Guardians, on Tues- day, made short work with an out-of-place communication on Home Rule; they de- clined to read it.

The Irish question is coming more and more to the front. It has been discussed, within the past few days, at St. Helens, Hay: dock, Earlestown, and Runcorn. This is as it should be. The People, as well as Parliament, are entitled to have a finger in the pie. There is nothing Mr. Gladstone likes better than to listen to the voice of the nation. How equal he is to the situation was shown by the splen- did speech which he made in the House on Thursday nights It carried the war into the enemy's camp. Lord Randolph Churchill is the fish-wife of politics, who makes it his business to vil- ify all good people who may pass his way. The better they are and the more foul-mouthed he becomes. Because Lord Ripon succeeded as no other Viceroy has ever done in winning the hearts of the, people of India, he is said to have " betrayed an altogether extravagant amount of mental instability." And this from a politician who will unsay to-day what he he said yesterday, and contradict both statements to-m orrow. Mr. Gladstone, he tells us, is "the deification of inconsistency." It would be impossible, of course, to say this of Lord Randolph ; with him, inconsistency is not deified ; it is diabolised.

FRESH DAILY.
LOCAL NEWS.

SAD DEATH OF AN UNEMPLOYED MAN AT RIINC)RN.—A. sudden death of a sad nature occurred at Runcorn on Tues- day afternoon. Edward Hughes, apparently about 40 years of age, came into Runcorn from Wales on Friday in order to look for work. He took up his residence at the common lodging-house, 4, Fryer-street, and he appeared to the woman of the house to be suffering from asthma. On Monday, whilst walking in the street, he fell in the snow and had a fit. He was subsequently seen at the lodging-house by Dr. McDougall. The man persisted so strongly on leaving the house that the landlady went down to the police station and Inspector Millington sent P.S. Neild to the place. The man died the following afternoon. On Monday night a cousin of the deceased gave him 5s to supply his immediate wants. It is believed that deceased had relatives at St. Helens. The Coroner was informed of the occurrence, but he considered an inquest unnecessary, as the doctor had cer- tified the cause of death. BETHESDA MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY:tit-On Wed- nesday night Mr. Thvdiate read a:Paper on special services. He treated on their need, the method of conducting, and their aim and result. Saywets Bank AT WESTON —ea branch of the Runcorn Savings Bank was opened at Weston on Saturday afternoon. The managers consider the tact that seven new accounts were opened as highly satisfactory. THE BISHOP OF SHREWSBURY AT RUNCORN.—The Catho- lic Bishop of Shrewsbury officiated at Mill-brow Chapel, on Sunday. At the early morning service he said mass, at the forenoon service he preached, and in the evening.he de- livered a lecture, and administered the sacrament of con- firmation. There was a crowded congregation on each occasion. THE ATTENDANCE OF CHILDREN AT SCHOOL AT RUN- CORN.—On Thursday afternoon the head teachers of the ' various denominational schools in Runcorn met the Attend- ance Committee of the School Board at the Town Hall for the purpose of devising means to secure the better attend- ance of children at school. An interesting discussion took place, bat no definite lines of action were decided upon. It is expected that the results of the interview will be bene- ficial. RUNCORN UNION AND THE COUNTY RATE.—At the last meeting cf the Runcorn Board of Guardians the county rate precept was submitted. It was as follows :—County rate, £230 165 101 •, constabulary and local expenditure, £230 163 , 10d ; total, £461 13s 8,1. For the corresponding quarter last year the figures were :—County rate, £535 65 84 ; consta- bulary and general expenditure, £l7B Sc 3d; constabulary local expenditure, £336 14; total, £1,050 Os; showing a de- crease for the present quarter of £5BB 15s 4d. WESTON WESLEYAN AUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.— The anneal meeting of the members of this society and their friends took piece in the Wesleyan school-room, Weston. on Monday night. After tea a programme of songs, recita- tions, &c., was gone through, and an enjoyable evening was spent. The tnanks of the society are due to Miss Ford, Miss Hibbert, and the other lady friends who so kindly contributed to the evening's enjoyment. Mr. James Ford was re-elected president of the society for the ensuing I season. SERVICE OF SONG AT RUNCORN.—In aid of the funds of St. Luke's Congregational Chapel, Pennington's-row, a service of eon c entitled "The Bow of Promise" was given in Eethesda Chapel, on Sunday eveninz, after the service. There was a numerous attendance. The musical port,on was rendered by the choir, who had the assistance of mem- bers of other choirs in the town; and Mr. George Lacy and Mr. A. Fox sang solos. Mr. Reyenscroft was at the organ.] The narrative was read by the pastor, the Rev. J. D. ; Thomas. OAKLAND-STREET WESLEYAN SCHOOL, WIDNES. On Monday evening the annual distribution of prizes to those scholars who had been of good behaviour and regular in at- tendance took place. The proceedings commenced with a tea, at which there was a good number present. Subseqently a public meeting was held in the chapel, under the presi- dency of the Rev. R. Bardon. Seventy scholars received ' prizes at the hands of Mr. B. Brown, and a pleasant even- ing was spent in listening to songs and recitations by the children. SCIENTIFIC DRESS CUTTING AT RUNCORN.-IIbIS Kevan, of the Scientific Dress Cutting Association, on Tuesday gave two lectures in Bethesda Schoolroom. The system of the association was fully explained by means of diagrams and examples. There was a very good attendance at ti-e even- ing lecture, and several ladies intimated their desire and willingness to form a class for the purpose of receiving instruction in scientific dress cutting." Miss Bevan Will visit the town in a short time, and it is expected a branch of the association will be formed. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.—Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, yesterday held an inquest at the house of Mr. W. R. Wass, Wellington Hotel, on the body of James Yates, three years of age, son of William Yates, a water- man in the employ of the Bridgewater Navigation Com- pany. The deceased, who had been delicate since birth. was taken ill on Thursday afternoon. Dr. Robinson was called in yesterday at noon, but the child had died before his arrival. He informed the mother that convulsions was the cause of death. A verdict was returned accord- ingly. SNOW STORM AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES.—A bitterly cold wind on Sunday night last was followed by a snow Storm which continued all night and on Monday. In some places the snow drifted to a depth of four or five feet, and all kinds of traffic was much impeded. At the Docks work was almost at. a standstill. Happily the railway traffic was carried on with very little delay. At Weston the poet-box was snowed up, and the postman had to use the spade in order to get the letters enclosed. On Tuesday tnorniug several gangs of teen, under the direction of Mr. Barker, surveyor to the Board of Commissioners, rapidly cleared the parapets of the town, and pedestrians reaped much bsne- fit. A similar practice was followed at Widnes. No easualities are reported. CANTATA AT WIDNES.—The cantata entitled "A moon- . .

light frolic in the valley of violets," was given in Lacey- street School on Tuesday evening, by a chorus of about 50 voices, including members of the various chapel choirs in the neighbourhood. Captain Brunner occupied the cnair. The room was filled with an audience which gave frequent signs of appreciation, the whole performance calling forth numerous eulogies. Under the leadership of Mr. Samuel Lamb, assisted by a full and competent string band, the chorus performed its work in capital style. The seloists were Miss Thomas soprano, Miss Owen contralto, Mr. Platt tenor, and Mr. Wilkinson bass, and they acquitted them• selves with credit. The customary votes of thanks were accorded at the close.

BURNING FATALITY AT WIDNES.—LiIy Pennington, three years of age, daughter of William Pennington, labourer, 81, Travis-street, died OR Wednesday night from injuries re- ceived on Tuesday morning. The deceased and her brother, aged seven years, had been left by their mother in a bed- room where there was a fire. The girl stood upon the fen- der to warm herself when a draught of wind sent her nightdress in contact with the fire, and it was soon in flames. Her screams brought the mother, who was down- stairs, upon the scene, and the burning nightdress was re- moved. The girl was very badly burned about the legs and body, and notwithstanding the attentions of Dr. McCarnbridge she succumbed to the injuries on Wednesday night. Yesterday, Mr, Brighouse held an inqueat on the body, and a verdict of accidental death was recorded. CATHOLIC BALL A'? WIDNES.—The seventeenth annuall Catholic ball was held at Widnes, on Monday night. The Volunteer Hall, where the ball took place, bad been effec- tively decorated with flags and limners, and presented a bright and attractive appearance. Despite the snow storm that was raging about 200 couples put in an appearance, visitors being present from Liverpool, Manchester, St. Helens. and Warrington, and the ball was one of the most successful yet held. The onerous duties of secretary had been ably carried out by Mr. S. Quinn. Mr. J. Tallon, jun., officiated as MC., and he was assisted by the following stewards :—Messrs. A. Treacy, J. Carroll, John Quinn, Jas. Quinn, J. Donoghue, jun., Edward Tallon, J. McMahon, J. Tracey, J. Pevlin, P. Whelan, T. 'Smith. G. Faulkner, J. Jameson, and C. Flinn. Dancing commenced at nine o'clock to the strains of Mr. Powell's quadrille band. Mr. Lynch, of the Commercial Hotel, Appleton, supplied the refreshments. THE PROPOSED COUNTY COURT FOR ,WIDNES.—Mr. W. T. Husband has received a letter from Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss, M.P., with respect to the above subject in which he say :—" It seems probable that the Government will shortly institute a regular inquiry into the division of Comity Court business throughout the country, and this fact may possiblo delay the settlement of the petition, but will in no way lessen the probability of its being eventu- ally granted. The objection of Jadge Thompson to the scheme is a serious matter, as I am under the impression that he will again be consulted. He may not appoint a deputy, unless from some cause or other be is incapacitated from performing his duties himself. I extracted a promise from the Secretary to the Lord Chancellor that the petition should not be " pigeon-holed " and the matter would be kept well forward until a decision was arrived at. I regret that I cannot send a more favourable report. VOLUNTEER CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—An audience of moderate proportions assembled in Runcorn Public Hall, on Wednesday, to hear a concert given in aid of the funds of the F. and G. (Runcorn) Companies of the 2nd C.R.V. The targets on the common have been condemned by the War Office, and before the member of the corps can resume shooting practice, it is necessary that new ones should be purchased. The proceeds of the concert will be devoted to this end. The programme of vocal and instrumental selec- tions was carried out by local amateurs, who, on the whole, succeeded in winning the appreciation of the company. Captain Hazlehurst, and Miss Wright, and Miss Hankinson were unable to fill their engagements through sickness, and the place of the first-named was filled by Mr. J. R. Lea, of Farnworth, who sang a couple of songs in fine style and was recalled. Miss N. Handley contributed the song "Needles and pins," new to a Runcorn audience, which she sang with her accustomed facility of expression and melody. She also appeared in the second part, when she gave an enjoyable rendering of "Molloy's London Bridge." Miss E Toft charmed the audience with a solo on the harp, and was enthusiastically recalled. In conjunction with her sister, who played violin, the duet "La Plainte" was skil, fully' performed. Miss K. S. Rigby, who possesses a voice with a good range, and of considerable expression, was very successful in her songs. Miss James, who is heard too sel- dam, was accorded a merited encore, and Private Fox was similarly honoured for his powerful rendering of "The warner bold." Lieutenant Joule gave an intelligent render- ing of "The mid,thipmite," and Mr. R. Morris contributed Ire capital style "Uncle Jack." Mr. James Kent sang " The message,', and was joined with Miss James in a duet. A vociferous recall rewarded Sergeant Woods for his skilful and tuneful manipulation of the cornet in the solo "Carnival de Venice." The concert concluded with the "Hallelujah chorus" by the band, which also rendered other selections in admirable style, Mr. Ainsworth conduct- ing. THE WIDNES WOUNDING CASE —John Reilly, who was struck on the head with a brick about two months ago, is still in a dangerous condition, and his assailant, Michael Carr, was again remanded at the Petty Sessions, on Thurs- day. bUNCORN PARISH CHURCH DISTRICT VISITING SOCIETY has during the past year distributed £35 to over families. The parish is divided into two districts, and are respectively under .the charge of the Rev. T. M. Armson and the Rev. R. Edwards. CAMBRIDGE LOCAL EXAMINATIONS.—The results of the Cambridge local ex animations show that Miss Cbristine Handley, daughter of Mr. James Handlsv, J P., of Runcorn, has pessed in the junior division with first-class honours and distinction in French. Mies May Beck, daughter of Mr. F. Beck, has also passed in the senior divi- sion. WIDNES NATIONAL ScilooLs.—On Wednesday evening Mr: J. lon, of Liverpool, gave a magic entertainment to a good audience. The proceeds will be added to the fund for the repair of the organ.—The weekly meeting of tee C.E.T.S. was held on Thursday evening. Tee Rev C. Rumfitt presided, and a programme of songs, dm., was gone through. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORE—At Whines Petty Session, on Thursday, Mr. G. H. Denby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted Coe following parents for neglecting to send their children regularly to school:—William Holland, James Houghton, Joseph Davies, John Fenny, Charles McKenna, William Fallon, and Thomas Burke. The usual penalty of 5,1 was imposed. Tne MEMBER FOR NORTHWICH.—In the discussion which took place in the House of Commons on Monday night on the Hyde Park Corner (New Streets) Bill. Mr. Brunner asked what was the principle of the bill. Was it that the management of these roads was to be placed in the hands of the Metropolitan Boards? If s, he should consider it his duty to oppose any further powers Neeing given to that body. THE" WEEPING PRESCHP.R " AT WIDNES.—The services which have been conducted by Mr. and Mrs. Henry wiggan, the London evangelists, at Hutchinson-street Primitive Methodist Chapel during the past fortnight, will be brought to a conclusion. The " Weeping preacher," as Mr. Wiggan is known, has achieved considerable success amongst the audiences which have nightly filled the edifice, and many have professed to have been spiritually benefited. UNJUST SCALES AT ASTON.—Jobn Davies, farmer and grocer, Aston-by-Sutton, was .summoned te Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, charged with having a pair of unjust scales. On the 23rd February Superintendent Leah visited the defendant's shop and found a small pair of flour scales, even after they had been well cleaned, half an ounce out of balatibe against the purchaser. He had warned the defen- dant 12 months previously.—A fine of 103 and casts 103 ad was imposed. Derroet BAND OF HOPE.—A public entertainment was given in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, Hough Green, on Wed- nesday, by the Goelder family, of Liverpool, assisted by Mr. and Mrs. Gibbs, of Bold, in aid of the funds of the society. The entertainment was a decided treat, and was arranged by Mr. Clarke, of The Hollies. A vote of thanks was accorded to the trustees, and to those who took part in the entertainment, on the proposition of Mr Hunt, seconded by Mr Stead. FUNERAL or A HELSBY LADY.—Theberial of Miss Chew, of the Poplars, took place on Monday afternoon at the Helsby Wesleyan Chapel. Miss Chew died at the age of 67 on the previeus Thursday. She was the principal of the ladies' bearding school, and in Helsby and the district,where she was we'l known and highly respected. The funeral was attended by several relatives and friends, but many were prevented from being present on account of the violent snowstorm which prevailed. The burial service was read by the Rev. E. Mosscrop. WIDNES BICYCLE AND TRICYCLE Cerne.—A meeting of the members of this club was held in Unsworth's dining , rooms on Thursday night. Mr. H. Handley was re-electect I captain, with Mr. Wm. Baker as sub-captain. Mr. George Baker was appointed hon. sec , and the committee consists of Messrs. J. Dorning, S. Matthews, W. Dixon, and J. Brookes. The treasurer reported a balance of £1 7s 4d from last year. A discussion on the advisability of permitting members to obtain machines on the Starr-Bowkett principle was adjourned. BRUACH C, MERCHANT SHIPPING Acr.—At Runcorn Petty SeseinAs, on Monday, Thomas Finegan, marine store dealer, Water-street, was summoned for not keeping his books ie the proper way required by the Merchant Sl4ipoing Act. Mr. Knowles, of Widnes, defended.—P. Clerk Wallace proved the case and produced the books, which were ex- amined by the Bench. In some instances the names and address of the persons purchased from were not insarted.— Mr. Knowles submitted that the offence was merely a technical one, and that persons in the position of the defen- dant could not be expeced to keep books with the precision of a merchant's cashier.—A fine of 20s and costs was im- posed. DRIFEN By HUNGER TO STEAL.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, Martha S mettnen was broug'it ap on remamd charged with unlawfully pledging two sheets, the Propsrty of Joseph Joynson, of Spring-street. —The prisoner and her femily took apartments at Joynson's house early in December last, and occupied them until Monday morning, when they left without giving rotice. Afterwards the two sheets were missed, and Neild discovered that they had been pl-dged at Mr. Craddock', Church-street, by the i prisoner.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and said she was driven to pledge the sheets in order to obtain bread.—ln de- I fault of pay Lee a fine of 10. and 9s costs, the woman went to gaol for 14 diva. A TEnnoß TO ITER NETMEOURR AT WESTON.—OD Mon- ! day, at Rancor Court, Margaret Kdgrest,, who lives with ; her husband at Banks-raw, Weston, was charged with assaulting Ann Griffiths, a widow, who keeps a small shop in the same neighbourhood, and possesses a cow and several pigs. On the evening of the 23rd February Mrs. Griffiths was passing the door of the defendant's house with some straw under her arm, when the defendant threw a large quantity of water from a bucket upon her. She made use of an nifensi4b expression at the tinae.—Mr A. Linaker, who appeared for the complainant, said the defendant was a terror to her neighbours, and had been twice flied for assaults.—She was now fined 103 and costs. PROPERTY SALE AT WIDNES.—At the Central Hotel, Whines, on Thursday •evening, Mr. Thomas Sutton. auc- tioneer, of Warrington, offered several lots of property for sale. The old established beerhouse fronting Lugsdale-road, Widnes, and the two cottages adjoining were purchased by Mr. Edwardson for £270; and Mr. Beasley gave £4OO for the two cottages, with workshop and gardens, fronting Marsh Hall Pad, Farnworth. £455 was the sum paid by Mr. Shuttleworth for the five cottages forming Barrows-row, Church-street. Two dwelling-houses and workshops with large gardens attached at Ditton, on the south side of the highway from Prescot to Warrington, were sold to Mr. James Burrows for £4lO. A couple of lots were with- drawn. TRANSFER DAY AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, Messrs J. Brundrit and James Handley granted transfers of the followiog licenses :—Of the Rifle- man Inn, Church-street, from Ellen Armstrong to Arthur Hough; The George Inn. Pool-lane, from Martha Robi.n- son to Thomas Robinson; The Mariners Hotel, Percival's- lane, from Thomas Lister to John Walker; The Mersey Vaults, Mersey-street, from Thomas Ashton to Thomas Blease ; The Norton Arms, Halton, from Edwin Field to Edward Badeley ; The Crown Vaults,. Heath-road, from Joseph Wilkinson to John Lawrence Winstanley ; The Camden Hotel, Sorry-street, from Charles Fradlaugh to Joseph Smith; The Sailors' Home, Regent-street, to Sarah Marsh, whose husband died recently; and the Albion Inn, Peel-street, from Elizabeth Williams to Sarah Littlewood. 'A NUISANCE AT WESTON.—Hugh Whaiton, of Weston Point, appeared before the Rnucorn magistrates to answer a summons charging him with failing to comply with a requisition of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority to abate a nuisance existing on certain premises, and which if temporarily abated would be likely to recur.—Mr. W. H. Linaker, solicitor. represented the Authority. From a statement by Mr. Farrington, it appeared that the privies were situate off South-road, Weston, and were used by the occupants of four houses. The Medical officer had certified that they constituted a nuisance dangerous to health. The defendant had been called upon to reconstruct the privies in a better situation, but he bad failed to do so. He now expressed himself willing to do anything the Authority required. The Bench accordingly made an order for the reconstruction and removal of the pretnises and the pay- ment of costs 40s.

Rusconx COUNTY COURT.—On Tuesday, before His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, there were one adjourned summons, three default summonses, 97 original plaints, and 20 judgment summonses. Application was nsade by the de'endant in the case of William Clark, farmer. Netherton, against Thomas Eistwood, potato° merchant, Huddersfield, for a new trial. The case was heard and decided a month ago, when the defendant arrived at the court too late. Mr. Carver, the deputy judge then sitting, granted stay of exe- cution until that application was made. His Honour said he could not take being too late as an excuse, and he re- fused a new trial. The defendant should have arrived in

town the night previous in order to be at court at the time , his summons directed him, viz., 10 o'clock. The claim was for £7 Os 3d for potatoes sold.—An order for immediate payment was made upon Robert Edwards, captain of the schooner Fay, who was sued by Joseph B. Bankes for LT for the hire of a chronometer. Mr. Hitchen represented the plaintiff. THE WIFE MURDER CASE AT WIDNES. A petition embodying the facts of the above case, and praying for the release of 'William Percy, farmer and contractor, Sutton's. lane, Widnes. who is serving a term of twenty years' penal servitude for the alleged murder of his wife at Widnee, in May, 1883, is being extensively signed. The petition is in charge of Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner for %Vest Derby Hundred of Lancashire, and alleges that there ' has been a grave miscarriage of justice, and prcceeds to give the details of the case. It is alleged that the blow which proved fatal to Mrs Percy was inflicted accidentally, and that the case against the old man was trumped up by the sou and his paramour. The petition contains many facts favourable to the convict which were unknown at the time of the trial. The petitioners pray that the prisoner may be released, "because he has been a6O ber, hard-working man; because he was blind of one eye and almost blind of the other, and could not have singled his wife out in the dirk ; because, if he did hit her, it was purely accidental ; because he had always loved his wife ; and because the character of the son was such as to render his evidence altogether unworthy lof belief, and that of the girl was open to the gravest sus picion." The object of the petition meets with great sVm- pathy, the convict having occtwied a most respectaUe, peel- tion in Widnes.

NEW MARMALADE, 31b. jars 9d. and 10d.—Law- lass Bros., 5, Market-place, Warrington.—Aikt. Dn. ADAMS, of Warrington, has been re-appointed medical officer of health to the Runcorn Rural Sani- tary Authority. EMIGRATION.—A list has been published of the steerage passengers landed at the port of New York during 1885, 1884, 1883, 1882, and 1881. The White Star line heads the list for 1885 with 24,123 steerage passengers, the Inman line coming next with a total of 21,112 steerage passengers. SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD.—Two meetings of this Board have been convened this week, but at neither was there a quorum of members present, and con- sequently the business has been left over. At the first meeting, on Tuesday, Mr. Turner, the chairman, ! and Mr. Kerfoot were present, and at the second, on ! Friday, only Mr. Kerfoot attended. ROBBERY IN CHESHIRE OF .£3,ooo.—At Nantwich, 1 on Thursday, six persons—three men and three ! women—were charged with breaking into the house i of Samuel Blud, a fellmonger, residing at Stapeley, and stealing over £3,000 in coin, which Bind kept in a box in his bedroom. The suggestion first was that Mrs. Blud and some of her relatives had stolen the money, and a Mrs. Bethell, sister-in-law to Mrs. ' Blud, was tried at the Knutsford Sessions for the robbery, but watt acquitted. Afterwards it was noticed that some of the persons now in custody were in possession of unusual sums of money, and they were arrested. Two of the male prisoners stated that the third man committed the burglary, obtained the money, and gave them £2O each, and from the man thus accused the police have re- covered nearly £6OO. The prisoners were remanded. THE SHIP CANAL.—The Bolton Corporation have I unanimously decided to support the application for the Money Bill in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal scheme, enabling the promoters to pay- interest out of capital during construction, and the borough members have been instructed to sup- port it.—The second reading of the Manciester Ship Canal Bill will be moved in the House of Com- mons next week. The Bill last Tuesday came before Mr. Campion, one of the examiners in the House of Commons, and was declared to have complied with the standing orders. The President of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce (Mr. E. Smith), speaking at the annual meeting of that body, on Wednesday, referred to the Manchester Ship Canal Scheme as affording ground for the " horrible tear" that the undertak- ing would assume the form of a public trust and be laid as a burden on the trade of the district. ile instanced in support of his apprehensions the case of Birkenhead, through which, he said, a loss of something like 16 millions had been incurred. • LIBERALISM IN CHESHIRE.—On Saturday night a large gathering of Liberals was held in the Mec- hanics' Institute, Hazle Grove, which is situated partly in the Altrincham division of Cheshire and partly in Hyde division. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Emmott Barlow, Liberal candidate at the last election for the Knutsford division, and he read a letter from Mr. T. G. Ashton, M.P., who wrote that "now they had secured the Hyde divi- sion, which they meant to keep, in spite of Tory explanations of the peculiar character of the elec- tion there, he hoped they might be able to assist their friends in the Altrincham division."—Mr. Joseph Leigh, one of the Liberal gandidates for Stockport, proposed a resolution expi•essing grati- fication at the return of the Liberals to power under the leadership of Mr. Gladstone, and trusting that the event would be signalised by the passing of the legislative enactments to which the Liberal party was pledged for the benefit of the people.--Mr. Killick, chairman of the Altrincham Division Liberal Association, seconded the motion, and it was adopted unanimously, after being supported by Mr. A. Bedell, of Wilmslow, chairman of the Knutsford Division Liberal Association.—A second resolution, proposed by Major 11. Turner, seconded by Mr. H. Milne, secretary of the Cheadle Liberal Association, and supported by Mr. S. Penney, viewed with satis- faction the return of four Liberal members to the house of Commons for Cheshire, and urged upon all the Liberal associations in the county to be pre- pared for any future election, in order to secure a majority of the seats for the Liberal party.
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMNIFS-lONERS._

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, Water- loo-road, on Thursday. Mr. P. SpPakman presided, and there were present—Messre. Dobson, Once, Mellor, Lake, White, Imison, Farrell, Meadowcroft, Lightburn, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), M. Barker (surveyor), and Dr. McDougall (medical officer.)

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY, The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday, at Dutton Workhouse. Present—Lieut.-Colonel Ashton (chairru an), Revs. J. Lockwood. J I Bryant, Messrs. J. Weir, E. Aaron, T. Hadfield, J. Parr, H. Linaker. (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Farrington (inspector.) GRANTS TOWARDS SALARIES.— k letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that they had paid to the treasurer of the Authority £l3O, being the Parlia- mentary grant in respect of the salaries of the medical offi- cer of health and the inspector of nuisances for the year ended 29th September last. THE WESTON POINT SEWER.—Messrs. C. Linaker and Davies, architects and surveyors, Frodsham, wrote that they had inspected that part of the Weston Point sewerage scheme constructed by the Mersey Brine and Salt Company. The foundation and subsoil was found to be solid clay, and there was no appearance of quicksands. There was every reason to believe the sewer to be an efficient one, but this could be better ascertained when the second minhole was built.—lt was decided on the motion of the Rev. J. Lock- wood, that the length of the sewer should not be passed until the second manhole bad been constructed by the corn- pany.—There was no other business of public interest.

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr. McDougall reported that the number of deaths regis- tered during the pas month amount to 36. Of these two were inquest cases. Of the remaining 34 deaths, nine were due to bronchitis, four to consumption, two to scarlet fever, one to dropsy after scarlet fever, two to paralysis, two to cancer of various organs, one to disease of the arteries, one to blood disease, one to convulsions one to defective nutri- tion, one to teething, two to heart disease, one to croup, one to natural decay, one to chronic dianteet, one to rheumatic fever, one to infl.mmation of the iining membrane of the brain, one to intestinal obstructioe, and one to premature birth. The above 36 deaths show an average death rate for the twelve months of a little over 25. per 1,000 of the esti- mated population. The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Commit- tee, which were passed ne the motion of Mr. Dobson, seconded by Imison, contained—r-c menendation that the tender of Mr. Thomas Itehinson,. or flagging a portion of Bridge-street be accep•ert. It was also recommended that the following t,lans f e-w huddino be approved :—Mr. Henry Dodd, for the erection of store- room at a shop in Princees-s•ree, ; William Firrell, for erection of eleyen cottages in Spealtmae !-te ; Mr. Henry Booth, for the erection of a house and shop 4,d two cottages in Ashridge-street. Toe Finance Committee reported that the receipts for the month amounted to £l3B 9s 9d, and -ce• wits amounting to £199 7s 1d were passed for paymeet he minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Imisoe, senonded by Mr. Mellor.

div.head: SANITARY CONDITIOX OP THE TOWN.
div.p: THE SANITARY CONDITIOX OP THE TOWN.

The minutes of the Health Committee contained the fol- lowing letter from the Lecal Government Board :—•• 2nd February, 1886. Sir,—l an directed thi t..ecal Govern- ment Board to state that they have had nod, r consideration your letter of the 7th met, and I am to exp, ess their satis- faction at the action which your letter stews to have been already taken by the Runcorn Imp-tivement Commissioners as regards the matters to which or. Airy drew attention on the occasion of his conference with the Commissioners on the 12th March 1885, and to which the Board roferred in their letter of the 23rd July last. The Boatd trust that the Widnes Sanitary Authority will not relax their efforts to improve the sanitary circumstances of their distr;ct Dobson moved, and Mr. Grice seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Mr. Dobson remarked with reference to the letter that the committee were adopting every means to put the town in a proper sanitary condition. He thought evtlry- thing was going on in a satisfactory way. Mr. Lake thought the emptying of aehpits was get- ting into arrears the arrears were Mcreasing instead of decreasing. Under the circumstances they could not congratulate themslves upon the sanitary conditions being satisfactory. They were doing something, but they were moving very slowly.—The Chairman said he was in a position to state that the nightsoil contractor was being dealt with very vigorously at present. .f he did not attend to his contract in its entirety additional men would be en- gaged under the terms of his contract, and the work done efficiently.—A circular:letter was read from the Royal Com- mission for the Calonial and Indian Exhibition, asking the chairman to enceurage the workmen of the Runcorn di-trict to go to the exhibition, where they would obtain much. valuable information by witnessing the finest examples of the productions of the British Colonies, and in the case of India viewing the practical workmanship. It was suggested that clubs should be formed to which the men should con- tribute is or 61 per week in order to raise the necessary funds. The letter has previously appeared in our columns. —The letter was referred to the committee.

div.head: DISTRESS AND THE SHIP CANAL EILL.
div.p: THE DISTRESS AND THE SHIP CANAL EILL.

Mr. Dobson said there was a bill before Parliament. for the purpose of giving the Manchester Ship Canal Company power to pay interest out of capital during the construction of the canal. If the Board could take any step to assist the passing of the Bill, it was important they should do so. There was a great amount of distress existing, and the scheme would find work for large numbers.—Mr. Grice thought this a siep in the right direction. The scheme would be a blessing to the commuaity these slack times. He thought the Commissioners ought to take a few shares to show that they had a real interest in the matter.—Mr. Mellor : You had better set us the example. —Mr. Grice : Wait until the borrowing powers are ob- tained.—Mr. Lightburn cordially eupportA the suggestion of sending a memorial in favour of the bill. The starving workingmen they met daily showed that something ought to be done at once.—Mr. Dobson moved and Mr. Grice -sec- onded a proposition that the seal of the Board be fixed, to a petition in favour ef the bill, and it was carried unanimously.

div.p: THZ COMMONS ACT.

Mr. Lake drew attention to the fact that some time ago— he was afraid to say how long—the Parliamentary and Legal Committee were deputed to consider the Commons Act as it referred to Runcorn. As that ommittee bad now no reports to make to the Board, he thought it was high time something was done in the matter.—The Chairman thought the mention of the matter would be quite sufficient to set the ball rolling.—The secretary said ,the committee had decided' not to deal with the subject in view of the County Government Bill.—Mr. Lightburn : That will not pass for years perhaps. (Laughter.)—Mr. Lake : Let us have a resolution brought before the Board, because the ' comnittee are simply docking the work without the Board knowihg anything.—Mr. Dobson said he would briog the matter before the committee. This concluded the business.

div.head: DISCUSSION ON HOME RULE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: DISCUSSION ON HOME RULE AT RUNCORN.

The second of a series of meetings und,er the auspices of the Northwich Division Liberal Association was held in Bethesda School-room, Runcorn, on Monday night. Con- sidering the very inclement state of the weather there was a capital attendance. Mr. S. Pope was voted to the chair. The subject for deliberation was 'Home Rule," and Mr. Edward Hill opened the discussion. At the outset, he asked "Had Ireland a case for National Self-governin'ent ?" He contended that it would be impossible for Ireland to be truly friendly and truly loyal so long as. the centre of government was fixed in London, and so long as five-sixths of Ireland's representatives were placed under the dominion and control of an indifferent and hostile majority. Ireland was capable of self-government, and independent manly Englishmen were bound to hold that in making that claim Irishmen were asserting their manhood and the dignity of their country, and deserved a fair and inipartial hearing. (Hear, hear.) Was it not clear that Ireland had a distinct nationality, a distinct history, distinct traditions, and a wholly distinct religion? What bound England and Ire- land together but that most unhappir and ill-assorted bond, the Act of Union? Englishmen hardly teemed to realise the fact that the Act of Union was a novelty, an innovation of the day before yesterday; and it had never been accepted by the Irish people. He referred to the agitation of O'Con- nell, and the rebellion of 1843, which included some of the purest and noblest Irishmen that modern times had known, who were ready to take the field, believing that by that means they could protest most effectually against the Act of Union. From that period until now in one form or another Irishmen had declared that force alone could com- pel Ireland to be bauod by the Act. At the present time for a man to obtain the popu- lar vote in Ireland, be must be or profess to be against the Act. Therefore he brought Eng- ishmen face to face with this fact that they were keep-

hg down a nation, that they were by their present system depriving a people of their rights as strongly, and as wrongfully, and by the very sort of oppression that keeps down the Poles or that kept down Venice. (Applause.) Nine out of ten Irishmen wert in favour of Home Rule. (Hear, hear.) And by what moral or political law were Englishmen justified in maintaining the present system. Two lines written by Dean Swift put the subject very clearly— West legislation that creates Divided hearts, united states. Hear, hear.), Mr. Hill pointed out that fcr generations f past the cry of Irish people for justice had been met with acts of Coerision. As to the power of England to do Ire- land jus..fiee, it would perhaps surprise Englishmen to hear how many great and fundamental differences there still were between the laws which related to Ireland and the laws which appertained to England on some most serious questions. On the question of education these was a fundamental difference between the law as it relaxed to Ireland and to England. The feelings of both peoples were not the same. The Irish people were devoted to one principle of education and the majority of the Eng- lish people bad different views, and yet the domination of the maji,rity in the House of Commons imposed a uniform system upon both Peoples. Was that justice? (Apithus,..) Speaking of the Land laws, he mentioned the fact that Mr. Gladstone made the first serious effort to deal with the Irish land system. but the misfortune was that Mr. Gladstone haying to think not only of the Irish people but the English

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Lieut.-Colonel Ashton presided over the meeting of the Board held at Dutton Wo! k house on Tuesday. Pressnt— the Rev. J. Lockwood ; Messrs. J. Weir, J. Parr P. Speak- man, E. Aaron, J. Stokes, J. Smith, J. Campkin, T. Hadfield, and the clerk and deputy clerk.

div.head: PARLIAMENTARY GRANTS.
div.p: PARLIAMENTARY GRANTS.

A letter was read informing the Board that the Local Government Board had paid to Mr. J. Dun, the treasurer, the sum of £343, being the Parliamentary grant in respect of the cost ef pauper lunatics in county and borough asylums and licensed houses for the year ended the 29th September last.

The Clerk had receivedi n-,;ti-e,3—t-h'a-t-T--hornas Jeffs, a pau- per patient admitted into Charter Asylum on the 8:h Nov., 1878, had died on the 15th February from nephritis and general dropsy.

• THE VAGRANT QUESTION. Mr. J. Stokes said he was under the impression that some time ago a resolution was passed that the experiment of causing vagrants to break stones should be made and he desired to know if the system had beeu Wed.—The Clerk said discretionary powers were given to the master.—Mr. Speakman remarked that from the returns he saw that since discretionary power was given to the master, there had been fewer vagrants.—The Rev. J. Lockwood said the books showed that since Decemt,er, 1884, 13 men were refused ad- mission simply on the ground of there being no room in the , house. At the last meeting the reflection was cast upon the Board that in some unions 41bs of oakum were picked by vagrants, and in the Runcorn Union only 21bs. In these places, however, where 41b3 were picked the vagrants staved two nights. In Runcorn they only stayed one night. 'Va- grants it was well known, would rather stay two nights than one. In the house there were seven wards for men and two for women. Before discretionary power was given to Mr. Jones there were constantly 14 men and four women in thee wards, and at the same time 13 men refused admission, showing that the present system was the best that could be adopted. Each of the vagrants con- tributed one-fifth of a penny towards their keep. Mr. Jones was of opinion that stone breaking would be an expensive luxury.—Mr. Stokes was quite satisfied with this explana- tion,.

THE BOARD AND HOME 'IDLE. The Clerk said he had received a letter, which had been addressed to all Boards of Guardians with reference to the state of Ireland, and asking them to petition to Parliament not to grant to the people of Ireland any greater amount of self-gevernment than they at present possesled.—On the motion of Mr. Speakman, it was decided that the letter lie on the table without being read,—Mr. Parr said it was a very good document, and several members expressed the opinion that he might keep it if Ns liked.—'.b a clerk
lett,

majority, and of the opposition of the English Parlinme... was not able to go the length that he felt certain Mr. Glad- stone was inclined to go. (Applause.) Ireland, the speaker stated was utterly opposed to most of England's wars and foreign enterprises, and he asked whether, in the face of this it was fair that they should be dragged into a war with which they bad no sympathy and against which very often their principles and consciences wete sternly re- solved. It might be asked whether there would not be a danger to the English people if Ireland had a native Parlia- ment, a..d whether an Irish Parliament would govern Ire- land as well as England had done. To the latter question be would answer with perfect confidence that a native par- liament could not possibly manage things worse. (Laugh- tor.) As to danger to England, he quoted from an article by Mr. JuAin McCarthy in the February number of the "Gentlemen's Magazine," to show that Home Rule did not mean dismemberment of the empire or any injury to the empire. "It does not mean separation nor anything like separation; it does not include control of an army or navy, or any power of levying what might be called impe- rial taxation,or of negotiation with foreign powers. It does not propose to abrogate in any way the imperial functions of the English Parliament." He was sure that all present would gladly see a thorough union of sentiment and sym- pathy between both nations. They wanted not the legisla- tion the, divided hearts and united systems, but the legislation which divided systems to unite hearts. (Ap- plause.) A discussion ensued in which Mr. Millingtcn and Mr. Kitto took part. Mr. B. Kniveton said the great cause of Ireland's sad state was, in his opinion, the land question. , (Hear, hear.) The laud laws of Ireland had been most abominable and had retarded the national progress. He did not see that a Parliament in Dublin would be a solution of the question. He believed that if they could put the land question right, thoroughly, ether things would right themselves. (Hear, hear.) Give Ireland the means and opportunity of increas- ing in wealth and in population, and he thought every other difficulty would son be cleared. He objected to a Parliament in Dublin at present, because he was afraid it wonici create as great if not greater difficulties than we had at the present time. The state of religious feeling that obtained in Ireland between Catholics and Protestants would, he epprehended, lead to serious trouble, and on this ground it would be better to keep Ireland united with England, and make a radical cure of the land laws, which lay at the foundation of the misery of the people, and then Ireland would be prosperous, contented, and happy Applause,) Mr. J. D. Jones, alluding to the religions aspect of the question, said the loyal Orange minority in Ireland really meant "ultra-Protestantism gone mad." (Laughter.) And what was to be done with them, because they undoubtedly would become the Fenians of Ireland when Home Rule was passed. (Laughter.) They would be stirrers up of sedition, and goodness knew they were mad enough for anything of that sort. (Laughter.) He was thoroughly in sympathy with the demand for Home Rule, and thought the Irish people would m.daage tbeir affairs quite well, and that Protestant views would be respected in every way.. (Applause.) The integrity of the empire, he pointed out, must be safeguarded. (Applause.) Tbe Rev. W. Vause, in a brief speech, said the opportne atunity for pacifying the Irish people with a Lard Act had iltogether passed, and he suggested that at a future meet- nn a resolution should be passed asking the Prime t Minis- .er to give as liberal a measure of Home Rule to Ireland as possible. (Applause.) The discussion was then adjourned.

EXTENSIVE ROBBERY OF COPPER AT WIDNES. At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday. Owen Ker- ley was brought up on remand charged with having during the last three months stolen 3iewt. of copper, value £7 173 4d from the copper works of Messrs. Bolton and Sons, Wid- nes. Alice Kerley, marine store dealer, Victoria-street, his mother, and Peter Kerley, her son, were charged with hav- ing received the copper knowiug it to have been stolen. Mr. J. W. Knowles defended.—Tbomas Kerry, a clerk in the employ of Messrs. Bolton, identified the copper. The copper was at the works in December last, and witness had missed quantities at different times. He had never sold any copper to the prisoners. The firm did not sell copper to marine store dealers.—Hecry Horabin, carter, of 4, Peel- street, Widnes, depose 4 that on Sunday mornieg the 21st ult., Owen Kerley enraged him to take a load, which he understood would be iron, on the following morning to Liverpool. The price agreed upon was 10s.—Joseph flora- bin, son of last witness, stated that when he took the pony and cart to the prisoners' house the next morning, the male prisooers placed three bags in the cart. He did not know what the bags contained. Alice Kerley saw all that was going on. Accompanied by Owen, he drove to Liverpool by way of Ditton and Hale, and on arriving they called at a marine store. The bags were thrown down a cellar to be weighed, and ha then discovered that the contents were copper, as tbe bottom of one bag gave way. The copper was not sold and three other marine stores were called at. At the last place Owen offered the copper for 3d a lb. A. man then came upon the scene and asked Owen to go to the police station with him and shortly afterwards a detective came and took him (witness) and the pony and cart to the police station. P.S. Robin- son deposed that when he received the prisoner Owen into custody from the Liverpool city police he in- formed him that his mother and Peter had been appre- hended. He replied that it was no use his mother and Peter suffering. They bad never seen the copper. He "stole it himself" from Bolton's and put it into an empty bouse in Peel-street.—Mr. Knowles for the defence contended that there was no evidence against Mrs. Kerley and Peter, and asked for their disckarge.—The prisoners were committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.
II
_RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Tc-a-w-n: Hall, Water- loo-road, yesterday morning. The Rev. Canon Barclay pre- sided, and there were present Messrs. W. Elandley, J. Prite chard, E Theisen, and F. Rigby (clerk). THE FINLNCES.—INCREkSED RATE.—The Clerk said the only business of interest to the public was the precept. Under the new system they paid £3OB 3s 2d a year for interest and principal on the money borrowed. They would not get over that for 30 years. Then they paid £35 a year for those offices and the salaries of clerk and officers amounted to £199. At Mill Brow School the teachers' salaries amounted to £l4l 7s, and fuel, lighting, and char- ing cost £25. Repairs, rates, and so on amounted to £lB. In respect to Greenway-road School they could only specu- late as to the expenditure. The salaries would amount to £340; charing would be £18; and fuel, lighting, and re- pairs would be, roughly speaking, £5O. In round numbers the expenditure for the ensuing year would 'be £1.200. Last year Mill Brow received in fees £7O, and the grant was £9l ; total £l6l. They could expect very little from Greenway-road School the first year. Everything was'in a state of disorganisation, the type of children was anything but an intelligent one; they knew little or nothing; and they could not expect good results. Putting the fees at £l5O and the grant at £2OO, that would give them £350 from the school. This sum added to the income from Mill Brow and other items brought the Board's Income to £533 This would leave about £7OO to be provided out of the. rates. The Board's present balance in the hands of the treasurer was £99 19s 9d, but unfortunately they were called upon to pay accounts amounting to £204, which would leave them a debit balance at the bank of £lOO. It was true they had a considerable credit balance in respect to the loan, but they would bave to pay it out before long. A rate of 2d in the £ for the half year would produce £420, and if they deducted the £lO4 overdrawn at the bank there, would be left £316 for the half year. He thought the Board were obliged to levy that rate because they were starting with new expenses and with a balance on the wrong side. He thought the rate for the half year commencing on the ,25th March would be Pei in the L.—Mr. W. Haedley said he went into the matter with the clerk on the previous day, and the figures were quite correct. The rate would be no heavier than it had been for the past half year, because the overseers had been required to pay £350 for the past half year.—The Clerk explained that the balance on the wrong side was caused mainly through the cost of removal to the present offices, namely, £70.-51r. Handley remarked that the overseers only spent £3O in removing.—lt was unanimously decided to issue a precept upon the overseers for £4OO for the half year.

div.head: DOCTOR'S DINNER AND ITS CONSEQUENCES.
div.p: A DOCTOR'S DINNER AND ITS CONSEQUENCES.

Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner, yesterday held an in- quest at Widnes on the body of Ann Whitfield, a widow,. who lodged at 15, Chatham-street, Widnes, with Mrs Burke. Mrs Burke dePosed that the deceased had lodged at her house for seven months. She was 64 years of age. /or several months she had suffered greatly from cold, and on Thursday morning she complained of a pain, in the chest.. Witness put warm flannell on her chest, but the deceased became so neuch.worse• that about a quarter past twelve witness went to Dr. Cooper's surgery. Dr. Cooper said he would come when he had had his dinner, and she returned home to find the deceased lying on the sofa in an insensible condition. Death ensued at half-past one:. Dr. Cooper did not go to the house until four o'clock when the woman was laid out. In reply to Questions wit- ness said she spoke to the doctor 'as follows t "Will you please come at once for a. person at . my house is either dying or in a fit. Do come at once."—Several jurymen expressed disset'sfaction at the conduct of the doctor. His house was enly about fifty yards from tne place, but just because it was a poor Person, they said, he did not attend until too late.—lnspec- tor Wood said Dr. Cooper had that morning told him that he would have been at the house sooner, if he had not been teld that the person was dead. He therefore thought it was no use going. He simply "looked in" at four o'clock, not because he thought he could do any good.—The Coroner said Dr. Cooper was the parish doctor, ard had entered into- a contract to attend poor people, and he should keep to it. He should have gone to the woman at once on receiving the, summons. If she bad been a private patient he could have. pleased himself.—The jury reterned a verdict of death from natural causes, but considered that a presentment was unnecessary, as the publicity the Press would give to the matter would be sufficient.

WARRINGTON BOROUGIi POLICE COURT. SATURDAY—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandley. AS UNTERACIOUS MILITIAMAN.—JOI Saunders, a pri- vate in the 3rd Battalion of the Liverpool Militia, stationed at Orford Barracks, was charged with having wilfully made a false answer to a question put to him on attestation on the 17th inst., namely, " Have you ever been sentenced to penal servitude ?" To this question he answered "No," although he had been twice sentenced to penal servitude. Prisoner was committed to gaol for a month. MONDAY—Before Alderman Davies and Councillor Green-

log. DurrucioncEss —The following were dealt with for this offence :—William Yates, in the Market-place on Saturday night, sent to prison for 14 days; Edward Moran, in Butter- market-street on the previous morning, fined 50, including costs ; William Taylot, in Rose-yard, sent to prison for 14 days; John Bibby, in Battermarlot-street on the 20th ult, similarly punished. Too MANY LODGERS.—SamueI Platt was summoned "for keeping lodgers without having his house registeled.—ln- spector Church gave evidence to the effect that in defen- dant's house in William-street, off School-brow, there were two sleeping and two living rooms, and seven persons were living there.—A fine of ss, including costs, was imposed. —Ann Yates, who also lives in William-street, was fined 2s 6d, including costs. A BuTcnEla FlNED.—Sidney Cooper, butcher, 35, Bridge- street, was charged on a summons with causing an obstruc- tion by hanging meat outside his shop so as to project over the footpath-, and was fined 2s 6d and costs. TUBSDAY—Before Messrs. F. Monks and E. J. Guest. DRUNKENNESS.—Pat. Murphy and Mary Ann Holmes were charged with being drunk in Leyland's Court at one o'clock the same morning. They were found lying in a corner beastly drunk, and with them was a little child. The Magistrates sent them both to prison for 14 days. WEDNESDAY—Before Mr. Jahn Fairclough, Alderman Pickmere, and Councillor Greening. KICKING Can.—Peter Fleming, an Army Reserve man, was charged with assaulting a man named Jonathan Back- ley Mellor, at 8-40 on Monday evening, in Market-street.-- Mellor said that a woman tried to snatch his watch-chain and he ran after and caught her. Thereupon prisoner came up, struck him twice in the face, knocked him down, and kicked him in the ribs.—The Magistrates seat him to prison for two months. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds. Dr. White, Dr. Gornall,

FALSE ATTESTATION.—Heary Mills was charged with making a false answer on being attested as a recruit at Orford Barracks, lie having said that he had never before belonged to the service, whereas in 1884 he was discharged with ignominy from the Royal Marines.—He was sent to prison for a month. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—Sarah Ellen Green was summoned for assaulting Sarah Ansbury, on the Zits ult.—The case was dismissed. MASTER AND SERVANT.—Margaret Burns, an apprentice to John Gallop, fustian cutter, was summoned for absenting herself from work on the 10th ult.—The case was adjourned for a fortnight to see if defendant would resume work.

The tobacco factory of Messr . Goodbody, at Tullamore, was burned down early on Thursday morning. The loss is estimated at £30,000, and it is stated that a thousand per- sons will be thrown out of employment.

This match was played at Si. Helens, on Saturday. Newton were beaten entirely in the loose scrimmaging. Tries were secured by the brothers Hankinson, but Pike failed to im- prove upon them, St. Helens Recreation winning by two tries and ten minor points to nil. WRSTON SHANTERS V. W MAN ST. JAMES' (2ND).—This return fixture was played at Weston on Saturday. The visitors arrived wiih three of their team short, but found good substitutes in Higgins, Pendleburv, and Stinger, and a pleasant game ended in favour of Weston by two goals, one try, and five minors to two minors. RUNCORN V. NEW BRIGHTON —The frost did not, as was quite anticipated, stop the fixture between these Cheshire teams being played off, although the principal Liverpool clubs scratched their engagements en Saturday. A good number of spectators assembled on the Liscard ground, when a very fast and interesting game was witnessed. New Brighton winning the choice of ends, W. Hughes set the ball going. The visitors won a capital game by two goals, three tries, and three minor points to New Brighton one goal and two minor points. For Runcorn, Woods, Hughes, and Andrews played a fine game behind the pack, and the for- wards played a very hard and quick game, whilst, for New Brighton, Rome, Couborough, and Barber.in the backs, and Dunn, Dodd, and Brown (forward) were the most prominent. RUNCORN (SECOND TEAM) V. RUNCORN RECREATION.—
Runcorn handsomely took down New Brighton andWigan ought to have appeared at Widnes last Saturday, but failed to do so for some unaccountabls reason.

Oldham very reluctantly turned out against Swinton, and I were a try to the bad at the finish. Manchester and Brough- ton Rangers, and Broughton and Liverpool, were cancelled! owing to the hard ground. The first round of the Yorkshire Cup Ties were played off on Saturday last, and furnished some remarkable sur- prises, the most notable being Wortley beating Huddersfield, Mirfield throwing out the 1883 cup holders, Thornes. Salter- hebble, in receipt of .£lOO, corSnted to meet Hall on their own ground, and a splendid fight they made, three minors only throwing them oat of the competition. Chief among others who were put out are Wakefield Trinity, York, Selbv,_Ossett, Sheffield, and Halifax Free Wanderers.

To-day (Saturday) Scotland and England meet at Edin- burgh to fight their battles over again. The teams selected for the occasion contain the very hest known exponents of the game of bath countries, and of course a very fine game is sure to result. In England public opinion la in favour of the Celt winning, and no doubt he will use his utmost en- deavours to bring about the defeat of the Saxon. Referring to the Liverpool Cup match, the Mercury says :—" Since winning the Liverpool Cup, Earlestown have altogeber failed to substantiate their claim to be con- sidered the first club of this district, and their overthrow on Saturday by Stanley will cause very little surprise. The present season has been as disastrous to the present holders of the cup as the previous seasou had been successful. Starting with a sensational defeat in the cup competition by Brombotough, they were only reinstated in that competition owing to some t.chnical infringement of the association rules by the riverside club. An easy defeat of Skelmersdale and a stubborn fight with Cambrian, brought them a fort- night ago f ice to face with Stanley, a drawn game result- ing. On Saturday the tie was brought to a definite issue at the Nursery Ground, Walton-stiles, and here, in the presence of 4,000 spectators, Earlestowu were completely routed. Although the verdict against them was but two goals to nil, Earlestown bad all the worst of the play. From start to finish Stanley had the upper hand, and their custo- dian had very much of a sinecure in both portions of the game. Taken all round, the play cannot be characterised as a scientific display. The winners alone showed any at- tempt at combination, whilst Earlestown relied principally on spasmodic dashes, which, however, were easily checked by a more than usually safe defence. Stanley assumed the offensive from the kick off, and the game was young when Smith, with a clever shot from out of a scrimmage, scored the first goal. Much long kicking was afterwards indulged in by the respective defenders, bat a capital passing run by the ~tanley forwards gave Culkin an opportunity, and he scored with a good shot. A third time the ball was spleadidly got through by the Stanley players, but unfortunately the point was disallowed for offside. In the second half play dete- riorated, and though Stanley still pressed their opponents no other point was scored, and Stanley won a very popalar vic- tory by two goals to nil." The conference between the representatives of the Scotch, Irish, and Welsh Football Associations at Liverpool last week is likely for proving successful. The resolutions passed acknowledge the fairness of the position take& up by the F.A., but the Scotchmen could not give in entirely, so to make the matter presentable to the " Scottish Paris's" they made the residence restriction three years instead at two. This, however, they are not likely to stand out, so that by Faster Lancashire patrons of the winter game may expect to see the leading Scotch clubs on their grounds.
This match was played on aturday, on the ground of the Runcorn Football Club. The match excited great interest in the town, and there was a Lirge number of spectators. _

The game ended in a win for the Runcorn team by a try and six minors to nil. For Runcorn Davies, Riley, and Whitby behind played a capital game, as also did Green (captain), Woodward, and Pendlebury for the Recreation. In the pack. Faulkner, Dolan, and Dunbavand for Runcorn, and Acton, Yarwood, Pennington and John Green did most work. The teams were as follo.s:—Runcorn: Booth, back: Davies, Riley, and Cawley, three-quarter backs; Whitby and Antrebus, half backs; forwards, Raffe, Dunbavand, Gittens (captain), Faulkner, W. Jones, Dolan, Andrews, Orme, and Ford. Recreation: Full back, T. Charleston; three-quarter backs, Green (captain), Clare, and Wishlade ; half backs, Woodward and Pendlebury ; forwards, John Green, Haitwood, Hayes, Pennington, Acton, Yarwood, Hughes, Bushell, and Stubbs. WARRINGTON Y. MOSSLRY.—The Warrington team on Saturday, without Warren, Fair. Turner, Tommy Barnes, and Hough, journeyed to Moseley to play their first fixture with this noted South-east Lancashire team. The weather was very favourable, but a bitter cald wind blew across the ground, which is situated at a good elevation, to the discom- fort of the 600 or 700 spectators who had assembled to- gether to witness the encounter. A cheer greeted the teams on their appearance on the field of play, and both sides being ready, Frith started the leather on behalf of Moseley, Jolley returning. After some exciting scrimmages, H. Ashton got in a short run, the ball now being in the home quar:ers, W. Winterbottom relieving by a short run ' and kick into touch. Some tough scrimmages Were the next item, Mosslev gaining ground. Billings was now allowed a free kick, and soon after Rigby was hurt and had to retire, his head coming into contact with J. Winter- bottom's shoes whilst in the act of tackling him. The visi- tors now pleyed with only eight men in the scrimmage, the consequence being that weight told against them, although Ashton, Povey, and Dillon worked like giants. some loose play took the ball to the home 25, but Lawton broke through with the hall at his toes and removed hostilities to the visitors' 25. Rigby now partially recovered, amidst the hearty plaudits of the spectators, joined the scriminagers, who worked with renewed vigoar and again transferred play to the home department. Sabs€quently good passing on the part of Billings and J. Winterbottom resulted in the leather being taken back again. Billings passed time after time to Winterbottom, and time after time Jolley came in full sail and made him bite the dust. Gilbert, Speakman, and Nevins gained ground by a combined dribble but Coxe saved, and shortly afterwards Billings, by a good piece of strategy, got past Gilbert and Jolley, and got over the line, but failing to hold the ball J. Winterbottom had the honour to score the first try, Lawton failing to con- vert it into a premier point. On the ball being restarted and kicks exchanged between the backs, Gilbert got hold and punted with good judgment. The forwards, led by ishton and Dillon, coming up quickly took the ball to the home 25. Speakman and Gilbert stopped rush after rush at this place, but eventually Coxe led the Moseley forwards to the visitors' territory. The home forwards, from now until the end of the game, persisted in playing off-side, their wingmen being greatly detrimental to stopping the passing of the visitors' half backs. Half time was now called with the ball in the centre of the field. On resuming, F. Turner kicked off, Ashworth returning. Nothing of any importance took place for the first half hoar, unless we take some very toughly-contested scrimmages into consideration. Billings obtained another free kick, but Ashton charged it down, arid led a good dribble to the home 25, being ably seconded by Povey and Davies. Massey next received the ball from Speakman, and made a pass without looking, which cost the visitors a try, J. Winterbottom again being the lucky individual; Lawton again failed to improve. By strenuous efforts on the part of the visitors' forwards the ball was taken to the borne 25, Fovea, getting over, but through some infringement the point was not allowed. A series of scrimmages took place on the line, and a good dribble on the part of the home team brought to a conclu- sion a very hardly contested game, the score being—War- rington, 2 minors; Mosley, 2 tries and 3 minors. Jolley I was the best of the three-quarters. Gilbert and Speakman played a grand game under great difficnities, whilst Ashton was most prominent in the forward rank, being well seconded by Dillon, Rigby, Povey, and Nevins for War- rington. Billings and J. Winterbottom were, by far, the best backs for Moseley, all the forwards playing a most derter- mined game. After the match a substantial repast awaited the teams, to which ample justice was done by the 70 or 80 persons who partook of it. Teams :—Warrington Back, Hewitt; three-quarters, Massey, Buxton, and Jolley; half backs, Gilbert and Speakman; forwards, Nevins, Frank Turner, Rigby, Povey (captain), Dillon, Ashton, Littlewood, Davies, and Heyes. Mossley : Back, Roylance ; three- quarters. W. Winterbottom (captain), Lawton, and J. Win- terbottom; half backs; Billings and Wood; forwards, Ash- worth. J. Winterbottom, Meakin, Mitchell, Firth, Rowan, Mayall, Coxe, and Walker. ASSOCIATION RULES.
