Scoot ArrE4lNcis.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday. before Mr. F. W. Earle and Captain Willis the following persons were each fined 6d and costs, 4s 6Y, for seglecting to send their children to school :—James Gilli- gan, Thomas Larkin, senr.. Michael Reddish. Daniel Murphy, Robert Atkinson, James Glover, and Thomas Hold- croft.

KNOWSLEY HALL.—Considerable alterations are about to be made to this seat of Lord Derby, which will materially alter the appearance of this historical mansion. The southern facade is to be raised with an additional story, which will add A suite of six bedrooms. A contrast will be shown from the main building in the materials used, but the features of the architecture will be maintained. ZION SCHOOLS.—On Tuesday evening there was a good audience assembled to hear the reproduction of the children's festival of sacred song. as recently rendered by the choir of the Liverpool Sunday School Union at St. George's Hall. A chorus of 200 voices were gathered under the conductorship of Mr. William Berry and a band of stringed instruments; leader, Mr. William Atherton. Miss Quick with her usual ability accompanied on the American organ. RBFORMATORY ARRZARS.—James Doddv, a labourer, liv- ing in erescot, was summoned at the Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Mr. F. W. Earle and Captain Willis, for failing to comply with a magisterial order for the payment of is 6d per week towards the maintenance of his son, in an industrial school.—Superintendent Barker stated that the arrears amounted to £1 16s, and the defendant had not paid anything since 28th August last. With the costs, the amount owing was £2 2s 6d.—The Bench made an order for payment within 14 days. INFIRM PARENTS.—Befere Mr. F. W. Earle and Captain Willis, at the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Martin Mullen Michael Mullen, and John Mullen, brothers, and all employed as chemical labourers at Widnes, were sum- moned to show cause why they should not contribute to the support of their father, 7$ years of age, at present charge- able to the Prescot Union. Neither of the defendants ap- peared.—Mr. John Scannell, relieving officer, stated that the father of the defendants was totally unfit to earn his own living, and was in receipt of outdoor relief.—The Bench made an order for each defendant to contribute Is per week. —Joshua Abbott, a chemical labourer at Widnes, was summoned for a similar offence.—Mr. Scannell stated that the defendant's father was 78 years of age and was receiv- ing 2s per week from the Union.—The defendant said he had always been willing to keep his father if he would come and live with him.—The Bench made an order for the pay- ment of 2s per week. BOARD OF GUARDIAIrS —The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held on Thursday. Mr. J. Leatherbarrow 'presided. On the motion of the Rev. J. Barnacle, seconded by Mr. W. Birchall, it was decided, sub- ject to the approval of the Local Government Board, to ap- point Dr. Andrew Murdoch medical officer for the Rainford district at a salary of £25 per annum, and as vaccination officer, with the usual fees.—The workhouse master re- ported that there were 510 inmates this week, against 515 i last week, and 457 in the corresponding period of last year. Vagrants relieved 31, against 61 in the corresponding period , last year.—The Clerk remarked that the number of inmates, which was satisfaotory considering the hard times, would have been lower if the master had discharged a number of persons in the usual way; but owing to the very severe weather he did not feel justified in turning them out.-Several Guardians remarked that the master had exercised a very wise discretion, and it was a very humane thought.— The Clerk drew attention to the alleged death of an old woman from starvation at St. Helens, and said he had thought it his duty to communicate with the relieving officer alluded to Mr. Tracey, for his observa- tions concerning the case. Mr. Tracey had replied that the deceased applied on the Bth October last. She was told to appear before the committee, but site did not come, and the committee told him (the relieving officer) to offer her an order for the workhouse. He did so, but she refused it, saying she would try and do without relief.— After some discussion the relieving officer was called into the Board room, and he added that the coroner called on him after the inquest to ask if he would bury the woman. He (Tracey) explained the circumstances, and Mr. Brig- house said that altered the circumstances, as both himself and the jury were under the impression that deceased had made a recent application.—The Board considered the ex- planation of the relieving officer satisfactory, and expressed their confidence in him. BRBsCoT LOCAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday evening, when there were present Messrs. C. Speecely (chairman), J. Hall, W. Hatton, T. Dennett, T. Preston, H Whitfield, H. Makin, W. Goulds- worth (s u y Dickinsonor ) H H. (nuisancer os(clerk), n ape Teal et pe rh o(collector),and A Clerk reported that he had exchanged agreements with the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephonic Exchange Company, for the erection of poles throughout the district.—The Board's Officers:—On the motion of Mr. Hall, seconded by Mr. Dennett, Dr. E. F. Hall was re-elected medical officer of health for the ensuing year at a salary of £25 per annum. Dr. A. Dickinson was re-appointed sanitary inspector at a salary of £4O per annum, on the motion of Mr. Hall, secon- ded by Mr. Makin.—The Fire Engine': The surveyor re- ported that he had made inquiries with regard to the par- chase of a good second-hand fire engine, and read a copy of letters sent to several makers. He bad as yet received no definite reply on the subject, and the matter was scarcely ripe for consideration at that meeting. It was decided to leave the matter in abeyance until the next Meeting.—Mr. NOTES BY THE WAY. Whitfield asked if there would be a guarantee that it was a To-day (Saturday) commences the first round of the better engine than the Old One.—The Surveyor replied there West Lancashire and Border Towns Cup Ties. It certainly would be no purchase until they were satisfied on that point will be a red letter day in the annals of football within ths —Arrears of Rates: The Board directed the clerk to give above district, and should prove very beneficial to the the usual notice requiring payment of rates before the 25th i tL verpool clubs particularly, as they require a great impetus inst., the end of the financial year.—Births and Deaths: o propagate the game, and to secure a gate in that part. Mr. H. Fogg (registrar) reported that during February there lwenty-four clubs contend for the trophy, and of those were 10 deaths against 18 in the corresponding month last

LITE.RPOOL Sr. JOHN'S T. Sr. HELENS VICTORIA.— Played on the ground of the former, the result being a tie— one goal each. WHOM!? T. LIVERPOOL Sr. BENEDICTS.—PIayed 011 the ground of the latter on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the home team by four goals to one. PARK LANE WANDERERS T. SANKEY REFINERS, EARLES- TOWN.—The Park Lane Wanderers journeyed to Earlestown on Saturday to play the Sankey Refiners' first team. The match was played before a large number of spectators. A pleasant game resulted in a victory for the Refiners by two goals to one. The Refiners' should have played Park Lane second, but did not put in an appearance. EARLESTOWN (A TRAM) V. OSWESTRY.—The Oswestry first team journeyed to Earlestown on Saturday afternoon to fulfil their engagement with the Earlestown first team, but as the latter were playing their cup tie with Stanley at Liverpool a strong "A" team was got together to oppose the visitors. The match was played 'on the Manes, and there was a fair number of spectators. The visitors won by two goals to none. WIGAN AND DISTRICT CHALLENGE Cup: HINDLEY T. GOLBORNE.—These teams met on Saturday, on the Wigan Rectory Ground, to play off the semi-final in the above competition, having played a drawn game the previous week. Hindley won by three goals to two, after a close game. There were 3,000 spectators. Golborne hive pro- tested against one of the goals given to flindley, and should the protest be upheld, the result will be another drawn game.

div.p: LIVERPOOL CUP TIE:

ZARLESTOWN V. STANLEY : THE CIIPHOLDERS DEFEATED. The Earlestown Club, last year's winners and present holders of the Liverpool and District Association Challenge Cup, were on Saturday thrown out of this season's compe- tition by the Stanley Club, who, after a hard-fought and rough game, defeated the cupholders by two goals to none. The two teams had played a drawn game of one goal each at Earlestown on the previous Saturday and their meeting at Liverpool on the Stanley ground on Saturday excited a keen interest. One of the largest " gates " of the season assembled, nearly 4,000 persons paying for admission into the field. Both elevens mustered their strengest teams, but the cupholders were not •in good form, Dagnall (captain) ' still suffering severely from the injury sustained at Black- burn, while Ellison was far from well. Then shortly after the game commenced Siddeley sustained an injury to his knee, which rendered him almost useless during the rest of the game, and early in the second half Ellison was violently kicked on the right cheek, severely lacerating the flesh and rendering him unable to play any further. These mishaps thoroughly disorganised the cunholders, whose accidents were crowned by a defeat of two goals to none. The redeeming feature on their side was the good defensive play of the brothers Green and Appleton (goal keeper). The Stanley team was much heavier than their light opponents, and the latter, who .were much knocked about, were treated to play of a rough description. Teams : EanLESTOWN.—Appleton, goal; J. Green and R. Green. backs; Bowker, Duxbury, and Whalley, half backs; Sims, Siddeley, Dagnall, Ellison, and Rich, forwards. STANLEY.—G. Wright, goal; A. Dick and R. Stevenson, backs; R. Pollock, G. Kerr, and A. McCallum, half backs; W. Wilson, D. Smith, W. Macgregor, J. Culkin, and W. Brown, forwards.

Tear; death rate 18.69 per 1,000, against 33.65 last year The births were 19 against 22 last year.—Firs: The Clerk read correspondence with Mr. Scratton' of the Pottery, Huyton Quarry, in reference to a fire which broke out on his premises on the 2nd ult., and to which the Prescot Fire Brigade were called. The caarge for their services amoun- ted to £6 1.9 a 6d, including the payment of several assis- tants. Mr. Scratton maintained that he ought not to be charged for the latter as he resided outside the Board's district and he had plenty of assistants on his own pre- mises. After some consideration the Board decided to with- draw the charge £2 for the use of the fire engine, so as to be able to pay the assistants.—This was the only busi- ness.

PRBSCOT HIGHWAY BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday foreaoon when there were present—Mr. , ' W. L. Evans J.P. (in the chair), 'Captain Willis Messrs. R. Tyrer, M. Lowe, H. Cross (clerk), and W. GoHaworth (surveyor).—Telephones and Telegraphs: The Surveyor re- parted that since the last meeting he had received a plan of the positions of the telephone posts proposed Is be erected by the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Company, and it was of a satisfactory character. With regard to the ob- jectionable Government telegraph post in Warrington-road, the chairman of the Board and the wavvarden for Whiston had had an interview with the engineers to the telegraph authorities, and they had agreed to remove the pest to the I Bide of the wall. The Board approved of the proposed re- moval.—The New Railway: The Clerk said he had presented a petition on behalf of the Highway Board against tke St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway Bill, and he had pre- pared a, draft agreement embodying the requirements of the Board in regard to the highways. A draft had been sent to the solicitors for the promoters, and they had endorsed It. He read the proposed agreement, which the chairman thought very satisfactory. Mr. Tyrer : I think it is quite so. The Board passed .a resolution approving of the agree- ment, and directing the seal of the Board to be affixed there- , to.—The St. Helens Water Works: The Chairman, in alluding to the road at Knowsley seriously damaged by ex- cessive carting in connectian with the St. Helens Corpora- tion Water Works, remarked that he saw the Board were doing something at it. The Surveyor replied that he was only making it simply passable. The Chairman: And keeping an account of the cost? The Surveyor: Yes.— Tender for Slag, #c.: The Surveyor submitted several tenders for the supply of slag material, ite„ required by the Board during the ensuing year, and a resolution was passed that the tender of Mr. Derbyshire, of Penmenmawr, for macadam, be accepted. The tenders for slag and carting were left over for further consideration —The Snowstorm: Mr. Lowe asked the Surveyor if anything had been done with respect to clearing the snow from the roadway, in order to prepare for vehicular traffic? %r. Goldsworth re- plied that on the previous day he sent instructions to all the road foremen that they were to open tie roads in their respective districts sufficiently to allow one vehicle to pass. They were to deal with the most important roads first, and gradually widen them out. He had men in every parish that morning following out his instructions. Mr Lowe said that in some places in the Holt., the snow was five feet deep, and the road almost impassable.—The Cleaning of Villages: The Surveyor asked the permission of the Board to engage an old man in each of the villaees in the Board's district at a few shillings per week to sweep the principal streets in each village. The Board granted the application,—The Expenditure: The Surveyor's statement of his expenditure for the four weeks ending 25th February was as follows : Bold, £24 17s 6d ' • Knowsley, £l2 18s 2J; Rainhill, £23 us Id; Whiston,£6 Is 61; team labour, £2O us 6d ; new materials, £l4 7s lid; incidentals, 17s 4d; total, £lO3 11s 6d.—This was all the business.

div.head: "THE CHURCH OF THE FUTURE."
div.p: "THE CHURCH OF THE FUTURE."

In connection with the educational fund of the Warrington Co—operative Society, the Rev. W. Tuck. well, rector of Stockton, near Rugby, gave his lecture in the Co-operative Hall, on Monday evening. Not- withstanding the very inclement weather there was a large attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Crostleld, J.P., and amongst those present were the Rev. 8.. Pilcher, 8.A., Mr. F. Monks, J.P., Mr. J. Greening, J.P., Mr. T. Birchall (president. of the Co- operative Society), Mr. Birtles, &a. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, said he did not know anything about the opinions of the rever- end gentleman who was going to lecture, and he did not know whether he should•agree with or differ from him. The subject was about the church, and he (the chairman) was not one of the extreme people who would have the claurches put up to auction and sold to the highest bidders, to be used as music halls, or pulled down and the streets paved I with their stones. ("No, no," and laughter.) But at the same time he thought there was plenty of room for reform in the church—(hear, hear)—and great as was its influence in this country, he thought it might have a still greater in- fluence. He was one of those that thought the bishops had no business in the House of Lords, and he was pleased to see that Mr. Peter Rylands had given notice that he would bring that matter before the House of Com- mons. (Applause).

. , The Rev. W. TUCZWELL, on rising, was greeted with loud applause. He said that a year ago he spoke a parable in that hall, and portrayed in terms of totally uninspired pro- phecy the possible future of England. He predicted an access of material prosperity to a class amongst which at had hitherto been a stranger, by means of the distribution of the land, with the gaiety of an irresponsible enthusiast. He substituted the state for the capitalist, co-operation for private enterprise; he swept away with one hand the deer forest and the private park, and with the other the slum, the workhouse, and the gaol; he parcelled out England into a huge allotment ground set with picturesque homes, yielding boundless produce, sustaining a free and equal ten- ant population. His prophecy was received with rapture, but with incredulity; as a dream, not as a programme, as the confession of an opium-eater, not as the forecast of a states- man. But the chimera of one age becomes the truism of the next, and the ages at this moment are moving with ac- celerated velocity. (Applause.) The old order had passed away and the political education of the autumn had given such a consciousness of their power .to the classes in whose behalf he spoke, that already the peasant tenancy was ac- cepted as the agricultural condition of the future, and park- ownicg squires and glebe-owaing parsons were offering the coveted holdings as a boon and the admirable Allotment Association with a 'powerful Parliamentary following was demanding them as a right, and no ridicule would be cast to-day upon the prediction that before many years, perhaps before many months were ever, compulsory purchase of the land will have bound the labourer to the soil, the cottage will have been added to the enlarged allotment, the conges- ted population of the towns will have begun to flow back into the country, and the historic cow will have calved. (Laughter and applause.) The workingman will have exchanged the slavery, the poverty and the over- work which has been his sole heritage for centuries for the social independence and the'financial competence which his productive toil will have deserved, and which his political sagacity will have won. (Applause.) Bat his (the lectu- rer's) dream soared above regions personal and domestic into an atmosphere of moral and spiritual elevation. He threw round his new Utopia the halo of a worship universal and harmonious, of a faith rational and fervent, and of a minis- try admired, followed, and believed, for he endowed it with a national church. With that problem, toe, they had been brought face to face. The question which a few months ago was a languid and a remote one has become imminent and a pressing one. (Hear, hear.) Popular feeling refused any longer to be shelved, yet if the public will was alive to the urgency of the question the public mind was unprepared for it, uninstructed as to its manifold complications anl not mastering its deep import to the national welfare. The ex- isting church was attacked and defended on a false issue; the alternative put before the public was a misleading one. Happily the necessity for a decision was not immediate; there was time for discussion, time for the application of principle and knowledge, so that the solution of the prob- lem when the time arrived might be submitted to the verdict , of democratic wisdom. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Look- ing at the question himself, not as a Churchman, not as a ' Nonconformist, not as a Liberationist, but simply as a re- ligious and patriotic citizen, it had occurred to him that he might lay before thew a few facts and considerations in the

hope that they might furnish them with the materials for leisurely and dispassionate study against the time when the call for irrevocable action had arrived. . (Applause.) In law and in fact the English Church was theirs. The fran- chise of the church was wider even than the franchise of the State. Women were not on the electoral roll of rate- payers, but they were constituents of the national church. They might not accept its doctrines, they might not attend its worship—that was, a matter of their own pleasure, or possibly of its imperfect constitution, but was in no sense a disqualification. The vestry or church parliament was a lineal descendant of the old folk-mote. He had taken great pains to explain to the labourers of his own village and neighbourhood that of these vestries they were members, and that it was their privilege and duty to understand the parish income and to control the parish expenditure, and to elect for themselves the guardians of the poor, the church- wardens, the oversees, the surveyors, and other parish offi- cials. He entreated them to remember that the Church of England, whatever it might be, and however it might need reform, was not a foreign citadel to be stormed, not a neigh- bour's territory to be appropriated, but absolutely, and in truth their own, not lightly to be thrown away if it can be maintained, and utilised and improved. (Hear, hear.) The essence of a national church was its nationality. (Hear, hear.) It must suit all religious natures, and respect all religious peculiarities; its standard of life and conduct could not be too high, for on this all good men agreed; its code of belief and doctrines could not be too wide, for on this most good men differed; but it must be national or nothing. It was in recognition of this fact that the English Church was originally founded, and might, he would fain hope, be reconstructed. Mr. Tuckwell then gave a brief history of the Church, and mentioned that in Cromwell's days Episcopalians. Presbyterians, and Independents were introduced into Church livings, but on the return of Charles 11. all but the former were ejected. The rector of Warrington at that time was ejected, and subsequently founded Cairo-street Chapel. The recent political crisis, the lecturer went on to say, had placarded unmistakeably the fact that in point of temper and feeling the Church was absolutely at isspe with those for whose sake it existed, and bad forced into prominence the alternpve of either nation- alising it y reforming or reconstructing it, or abandoning as impracticable the idea of a gate controlled ecclesiastical system. (Applause.) Contrasting the theoretical position of the Church as belonging to the w i hole people in its real position and practices, the lecturer said that f a clergyman of the Church of England were honoured by the request to preach in the Cairo-street Chapel and consented, he would

lay himself open to penal treatment from his bishop. ("Shame.") And they must also remember the intellectual incompetency of the clergy, for instead of being selected by competitive examination the bishops took almost all who came. The best students of the universities passed into secular life, and the dregs, as it was callel, took orders. (Laughter.) Their special preparation was infantile. A few exploded text books were thought sufficient for mini- sterial initiation ; their literary proficiency was in most oases ridiculously imperfect, whilst towards science they comforted themselves with the hostility of absolute ignor- ance. They did not know sufficient music to conduct the choirs in theirchurches, and their sermons were exaspera- ting or common place. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) His statements with regard to the ignorance of the clergy had been disputed by au eminent clergyman of the Church, but he challenged him to put them to the test, and this gentle- men afterwards admitted that after carefully inauiring amongst the clergy ef his archdeaconry he found that nine- tenths of them were not aware that there was any valid ob- jection to the literal acceptance of the six days creation. ("Oh," and laughter.) They must also remember that the relation of the Anglican clergy to their flock was not mini- sterial, but autocratic. (Hear, hear.) Who had not seen a congregation broken up by the advent of a new clergy- man determined to carry Out a system of worship and of teaching wholly alien from that which under his predeces- sor they had loved and enjoyed? (Hear, hear.) Who had not pitied the frogs into whose peaceful pool, where 'the clerical King Leg reigned fraternally for years, Juniter sends down a clerical King Stork of potentous spiritual activity and unappeasable spiritual hunger. (Laughter.) Here was the Church to-day in its narrowness, its incompetence, its tyranny, whilst still theoretically national, still retaining in its fabrics, in its endowments, In its parochial machinery, three momentous survivals of its past ideal. Could that ideal be reconstituted? That was the problem they had to solve. Having pointed various dis- advantages connected with the disestablishment of the Church, Mr. Tuckwell said they had another alternative, that of reconstruction. Let them reconstitute it on entirely new principlee, reassert its nationality, proclaim the in- herent right of every citizen, no matter under what denom- ination he might range himself, of partnership in its con- stitution, and of a share in its endowments. Let them re- form their ministers in tlaree directions; let them be com- prehensive, not bound up in narrow sectarianism, but open their ranks, as Dr. Arnold pleaded for 50 years ago to all who professed and called themselves Christian. (Hear, hear.) Let them be educated in literature, art, science, music, oratory—(laughter)--and tested, as the civil servants of the State were tested, by some such governing body as that which Cromwell established ; and let them be popu- lar, each parochial minister elected and controlled by the entire population of the parish. (Loud applause.) Mr. F. Motexs, in moving a vote ef thanks to the lec- turer, said that they were aware he was a member of the Cairo-street congregation, which was started by the rector of Warrington when ejected in 1662, and for his part he should welcome such a Vansformation or reconstruction of the Church upon the lines which had just been sketched. (Hear, hear.) He himself was not a Liberationist, and he did not believe in disestablishment and disendowment of tne Church. He thought it would be a great misfortune to this country if the vast endowments which the Church owned, just as much as any of them owned their own pro- perty, were taken from it. He preferred that they ahonld bide their time until they could reconstruct the Church upon some such basis as Mr. Tuckwell had shadowed forth that night. (Applause.) The Rev. R. PILCaRR, in seconding the proposal, said he had never been a Liberationist, and he had always felt the enormous difficulty which lay in the way of both disestablishment and disendowreent. He wished he could think it possible that such a dream as their magnificent dreamer had had could come true,because he had not intelligence enough, he suppcsed, to discriminate be- tween Episcopalian and Nonconformist bigotry. (Laugh- ter.) The Nonconformist" damn "came to his ear quite as frequently and sounded quite an offensive, and he had al- most said more so, than the Episcopalian " damn," and he thought that before their friend's dream had a chance of coming true, he would have to come down and lecture some of their dear Dissenting brethren, and win them over to Christianity. (" Oh," and laughter.) The CHAIRMAN having also spoken in high terms of the lecture, the vote of thanks was enthusiastically accorded.— A similar compliment, on the motion of Mr. BIRCHALL, seconded by Mr. JIMITRIRS, was passed to the chairman, and the proceedings terminated.

A fire broke out on Thursday morning at the tobacco and snuff factory of Messrs. Goodbody, Tallamore, and con- tinued for five hours. The loss is estimated at £B,OOO. OUTRAGB.—John Cronin, Lord Kenmore's lodge keeper, at Mahony's Point, County Kerry, was fired at from behind a fence on Saturday, and, it is feared, mortally wounded. EVICTIONS ON AN ARCHBISHOP'S ESTATB.—A force of constabulary, under the command of District Inspector McKean, recently aided the sheriff to carry out evictions on the estate of Dr. McEvilly, the Roman Catholic Arch- bishop of Tuam, in the neighbourhood of Gleunamaddy, County Galway. AN IRISH BAILIFF SHOT DBA.D.—A Ballinasloe corres- pondent says a sheriff's bailiff has just been shot dead at Derry-woolen Wood, near Woodford, Galway. His revolver was found by his aide, and there were indications of a struggle. There had been evictions in the neighbourhood recently. The murderers have not been traced. IItaLAND AND IMPIRIAL TAXATION.—The Dublin Tru- man, repudiating Mr. Giffan's statistics, says :—Mr. Giffen acknowledges that we pay three and a half millions over our just proportion of imperial expenditure. For the last 85 years we have paid England an excess of 113 millions, and, roughly, 184 millions interest. Upon Mr. Giffen's own figures, in one item of taxation alone, England stands convicted of having robbed Ireland of 130 millions. Is it any wonder that Ireland has in population sunk from one third to one seventh, in taxable resources from one tenth to 1 in 50 ? •

DUBLIN UNITIIRSITY AND HOME BULB. ^ There was a stormy scene at a meeting of the Senate of Dublin Univer- sity on Saturday, convened for the purpose of adopting an address to be presented to the Lord-Lieutenant. The Right Hon. Dr. Ball, ex-Lord Chancellor of Ireland, pre- sided, as Vice-Chancellor of the University. The draft address submitted by the authorities of the University for adoption contained one political allusion which was much discussed. Eventually Professor Ma- huffy modified his amendment as follows, and it was adopted almost unanimously, Dr. Galbraith being the only dissentient :—" The peace and prosperity of all classes are in our judgment indissolubly connected with the legislative Union between England and Ireland. We there- fore conclude with the earnest hope that this and every other tie which makes Ireland part of the United Kingdom will be fully maintained." POSITION OD PROTBSTANTS IN IRBLAND.—Mary Hamil- ton, Larigan, Ballyfarnan, county Roscommon, writes to the Daily Express as follows :—I am a widow in the county Roscommon. I have got my rent fixed, and am satisfied to pay same. lam now boycotted, and my name put on posters all round Ballyfarnan, for ne reason snip that my son bought 2s &I worth of timber from the Earl of Kings- I ton. My hay has been burnt about three years ago. I know no reason why I should be boycotted only that I am a Protestant. If this state of things is not put a stop to I do not know what honest, peaceable people will do. We are compelled to pay money to every collection that the ruffians choose to demand. They now have my servant boy taken from me. They also cautioned my messenger not to bring me any shop goods. This is the position that the county Roscommon Protestants are placed in. There are three Protestant families boycotted as well as me.

MURDEROUS 017TRIGEI NEAR KILLLR-N-E-ZIA-110ther Out- rage of a desperate character is reported from the Killarney district. The victim is a respectakie farmer, a member of the local branch of the National League, and said to be highly popular in the district. Randall McSweeney, who is unmarried and lives with his mother and brother at Tiem- aboul, within a couple of miles of Killarney, had returned from market aPd was engaged in attending to some cattle in the backyard at half-past four o'clock, on Saturday, when he was accosted by three men who carried pistols, but were net disguised. One of them demanded his gun, and when McSweeney denied their right to take it, they tried to push him aside with the view of entering the house to get the gun. McSweeney barred the way, and seized one of the men. A struggle ensued, and one of the men fired at McSweeney's breast. The bullet smashed his wrist, passed along the arm, lacerating it, and struck McSweenev's watch, off which it glanced without doing farther injury. McSweeney still held the man he had caught at first, and shouted for help. His brother and a labourer, named O'Shea, who were working in the haggard, ran to his assistance, but before they reached him a second unsuccessful attempt was made to shoot him, and he was beaten on the head with the butt ends of pistols until he was obliged to relinquish his hold. The three men then ran off, followed by Mc- Sweeney'm brother and O'SE4sai and, although one of them was almost captured after he fell into a stream, the three succeeded in escaping. Four arrests were made, but Mc- Sweeney failed to identify two. The others have not yet been confronted with him, but one of them has a large wound on his face.

The petition presented against the return of Baron Fer- dinand de Rothschild (L) for Mid-Backs was on Thursday dismissed with costs, Mr. Justice Field holding that there had been no corrupt practices. SMALLPDX EPIDRMIC.—In consequence of severe out- breaks of smallpox at Hyde, the public were excluded from the police court on Monday. One school has been closed, and a bazaar postponed. The authorities are trying to localise the epidemic, but various parts of the borough are affected. The worst cases are those of unvaccinated pa- tients. There has been one death, and, there are no fewer than 30 cases.

The Queen held a Drawing Room at Buckingham Palace on Thureday. .
A fire occurred at Wateringbary Church, Kent, on Sun- day, and the steeple was entirely .destroyed. A fireman was severely injured.
The first stone of the chapel to be erected at Cannes to the memory of the late Duke of Albany was laid on Satur- day by the Prince of Wales.

Mr. Samuel Morley has adopted the allotment system on his estete at Leigh, near Tunbridge Wells. He has cut up the land into plots of about twelve rods, and these he lets to bonalAde working-men at the rate of 6d per rod per annum. The experiment has proved an unqualified BICCe.IIII.

Robert Nash, who was executed at Swansea on Monday for the murder of his child, whom he threw into the sea from Swansea Pier, left In the band of the chaplain a long letter containing a confession of his crime, admitting the justice of his sentence, and declaring that he preferred execution to reprieve.

While ascending his staircase, which overlooks a' garden, a shot was fired. The bullet broke the window, and was flattened against ths wall and fell at his feet. There is no clue to the would-be murderer. EIGHT &CAW SUFFOCATED—The master of the In- dian steamer Nederlanden-Organe, which has arrived in the Tyne, reports that while the vessel was in the Baltic eight of her crew were suffocated in the forecastle by char- coal fumes, and seven others of the crew were taken out unconscious, and are new under treatment suffering from the effects.

STRANGB rim) or LOST PROPERTY.—About four years ago some sensation was caused by the rai.sterions disappearance from Brvnkinalt. the Denbighshire residence of Lord Trevor, of the whole of the family jewelry, valued at £30,000. All efforts to recover the valuables then failed, bat on Sanday morning last a servant found them amongst a heap of rubbish in a disused cellar of the mansion. COAGAILINE.—Cement for Broken Articles, 6d. Is, 2s: postage 2nd. Bold everywhere. Kay. Bros., Stockport.—Advt. FATAL FIRE-ARMS ACCIDENT.—A shocking accident is re- ported from Sully, near Cardiff. A boy named Thomas James, aged 16, in company with two other boys named Brown and Perin, went out with a gun. Perin took the lweapon in his hand, not knowing it was loaded, and it acci- dentally went off. The contents, consisting of powder and a marble, lodged in James's neck, killing him on the spot.

FIRE IN MANCHRSTER.—ShortIy after six o'clock oq Tues- day morning a fire was discovered in the baker's shop of Mr. G. F. Griffiths, 11, Daniel-street, Bradford, Manchester. A deal 'ef excitement prevailed, and as Mrs. Griffitbs and her children were in bad, in the room above, fears were at first entertained of their safety, Mrs. Griffiths, however, opened the bedroom window and dropped Tier two children gently into the street, where, falling on a quantity of snow, they were not hurt. She then descended in a similar man- ner herself. No injuries were sustained. The fire was soon extinguished. TRAGIC AMIL—A. young private, named Richard Thomas Bullock, of respectable position, enlisted as a soldier, and was taken to Chester Castle, where he was lodged with a number of disreputable characters. He could not soar their company, and got leave of absence to visit Colour-Sergeant Wallace at Bury on Monday. Before going there he purchased a revolver and ammunition. He asked his uncle if he could be transferred to another regi- ment, the reply being that it was doubtfui, whereupon he drew the revolver and shot himself, as he thought, through the heart. The bullet, however, passed through his body, just over the stomach. His dying depositions have been taken. Tnu MURDER 07 A MunnEn.—The inquest on the body of William Daniels, who was shot by his brother, John Daniels, on Saturday night, at Dale House Farm, Rough Close, North Staffordshire, was held on Tuesday. The father of the deceased gave evidence to the effect that the brothers were on good terms, and left home together on Saturday morning to go to market. Shortly afterwards witness heard a shot, and go- ing out found the dead body of his eldest son in an adjoin- ing field. The other see returned to the house and pre- pared to surrender to justice. A niece, aged 10, said she sa% her uncle John follow William out with a double- barrelled gun. He fired twice, the first shot missing. From other evidence it appeared the accused was angry at some remark about his wife made by the deceased. A verdict of wilful murder was returned against John Daniels. Bee Advt. SCENE AT AN ExeCuTzoN.—ALLEGED BUNGLING.—David Roberts was executed in Cardiff Gaol, on Tuesday, for the murder of David. Themes, a cattle dealer, of Cowbridge, last October. Berry, of Bradford, was the executioner. The culprit had maintained his composure and cheetful demean- our almost to the last moment. He partook eof no break- fast, contenting himself with a cup of tea. On being pinioned he walked steadily to the scaffold, where he stood firmly till the bolt was drawn. Berry had only allowed a drop of 3ft. 71ns., as the culprit was a man of 13 atone. This, however, seemed insufficient, as the man was seen to strug- gle for three minutes, and apparently was not dead when the reporters were requested to withdraw. Another cerres- pendent says that when the lever was pulled and the drop had fallen it was seen that the neck had not been broken, and the culprit straggled convulsively for fully three minutes, during which the horrified spectators watched the struggling man. Theegovernor or the gaol then ordered the chief warder to conduct the reporters from the yard, though Roberts was not then dead. The usual inquest was held. RECEPTION OF A BAPTIST Minisiuu.—On Tuesday evening the members and congregation of the Baptist Church worshipping in the Victoria Tent, St. Helens, held a tea meeting, after which the special business was to wel- come the .Rev. W. Arthur, late of Marples, as their pastor. Mr. J. Leith (in the absence of Lieut.-Colonel W. W. Pilk- ington) presided, and was supported by the Rev. W. C. Tavler (Baptist), Rev. R. J. Ward (Congregational), Rev. J. Brown (Presbyterian), Mr. W. P. Lockhart (Liverpool), Mr. S. Menzies (founder of the church), Mr. S. Green (senior elder), and Mr. Thomas Penlington (secretary). Mr. Green delivered the charge to the new pastor, after which the Rev. W. Arthur expressed his thankfulness for the way in which he had been received and welcomed.—Mr. Penliug- ton read the annual report, which showed that the work was progressing satisfactorily, and from a sale of work they had £2OO in the bank.—Mr. W. P. Lockhart said one of the difficulties to be encountered was that this is an age of sen- sation' love of novelty, and craving for excitement. There was always something to occupy the minds of men and turn their attention away from the things of God. He did not think they realised as they ought to do how the proceedings of the world were focussed in the daily papers, which they received at such a small cost as a penny and a halfpenny. Well, that caused a gt eat deal of excitement in the human brain, and a good deal of talk and occupation; and that, he believed, in One sense, had been a serious hindrance to the cause of religion. Loup R. CHURCHILL AT MANCHESTER.—Lord Randolph Churchill was the principal speaker at a great Conservative meeting held on Wednesday night in the Free Trade Hall. An address was presented to the noble Lord by the Conser- vative Associations of Lancashire, recognising in particular his services at the India Office, and " the energetic, able, and spirited manner in which you exposed the weak, vacillating, and nn-English policy of Mr. Gladstone's late Government." Lord R. Churchill pointed to Mr. Gladstone as "the deification Of inconsistency," and said that but for the interposition of Providence the Prime Minister might also in his time have belonged to the Fourth Party. Refer- ring to his work at the India Office, he said nothing was more satisfactory with regard to the future of our great dependency than the development of the railway system and the profits it yielded. He took credit ter having been able to open up a new market for British industry in Thibet. He could hardly estimate the harm which Lord Ripon had done to India. There was no reason, said the noble lord, to be alarmed for the safety of the Indian Empire. The only question that need give us trouble was Indian finance. The continued fall in the value of silver, the continued fall in the price of the rupee, was a source of extreme anxiety to the Indian Governors. Leaving Indian subjects, he twitted the , Government with having no policy in regard to the unem- ployed, and condemned their proposals to "enormously re- duce" the naval and military establishments. In conclu- sion, his lordship asked if it was not time to establish a new political party in England—an essentially English party, combining all that was best of Tory, Whig, and Liberal—a party calling itself by the new name of "the Party of the Union," as distinguished from "the Party of Separa- tion."

I THE DISTRESS IN WARRINGTON. fit- 1 ' A meeting of the Executive Committee appointed : to consider the best means of meeting the prevalent distress in Warrington was held at the Town Hall, in the Mayor's Parlour, on Tuesday afternoon. The A Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and there were ' present the Revs. M. Stephenson, G. Allton, Major Litton. and Messrs. Beamont, R. Davies, R. Garnett, - _ 4 Jolley, Smethurst, Monks, Greening, S. Davies, W. Diggle, and J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk).—The MAYOR said that the amount paid into the bank wail now £342 7s, and the total amount contributed in money, material, and provisions, up to the present, was £466 12s 4d.—Mr. MoNrs then read a report of the sul>committee, which was as follows : ' Tour committee have to report that they immediately took steps to organise a system of distributing relief which should at once be effective in checking immature, .i and at the same time giving freely to all deserving 1 cases. One of the first questions to decide was , whether the visiting should be done by voluntarY assistance and by paid agency, and in deciding. in favour, of the latter your committee have had in view the desirability of having a thorough control, and an uniform system of relief throughout with the most effective inquiry into the circumstances of those seeking assistance. We believe the plan adopted will • a be efficient, and will reach all the tia,erving eases, but there will be an amount of distress which we think will be better left to be dealt with through the oral"- nary channel of the Poor Law Guardians. We have t decided no assistance shall be given to those in reeeiPt ' of parochial relief, and the relief that is given shall • " be in food, clothing, and coals. We have also found , it desirable to abolish the system of giving dinners at the Drill Shed, as it was open to abuse, anti' 1 since Friday last no dinners have been given ' to either young or old. In the matter of clothing we have requested the Ladies' Committee to organise sewing classes for making and distribut. .. lug the clothing, and the names of the most deserving cases will be given to them for their attention. Briefly stated, the plan now in operation is as fol , lows. All applicants for relief attend at the inquirl, , office at the Drill Hall, and give in their names, ea.''., dress, occupation, income, and any other details they' - think proper. These names are immediately banded to the inquiry officer, whose duty it is to visit the family, and make the necessary inquiriee . on the spot, and if found to be deserving ° i assistance a card is given with the name, num" ber of family to be relieved, and for bow long. These cards are brought to the Drill Shear examined and stamped every time they are presented. and the bearer then has handed to him the amount of relief as stated upon the card. All goods accounted to the committee are checked and the accounts elnli„ examined before being submitted for payment, and it s is proposed to settle up week. by week, that no armful,- may accumulate, and also that you may see exactly‘ ' I how the account stands from week to week. All the necessary details for giving effect to these arrange" ments are carried out by the members of the CO mittee, or by duly qualified officers appointed 131 I them, and so far as we are able to judge the work,e w , being done satisfactorily. The total number of apiyn' cants up to Saturday evening has been 385, as fol-e lows :—Wednesday 192 Thursday 117, FricleY 51' Saturday 25. Out of this number 263 females have been visited and assistance granted to 217, 46 having been refused as undeserving or not ree quired. In conclusion, your committee have to' acknowledge with thankfulness the very valtiablet assistance received from Mr. Harbourne, Mr. Shearer., and Mr. Garnett, whose ready help has greatlt facilitated the visitation and prevented any' serious delay." At a meeting of the sub., committee held on the 23rd February the following resolutions were adopted :—(r) That no relief be given to any person in receipt of parochial relief. (2) That the allowance per head shall be half a pint of soup and Ps of bread. (3) That all relief be given in food, clothing, and coars. (4) That the ladies be requested to form themselves into a sewing committee to superintend the making and distribu• • tion of the clothing, and that the sum of £ro be placed at their disposal for the purchase of materials. (5) That after Friday next no dinners be given to either young or old at the Drill Shed. (6) That all accounts be made up to the Saturday evening of each . week and presented to the general committee for 1 settlement on the Tuesday. (7) That the distribution of food should begin each day (Sunday excepted) at 12 a.m. (8) That Mrs. Booth be appointed cook at 20S per week, with an assistant at 129. (9) That Major Litton and Mr. Smethurst be appointed the buyers of goods, &c., for this and next week. (TO) ' That a paid agent ct be engaed to visit the cases, and that he shall give such relief as he thinks the case de- mands, and that Mr. Suter be appointed to this posi- tion at a salary of 258 per week. (II) That Sergeant Blease be appointed clerk to receive all applicationS for relief, and shall enter the names, address, occu- pation, income, and any other particulars, and shell at once hand over these names to the inquiry offioers for their immediate attention. (12) That the inquiri office shall be at the Drill Hall, and be open nine to five daily.—The minutes were confirmed oft the motion of Mr. R. DAW Mr. B ES, seconded by from, 4 Gensnere.—The TraTort then read the names of those who have made contributions of bread, meat, and other materials for the benefit of the poor.—Daring 3 discussion that took place regarding the mode of re- lief, Major Lrrroer remarked that there were between thirty and forty poor women working in the Drill Hall at making up clothes, which they were allowed to take for themselves when made up. The clothee were cut cut by ladies in the Town Hall.—Several bills were passed for payment, and Mr. Whittle vette appointed deputy treasurer on the motion of gr. Morrirs, seconded by Major LrrroN.—This was all the business.

SIR HENRY JANIE% M.P., AND THE GOVERNMENT.—Sir H. James, M.P., addressed a meeting of his constituents in the Phillips Hall, Bury. He explained the views which led him to vote against the bulk of the Liberal party on the motion by which the late Conservative Government was • turned from Office. He proceeded to explain his position With regard to the present Liberal Government. A high office in the Gevernment had been offered to him by Mr. tt Gladstone. This he could -lot accept, because he did not Ee- receive, and could scarcely expect to receive, sufficient as- surances to make it clear to him that if he undertook to sup- port the probable policy of the Government, se far as it affected Ireland, he should not run the risk of failing fully to redeem the election pledges which he had given. He was as good a Liberal now as ever he was. The general Policy of the Government he was prepared fully to support. On the Irish question he was one of those who would take on themselves the duty of endeavouring, on the one hand, to maintain intact and unimpaired the authority of the Queen of the Empire, and, on the other, to protect her Majesty fr ,m the horrors of bloodshed and civil war. Hav- ing proposed no policy himself, he was willing to give the fullest and fairest consideration to the policy of others. The address was received with every mark of approval. A resolution was passed, with enthe unanimity, approving of the statement of Sir Henry James, expressing a sense of the sacrifices which he had made in carrying out his pledges to the electors, and cordially welcoming the expression of bin devotion to the principles of Liberalism. Very stale bread—The crust of the earth. An insolvent actor made a statement of his indebtedness, and, with the ruling spirit strong in bankruptcy, he added, "For further particulars see small bills." Visitor to a show, to the little girl who takes the cash: We have made a bet, and we want you to settle it. Is the bearded lady your mother or your aunt ?—Little girl: She is my father. "Did you divide that chocolate with your little brother?" asked a mother of her greedy little Johnny. "Yes, ma: I ate the chocolate and gave him the paper it was in with the pretty pictures. He likes to look at the pictures," was her cherub's reply. WHAT A KERRY BOY SAID.—A sharp bit of repartee was overheard the other day at Killarney. A guide with a tourist scowled at a peasant who stared well at him. "You'll know me again if you meet me," said the guide. "Not if you wash yer face !" said the peasant. "Bromley, here's an account of a Georgia woman who lived forty-eight days on water." That's nothing, Dar. ringer. My father has been living on water for the last ten years." "You expect me to believe that, eh? Why don't you add that he grew fat on it ?" "Well, he did. He's a sea captain." Among the many stories Abraham Lincoln used to relate was the following :--" Trudging along a lonely road one morning on my way to the County Court-house, Judge X. overtook me with his carriage and invited me to a seat. We had not gone far before the carriage began to wobble. Said I, 'Judge, I think your coachman has taken a drop too much.' Putting his head out of the window, the judge shouted, Why, you scoundrel, you are drunk!' Turning round with great gravity, the coachman said, 'Boded, but that's the firs' rightful s'cision your honour's giv'n for a twel'mont' !' " DISTANCE AreatutruerED.—Two Irishmen, brothers, were engaged as navvies on one of the American Grand Trunk lines, and it chanced that on one occasion they did not see each other for a considerable time, being at stations far apart. One day, however, telephonic communication was established between the two points where Pat and Mike re- spectively toiled, and of course every one had an opportu- nity of testing the wonderful invention. After waiting till his turn came, Pat applied his month to the apparatus. "Are ye there, Mike avourneen ? " cried he, and then listened several seconds for a reply. " Bedad, an' lam that, praise Le to the Vargin !" came the expected response; but so close seemed the voice of the speaker that the astounded Pat for- got the hundred miles which lay between him and his brother, and instantly returned, " Efurroo—the saints be wid you! Give us a shake o' your fist ! " TRYING TO Ed:VALISE THE RISK. A good story about the unending duel question in France comes from Bordeaux. Three years ago a young naval officer, having quarrelled with a corn-merchant of the town in a club, sent him his seconds on the following day. "Gentlemen," said the corn merchant, "I am quite willing to fight a duel with the lieu- tenant; but Ido not think that our risks are equal. He is a bachelor, and I have three children. When he has three children, I shall be at his disposal." Lieutenant Carjuzac was obstinate. A barber of the neighbourhood had a pretty daughter. He immediately courted her, obtained her parents' consent, and married her in October, 1882. Ten months later he was presented with a boy, and in 1884 the young officer was blessed with a daughter. At last, to his great , joy, a third child was born three months ago. He lost no time. Taking the first two children in his arms, and order- I ing the nurse to follow him with the baby, he called on the corn merchant. "Well," said he to him in a triumphant I tone, "we can fight now ; I have three children !" "Ah," retorted his antagonist promptly, "but I have five now." Anderson, the "wizard," once met with a Scotchman who stole a march on him in the following manner :—Enter Scotchman. "I say, are you Professor Anderson ?" "Yes, , sir, at your service." "Wed, you're a smart man, and I'm ! surathin' at a trick, too, you know." "&h, indeed! And what tricks are you up to, sir ?" asked the professor, I amused at the simple fellow. "Weal, I can take a shilling and change it into a gold piece." "Oh, that's a mere sleight-of-hand trick; I can do that, too !" "No, you can't. I'd like to see you try." "Well, bold out your I hand with a shilling in it." Scotty stretched out his hand with a shilling in it. "This is your shilling, is it?" "Sire I it's nothing else." "Hold on to it tight. Presto, change! Now, open your hand." Scotty opened his fist, and there was a gold sovereign on his palm. "Wed, you did it, I de- clare! Much obleeged to you!" and the Scotchman turned to go. "Stay." said the professor; "you may leave my , sovereign." " Yours ? Man, warn't that my shilling, and didn't you turn it into this here yellow thing, eh? Good-bye !" And as he left the room he was heard to say, "I ken there ain't anything green about this chiel !" NEW GAME—An amusing story is told of an American millionaire from the far West. As he was walking down a quiet London street one morning, his eye was attracted by an organ-grinder. The top of the organ was covered with a smooth green cloth, and it was this green cloth that attrac- ted the attention of the Transatlantic Crceaus. For him the green cloth suggested only, one thought, and that thought I was gambling. He fancied himelf in the presence of some peripatetic roulette player, and he could not resist the I temptation of taking a tarn. So he stopped opposite to the musical Italian, who was grinding away, and tossed a gold coin cheerily on to the green surface of the organ. The astonished foreigner stopped playing, grasped the coin, pocketed it, removed his hat, grunted out some voluble Tus- can thanks, and resumed his music. "Lost that time," the millionaire murmured to himself, and produced another coin. He tossed it again upon the board, from which it was again no less promptly and no less gratefully removed by the delighted musician. The millionaire shook his head. " Ah, luck' against me." he remarked, as he sent a third gold coin to gleam for a moment upon the green surface before it , rapidly disappeared in the Italian's pocket. Another and another coin went the same way, without wearing out the patience of the American. But at last, when some six sovereigns had transferred themselves from his keeping to that of the organ-grinder, the American bent forward, and in a tone of the intensest curiosity whispered into the ear of the amazed Italian, "Say, stranger, what do you call this game, anyhow ?" Two VANDERBILTS ON TRH ROAD.—A gentleman was riding with W. H. Vanderbilt on Harlem-lane while the old Commodore was still alive. A pair of very speedy horses whirled the wheels of the light road wagon so swiftly around that they ate up the distance between themselves and whatever wheels were ahead of them. At length, how- ever, the sound of the hoof-taps approaching from behind grew clearer and clearer. " C-1-c-c-le," said Vanderbilt to his horses, and he smiled as he made the noise, for instantly they started ahead faster than before, and left the approach- ing hoofs sinking backward. But no—thump-thump, thump-thump, came the sounds nearer and nearer. The millionaire looked anxious. Out came his whip and down fell its lash with a flick, flick oa the neck of each horse. What followed was described as being like the sudden lengthening of a closed telescope, so suddenly and far did the startled team leap ahead; but it was of no use. Thump- thump, thump-thump came the still approaching horses, and presently, as Vanderbilt sat frowning and biting his lip, their heads were up to the tails of his steeds and in an Instant he was being passed. He looked out of the side of his eyes to see his rival, and suddenly heaved a sigh of re- lief. "Why, it's father!" said he. It was the old Comino- dore, humped up behind Mountain Boy and Mountain Girl, and smiling broadly. "Good road-team you've got there, Bill," said be; "but you need another pair if you're racing."

GREAT SNOW STORM -BLOCK OF TRAFFIC, AND TRAINS SNOWED UP. Since daybreak on Monday over 100 men were engaged fighting the snow-drifts between Aber and Penmaenmawr, on the Cheater and Holyhead Railway. As rapidly as they cleared the line at one point they became blocked at another. The up Irish mail was delayed an hour and a half, and the down Irish mail over two hours. Hundreds of tons of snow had been swept from the mountains on to the 'railway. Traffic was entirely suspended on the Bala and Festiniog line. 'The five minutes past eight o'clock a.m. train from Festiniog to Bala became deeply embedded in the snow. The following fairly indicates the wide area affected by the storm :—Between Pentland Forth and Inverness the storm threatened to block the northern railways. All com- munication between land and sea was interrupted, and a keen frost prevailed. As far south as Dorsetshire the ground was covered for several miles to a depth of five or six inches. North and South Shields experienced the fury of the storm, and the Tyne fishing fleet did not proceed to sea. Snow fell continuously from noon till night in Leeds and district. Tramcar.and omnibus traffic was interrupted rand railway trains were delayed. South Lincolnshire ex- perienced the severity of the storm, snow falling without Intermission for 24 hours, preventing all outdoor work. In ' Essex the fall was particularly heavy, as well as in the Lea valley and parts of Hertfordshire. All day snow fell almost continuously in Newcastle. At five o'clock on Mon- day morning snow -began to fall with unusual severity in Derry and County Donegal, and continued till evening. Stormy weather raged throughout the whole of Fifeshire, snow falling at intervals, and towards evening increasing in violence. Sheffield and district were visited with a heavy snowfall, and the tram lines were kept open with difficulty by use of snow ploughs. A gale from the south-east, ac- companied by snow, prevailed from morning till night in and around Sunderland. The drifts on some of the roads almost stopped traffic. The blocking of the tramway lines caused two fatal accidents in Birmingham. On the Bir- mingham and District Line, the cars were sent out each with two engines. At the Smethwicle terminus, while shunting the rear engine, a man named George Wall was crushed to death, being caught between the car and the en- gine. Scarcely half an hour later Joseph Purnow was killed in a similar way, his head being crushed. A goods train became fixed in a snow wreath near Dalwhinnie, on th e Highland ecanbdaßailway.m ech deta Sedev. eral waggons left the line, and thet e g At Douglas. Isle of Man, the drifts were in some places twelve feet high. Traffic on the, Port Erin line of railway was suspended. It is anticipated that flocks of sheep and lambs will have suffered severely. In London all trace of the storm had practically disap- peared on Tuesday. A serious block occurred on ;Tuesday mornieg on the London and North-Western Railway. The limited mail from Scotland to London, due at Wigan shortly before midnight, did not pass until between eight and nine o'clock, having been stopped by a snawdrift between Preston and Wigan. There has been a general snowing-up of trains in Dorn- fries,sbire and GallOway. The Irish mail froe^ Portpatrick, due at 11 on Monday night, had not reached Dumfries at 11 on Tuesday morning.

1 Snow fell at Crews on Tuesday. Drivers of trails re- ported fearful weather. The Scotch express for the south, due at Crewe shortly after midnight, had not arrived by noon. Several trains are snowed up near Tebay, where it is reported there are two miles of snow blocking the lines. At six o'clock ou Tuesday evening the snowstorm which commenced at Sunderland early on Monday morning con- tinued, causing partial suspension of the railway service and a complete block on the country roads. The main line south was kept fairly clear', and the trains were not greatly delayed; indeed, the London newspapers were delivered three hours before those from Newcastle, only twelve miles distant. The Mid-Scotch express, due at Leicester at five o'clock on Tuesday morning, did not arrive till noon, having been set fast in a snow drift. Throe trains got embedded, the first being the Scotch express from Glasgow. Three engines were attached, but failed to get the carriages through, and one engine broke away. The railway at Huntcliffe, be- tween Brotton and Loftus, is completely blocked, and two trains are embedded in the snow. The furious snowstorm which commenced in the Richmond district (Yorkshire) on Monday morning continued with un- abated severity on Tuesday. Communication with many of the villages end dales around the town has been cut off, and, in order to effect communic.tion with Gilling, a cutting seven or eight feet in depth has had to be made. The tele- graph wire between Richmond and Reeth was broken. The general traffic in the town was almost entirely suspended. Several salesmen who had attended Darlington March fair were prevented from getting home. At three o'clock on Tuesday the schooner Emily (Pyeraft master), of Dover, in ballast, from Lowestoft to Seaham Harbour, went ashore at West Hartlepool during a severe snowstorm. The crew were rescued by means of the rocket apparatus. . During the snowstorm on Monday the screw steamer St. Andries, of Cardiff, went ashore on the foreland above Lyn- lon and remained fast, all efforts to get her off proving un- availing. The crew put off in their boats and landed in safety. The vessel has become a total wreck. On Wednesday, though the snowstorm had abated, the blockade of railways in Scotland and the North of England continued. Reports are to hand of trains being snowed up and travellers imprisoned in railway carriages throughent Tuesday night. The Midland line was blocked at Skipton and Hellifield, and the express trains from London to the north were brought to a standstill. The passengers snowed-up in a train at Acklington drank water from foot-warmers, pillaged parcel post hampers. and ate what provisions they could discover. A number of cattle In another train perished. A cattle train was relieved on Thursday morning from a snow block near Morpetb, after being in the snow 54 hours. Several animals died, and the pigs suffered terribly. On Thursday the railways in the north had been almost entirely cleared of the ono% blocks, but in the upland dis- tricts country roads were still impassable, and there is every reason to fear than an enormous amount of injury has been done to cattle and sheep stocks.

[ADVERTISE-104NT.] TO THE TRADES UNIONISTS OF WARRINGTON AND DISTRIOT.

Tamose UNIONISTS, OuT Unions, to possess the power and influence which properly belong to them, should not only look closely after the interests of their own Members, but, if animated by the true spirit, should have sympathy with, and a desire to help, those belonging to other trades who are associated for the same purpose. This is the feeing which calls into existence and secures support for our Trades Councils and Trade Union Congresses. The true Unionist will not knowingly encourage capitalists or employers whose deal- ings with their workpeopte are known to be of an unsatis- factory nature. The true Unionist, if he happens to be a tailor, will not, if he knows it, get his clothes from a man who does not pay fair wages, nor witl the shoemaker, if he ha the true spirit of Unionism implanted in him, be less careful in looking after the interests of his fellow-workman —the tailor. As Printers, we now appeal to you for proof of your fidelity to Union principles by asking your sepport for Bach employers only as conduct their offices in accordance with the rules and principles of the Association of which we are Members. This appeal has been prompted at this particular I period by the fact that within the past few weeks the printer of a newspaper recently published in the town has discharged Union men, and, following the example Of two other local newspapers, has commenced to employ females, the only man remaining at work having forfeited his con- nection with the. Society. Thus three newspapers pub- Baited in the town employ this class of labour, and afford no Opportunity for the Union Printer. The following are the Offices where Union Printers are employed, and the recognised wages of the town are

• paid : " THZ EXAMINER" PRINTING WORKS, BEWSBY STREET; EAGLE PRINTING WORKS, UPPER BI,NK STREET; Join; S. GREEN, BRIDGE STREET; A. E. SMITH, WINWICK STREET; "TEE MAGPIE" OFFICE. Trusting that this appeal may not prove to have been made in vain, but that it will receive the consideration we feel it deserves, We remain, yours in Union, THE MEMBERS OF THE WARRINGTON BRANCH OF THE TYPOGRAPHICAL ASSOCIATION.

The above appeal has been considered at a meeting of the Warrington Trades Council, and they heartily commend it to the consideration of allplovers of Unionism and Fair Play. Signed, on behalf of the Council, J. GREALEY, President. J. WILD, secretary.

Secretaries and Members of Friendly Societies, who are Trade Unionists, should see that their Printing is done in Union Offices. Farther information will be supplied to those desiring it en application to Mr. ARTHUR CaomYrow, 279, Winwick-road, Warrington. February, 1886.

A MYSTERY AT WESTON POINT. SUSPECTED MURDER. An occurrence has taken place at Weama Point which is surrounded by considerable mystery, and there is a strong suspicion that there has been some "foul play" practised. About seven o'clock yester- day morning a waterman named Thomas Bostock found the dead body of a man on the river bank near Weston Point Docks. He was apparently about 26 years of age, had a light moustache, and his chin had not been shaved for several days. Although only about five feet two, he was well made, was wearing a blue guernsey, and had every appearance of being a seaman. At first it was thought he had been drowned, but tn. th 6 body being washed two deep wounds were found on the forehead, and one on the skull, all evidently inflicted with some long sharp in- strument, and that very recently. Yesterday after- noon Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, opened an inquest on the body at the Weaver Hotel; but it was adjourned without any evidence being taken in order that the police may make full inquiries. The body had not been identified last evening.

LAND GRABBING AT HIGHER-WAL I ON.

Sir,—l beg to call the attention of the public to the fol- lowing facts. A very old foothpath, on Mr. Ball's farm lead- ing front the Moore-road and back of the Parsonage, has been ruthlessly ploughed up. An old inhabitant of the vil- lage told me last week that he could lemember the said footpath for 45 years. So you can at once see that it is a Ipure case of filching from the people their ancient right of way. I hope that the public will make an earnest protest and take action against all such encroachments.-1 am, yours sincerely, EDWAEtD WRIGHT, Secretary pro. tem. of the Warrington Footpath Preserva- tion Society. March sth, 1886. P.S.-1 may just state that Mr. Baxter, who was there before Mr. Ball, never interfered with the said foothpath, but always kept the byepatha on his farm in good repair.

It now turns out March 4th, 1886. that a dog may not look at the Queen. An order has just been promulgated from Windsor Castle prohibiting the entry of all dogs. The detachment of the British army on guard at the Castle have orders to use armed force against any dog attempt- ing to obtain an entrance, and we have faith in our soldiers that in this case, as in other, they will do their duty. There is, perhaps, no more pitiable object in Europe than the poor Emperor of Germany. If he lives till Monday fortnight he will have reached his ninetieth birthday. His four score years are far past, and for a long time now his life has been one of labour and sorrow. He clings with child-like affection to all the pageantry and ceremony of his earlier state. He will insist upon wearing his stiff uniform when he were better in bed. He tries to get up early in the morning, as was his military habit, and goes through certain formulfe of signing papers and discussing public affairs as if old age were a myth and failing powers a phantasy. The poor old man refuses to believe that an Emperor can be so weak that it is dangerous for him to totter across the roorn. He is just now suffering from a contused thigh brought about in one of these excursions, and there is some fear that he may not Jive to see his, ninetieth birthday. It is impossible that the Emperor should last long. But the extension of his life, even by a few months, is a matter of keenest interest to Europe. Far-reaching changes will follow at his demise. In the first place it is certain that Prince Bismarck will retire from active politics. He too is old and weary. At least ten years ago he expressed his de- sire to spend the rest of his days in private, yield- ing only to the tearful solicitations of his aged master. But When the Emperor dies Bismarck will feel himself relieved from all further obligations to the country he has served so long. With the founders of the empire gone, my own opinion, based upon some personal acquaintance with the country an d the people, is that the empire will not long survive. With Germany hoisting the Republican flag, there will be a terrible tottering of thrones in Europe.

HARD TIMES AND HOW TO MEND THEM.

Sir,—Tbe prevailing distress that we are constantly hear- ing about, demands our thoughtful consideration, and with your permission I will give your readers a few ideas, which if acted upon, cannot fail to mitigate the evils complained of. As a vegetarian of many years practice and observa- tion, I can speak with authority respecting the advantages to be gained by following a simple course of diet. Let any of your readers try the following three-course dinners coat- ing about is 9d, and which will be sufficient for a family of six persons : Scotch broth.—Two ounces each Scotch barley and groats or oatmeal, Id ; llb. carrots, 43 ; 11b. turnips, 4d ; lib. onions, id; pot-herbs, pepper, and salt. ird. Direction.: Put the barley and groats into two quarts of boiling water, ' with the vegetables cut small. Boil for three hours. Add the herbs and seasoning half an hour before serving. A head of celery added is an improvement. I Haricot Stew.—One and half lbs. beans, 3d; loz, butter, id; large handful of parsley, id ; pinch of bi-carbonkte of soda, pepper, an salt to taste, kI. Directions Wash the beans, and throw them at once into three quarts of boiling water, with the butter. Let them boil about an hour, then put in the soda and when tender add the parsley (chopped), and pepper and salt, and boil for a qoarter of an hour longer; time required, about three or four hours. Four lbs. potatoes, boiled or roasted.

LORD SALISBURY* AT THE CRYSTAL PALACIL—TtIe Mar- quis of Salisbury spoke on Wednesday night at a Conserva- tive Banquet at the Crystal Palace. He denied that the Conservative party had ever given pledges to the Parnellites with regard to Home Rule, and expressed the opinion that Mr. Gladstone's present Administration had been expressly formed for the purpose of bringing such a measure into operation. Were such a measure brought forward it would, he said, probably meet with the strongest opposition in the House of Lords. The opposition would be backed up by the loyalists of Ulster, who were naturally greatly perturbed at the thought of their hereditary enemies ;being placed in power over them.

Tire LONDOX SOCIALIST TRIAL.-At Bow-street Police Court, London, on Saturday, Burns, Champion, Hyndman. and Williams, were again charge 4 with inciting to riot. There was a considerable abatement evident in the public interest in the proceedings.—Hyndman complained of the magistrate deciding to seed the case for trial without hear- ing the defence, and of the remarks of the Home Secretary, whom he called "coercion Childers."—The magistrate de- clined to discuss the subject right, and Hyndman thereupon protested against his animus.—Sir Edmund Henderson. late Chief Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police, was called by the defendant. He stated that nothing occurred at the socialist meettng on the night before the Trafalgar-square demonstration to excite his apprehensions. He had no reason on the Monday to expect any disturbance in the West End. It was totally unexpected and wholly unpro- vided for as regarded any special precautions. The only special measure he took was to order a reserve of police to Pall Mall.—Cross-examined by Hyndman : The Socialists had geserally communicated with the police beforehand about their meetings. So little expectation had he of a disturbance that bad it not been for the interregnum at the Home Office he should not have sent so many policemen as he did.—The Hon Guy Dawnay deposed that he was aronbdbehdisofbraowthaetrchpbroytecthteed chroimw.cl2...mbunt sthtese dd,efeednditoaart oßfutrhnes Pall Mall Gazette, said be believed there were many thieves in the crowd in the square. The impression 'on his mind was that Burns and others were good honest men, who were soniewhat cracked, and saw an evil they wanted to remove, and used very strong speech. Witness anticipated no disturbance. The crowd was very good humoured, and as for the thieves there were the police to look after them. But their business seemed to be to look after the Nelson column, and in this they were absolutely successful. Other witnesses were afterwards called and the case adjourned. On Wednesday Messrs. Hyndman, Burns, Champion, and Williams, were again brought up at the Bow-street Police Court, and after a -number of witnesses had been examined on their behalf were committed for Ws at the April Session' of the Central Criminal Court. Bail was accepted.

Plum Pudding.—Tialf lb. wheatmeal, id ; Vb. bread. td; Vb. raisins, 2d; lb. currants, ; Ilb. toots or moist sugar, td; 11b. carrots, id ; loz candied peel, ; saltspoon of grated lemon peel, and a little spice, id. Directions: Stone the raisins, pour boiling water over the bread, rub the butter into the meal, mix all well together, tie in floured cloth, and boil for about three hours ; the longer the better. A 21b. wheatmeal loaf; cost 3d. .

The above dinner will be found far more substantial than the wretched fare that too often graces the tables of our poorer classes, and costing only 3bd per head. Of course the above can be varied according to circumstances; for example the Scotch broth can be made in sufficient quantities to serve for the meal with the bread added, or the second course can be treated in like manner. Next week I will give another dinner if you will kindly permit me. In conclusion let me appeal to the better classes to try the above dinner as an experiment, and let it form a por- tion of their gifts to the poor, not because it Is cheap, but in order to teach them how much farther money will go, with la little knowledge of domestic economy. Warrington, March 3rd, ISM. W. H. CHAPMAN.

1103 IE Rum—The Press Association, professing to have "the most reliable authority," furnishes a report to the effect that Mr. Gladatone's scheme for Ireland is one of Home Rule pure and simple, that he is determined to stand or fall by it, and that at least one member of the Govern- ment—Mr. Trevelyan—is expected to resign within a few days. SIR CHARLES MUCH AND TRH TEETOTALLERS.-0/1 Wed- nesday sight, Sir Charles Dilke, M.P., addressed a social meeting of workers of the Chelsea Temperance Society at Sydney Hall. Chelsea; Mr. J. S. Brass presiding. The right hon. baronet pointed out that hitherto temperance legislation had been delayed by the block of Parliamentary business, but would be secured when the Local Government Bill came to the front. That bill when passed would ron- stitute undoubtedly the greatest revolution that would over have taken place in the affairs of this country at one time. He understood Mr. Chamberlain was to receive a depot ttion on the subject, and be (Sir Charles) hoped that tem- perance reformers would find their hopes realised in the measure. STEPNEY ELECTION PATITION.—EH-COUNT ORDERED.— At the hearing of the Stepney election petition on Saturday the Court decided, counsel on both sides consenting, to send to the Court of Appeal for argument the question whether a person born in Hanover, and whose father was born in the same kingdom during the time that it was attached to the British Crown was a British subject, and therefore entitied to a vote. The question affeeis 20 votes. Mr. Gully, Q.C. (for the respondent), afterwards asked for a recount of the whole et the votes, and the judges granted tbe application. , —On Monday, Mr. Justice Denman announced that the re- count of votes had resulted in giving Durant 2,14 C, Isaacson 2.116. Deducting from this the votes struck off on the scrutiny, the record stands—Durant 2,052, Imac- son 2,051. The sitting member will, therefore, retain his seat, subject to the reserved decision on the validity of the Hanoverian vote.
