div.p: THE EXAMINER, SkirtißDAY, MARCH 6, 1886.*
Xettero to the editor.
Tce Viceroy and Lady Dafferin left Madras on Friday for Calcutta.
Lord Salisbury left Charing Cross on Friday morning for Cannes, travelling via Paris. At a meeting of the Bristol Trades Council it was stated that 3,000 men were out of work in that town.
The ship Cinderalla was found capsized on Friday morning at Tarbet, four miles from Listowel. There is no trace of her crew.
Three more deaths have occurred from famine near New- port, county Mayo. Shopkeepers are on the verge of bank- ruptcy, and refuse credit even to the priests.
FIVE MEN DROWNED.-Dr. Sutton and four men were returning in a lugger from Ballymlongford to Listowel on Thursday evening, when the vessel capsized and all were drowned.

The Queen, accompanied by the Prince and Princess of Battenberg, and the infant children of the Duchess of Albany. arrived at Windsor from London at a quarter to six on Friday evening. Tke Central News is requested to contradict the state- ments contiinad in a paragraph communicated to the news- papers by the Press Association in reference to Mr. Glad- stone's plans respecting Home Rule, and to state that they are without foundation. THE PIMLICO POISONING CASE.—Hearing ef the charge of murder against Mrs. Bartlett and the Rev. Geo. Dyson was resnmed at Westminster Police Court, on Friday after- noon, when Dr. Leach deposed to the circumstances under which post morterta examinations of the deceased were made. During witness's examination he was excitedly accused by Dyson of telling lies. Witness repeated the evidence he gave at the Coroner's inquiry, as to Mrs. Bar- tlett's statement to him of the peculiar matrimonial relations between herself and her husband. The case was adjourned until to-day.

THE SNOWSTORM. - The dead body of a shepherd named Henderson was found in the snow near Berwick on Thursday —On Shan Fell, in Westmoreland, a man on horseback trying to get through the deep drift came upon a woman and two children lying beside her. The woman was dead, but the children although suffering dreadfully from the intense cold and hunger were alive.—On Thurs- day one of the men employed by the North Eastern Rail- way Company to clear the line in the Fulwell cutting be- tween Newcastle and Sunderland, was killed. He was caught in a snowdrift by the engine and carried a distance of about 50 yards. The body was dreadfully mangled.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The House met at four o'clock.

MISCELL&NEOUS.—The royal assent was given by com- mission to the Land Registration Act, the Lord Chan- cellor, Lord Monson, and Lord Sudeler being the Royal Commissioners. The Drill Ground Bill, giving the Secre- tary for War extended powers for providing drill grounds for volunteers was read a second time. The Marriage Validity Bill was read a third time and passed. The House adjourned at 4.40. ROUSE OF COMMONS

THE GOVERNMENT EMPLOYES.-Sr H. TYLER gave notice that on going into committee on army estimates, he should move a resolution stating that it was undesirable to discharge workmen from Government factories at the pre- sent time of depression.—Mr. CAMPBELL BANNzamex, re- plying to Sir H. Tyler, 'aid the final arrangements for dis- charging workmen from Enfield Sinai! Arms Factory would not be abrupt or cause the discharge of men to any large extent.
Tug LONDON Ml:yrs.—Sir R. PEEL gave notice that he would move the rejection of the Compensation for Damages Bill.

Tina HOUSE or LORDS.—On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Mr. LABOUCHERE moved as an amendment that in the opinion of that House it was in- consistent with the principles of representative government that any member of either House of the Legislature should derive his title to legislate by virtue of hereditary descent. He obected to the present system as clever men had not always clever sons, and because there were no less than 207 peers connected with the two services. The House of Lords, he contended, was an assemblage of Conservative partizans, and that it was uselest, as when the Liberals were in office it obstructed, marred, and mutilated the measures that the representatives of the people had passed. The action of the House of Leeds had been one persistent war against all reforms, parliamentary or municipal, and against all sound doctrines of political economy.—Mr. DILLWYN seconded Mr. Labouchere's resolution.—Mr. BRODERICK opposed it, and he advised the House to think once or twice before it condemned the hereditary principle. He was in favour of strengthening the here- ditary principle by the creation of life peers.— Mr. Gladstone said he had never, he believed, votedlon a question of importance for an abstract resolution, unless he was able to follow up his vote by action. As regarded the legislative action of the House of Lords he cold not deny that there was a case for large and important change, but the case was one not to be dealt with piecemeal. He certainly should not vote for a motion that he could not give effect to, and he considered the words of the present amendment far too wide and sweeping.—After a few words from Col. Verney. the House divided, when Mr. Laboucheres proposAl was rejected by 202 to 166. FISHERY INDUSTRIES.—Sir E. BIRKBECK called atten- tion to the great want of a central department for all mat- ters connected with our tishery industries.—A discussion ensued, in which Mr. MIINDELLA admitted the necessity of something being clone, and the Government were quite prepared to co-operate with the honourable baronet by creAting in the Board of Trade Department for purposes suggested SUPPLY.—Tbe House then went into Committee of Sup- ply, and progress was immediately reported. The Freshwater Fisheries (Eels) Bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at ten minutes to twelve.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

THE DISTRESS IN WARRINGTON.—During the present week more soup and bread has been distri- buted to destitute people at the Drill Hall. In addi- tion to these clothing and fuel is also being given in necessitous cases. The members of the Ladies' Committee have been very industrious in providing clothing, and at the Drill Hall a large number of poor women have been employed, under the super- vision of Mrs. O'Brien, in completing ;the garments which have been cut out and prepared by the Ladies, Committee.

THE LATE MR. CASSIDY.—On Sunday the Rev, J. Warnock, 8.D., preached in St. John's Presbyterian Church on "A good old age," the subject having special reference to the late Mr. John Cassidy, who died last week at the ripe age of ninety-five years. Mr. Warnock selected as his text Genesis 25 c. 8 v., "And Abraham gave up the ghost and died in a lgood old age, an old man and full of years, and was gathered to his people." Turning to some of the features in the deceased's character that wore worthy of their emulation, Mr. Warnock said one of these was his scriptural knowledge. No one could have talked long with Mr. Cassidy without learning that the patriarchs and prophets and apostles were much in his thoughts. The words and deeds of Abraham, Moses, Peter, and John were all known to him. Another trait worth notice in their friend's character was his steadfast adherence to the principles and practice of Christian temper- ance. In the history of the temperance movement, he (Mr. Warnock) found an account of the origin of a temperance society in Warrington, which took i place more than 50 ears ago, and amongst those who were first to sin the pledge he found the name of John Cassidy. o far as he had learned, Mr. Cassidy had been a practical abstainer ever since. In conclusion, Mr. Warnock referred to the regular attendance at that place of worship of Mr. Cassidy whilst his health permitted him. On looking over the communion roll, he found that up to the year 1883 Mr. Cassidy was present at every communion almost without exception. His example in this respect might well be followed by younger men. , If a man of ninety was able to honour God by ; waiting upon Him in public worship then truly everyone else was without excuse. I

div.p: LYMM.

COOEBRY LECTURES.—A. series of lectures on cooking by means of gas stoves has this week been given in the Drill (late Mission) Hall, Lyram, by Mrs. Thwaites, of Liverpool, who has succeeded in interesting very good audiences. The lectures were practically illustrated. The exhibition was got up by Mrs. Wright and Son, who had the assistance of the Lymm Local Board, with the express purpose of recommending the gas cooking stoves to the notice of the public. On Thursday evening the members of the Lymm Local Board and a number of guests partook of supper at the Hall. In addition to the stoves that were on exhibition there was a number of gas meters, gauges, and other gas apparatus.
LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting at this Board was held in the Board- room, Lymm, on Thursday evening. There were present— Messrs. Cameron (chairman). Dewhurst. Rogers, Woolley, Hall, Gibbon, Forster, Thomason, Appleton; J. C. Ridgway (clerk). A LEGAL Poterr.—On the minutes of the previous meet- ing been proposed for adoption, Mr. Hall inquired whether or not it was legal for the Board to accept the protest of Messrs. Rylanda against the proposal to establish soap boil- ing, &c., at Massey Brook, as Messrs. Rylands lived out of the parish.—The Chairman: I suppose it is legal to re- ceive such a communication.—The Clerk : There is not the slightest objection to anybody writing to the Board that I am aware of.—The minutes were thyn passed. THE ADMISSION OF RATEPAYERS.—LIVELY DEBATE.-- The Clerk said he understood that Mr. Gibson, whose appli- cation for permission to establish soap boiling, tic., at Mas- sey Brook was to come before the Board, was in attendance, and claimed as a ratepayer to be present at the discussion. —The Chairman: That is a new claim to make.—The Clerk : It is the first that has been made.—Mr. Hall : It is legal, though.—The Clerk: It is in the power of the Board to do what they think right.—Mr. Hall said he could bring forward a parallel case, in which the Manchester Town Council had allowed a person to be present at their meeting.—The Clerk thought it was a question of conveni- ence; it depended on their accommodation.—The Chairman said there were reporters at their meetings to report what took place, so that the public might know what was going on.—Mr. Hall remarked that there were meetings of the Board to which reporters were not allowed to come.—The Chairman: That is so, and will always be so; the Board has a right to consider its business in committee.—Mr. Hall said that in the case of important matters which in- volved the spending of money it was unfair to keep the ratepayers in the dark. They might take, for instance, the special meeting they had about the gasworks, which was not a committee meeting, yet the reporters were not ap• prised of it. The business was most important, and showed clearly the deficiencies in connection with the gasworks. Everything should be done justly and fairly towards the ratepayers and it was perfectly right that they should know what was being done. The Gas Committee, Mr. Hall added, once or twice took upon themselves the responsi- bility of purchasing various things which they ought not to I have done without consulting the Board.—The Chairman said he did not know that it was the duty of anybody to give uotice to the reporters of special meetings of the Board. I —Mr. Hall said that if it was nobody's duty to give the re- porters notice of special meetings, important business should only be brought forward at the monthly meetings.— The Chairman : This matter of Mr. Gibson's is one en- tirely in the Board's hands.—Mr. Hall : As you have turned to that subject, Mr. Chairman, I suppose there is no reply, and I am perfectly in order in making my remarks. —The Clerk said that as orders passed through his hands he should like to ask what Mr. Hall meant when he said that things had been ordered without the sanction ef the Board.—Mr. Hall said he alluded to the purchase of a new exhauster, and he brought the matter before the Board at the time when Mr. Dewhurst was kind enough to offer them a cheque. It ,was explained at that time by Mr. Rogers that the necessity was so urgent that they were com- pelled to buy the exhauster before a meeting of the Board. ' —The Clerk, referring to the minutes, said that on the sth November, 1885, the Board sanctioned the purchase ,ef the exhauster, and the order for it was given lon the same date.—Mr. Hall : I beg pardon ; and then the other things were a number of retorts.—The Clerk said the order for them had not yet been given.—Mr. Hall re- marked that they had been knocking about the station.— The Clerk: If you have anything else to charge against the clerk perhaps you will do so new.—Mr. Hell denied that be was charging anything against the clerk.—After a few further remarks, the Chairman said he thought Mr. Hall had got into a mare's nest. (Laughter.)—The Clerk : The clerk has had to meet Mr. Hall before, and the clerk will meet Mr. Hall again in a public manner if he does not mind how he addresses the clerk.—Mr. Hall said he had a right to maintain that it was not proper for any committee to order anything without first coming before the Board.— Mr. Dewhurst : Would von like to have the whole village I in darkness P—Mr. Hall : Thank you, sir, that is quite suf- ficient- that was what was said at the time. Mr. Hall then went on to say that it had been found that they were in so deplorable a position in regard to the gasworks that it required £5OO to be spent. Mr. Rogers with his deplorable theories made a mistake at the Outset which the public knew nothing about. Theory was all very well, but when it was put into practice everything turned out wrong with Mr. Rogers.—The Chairman: We have not that question before us.—Mr. Hall: It is no mat- ter, I have got it in.—Mr. Thomason said it was Mr. Hall's great idea to get what he said into the newspapers. He came there for nothing but to epout.—Mr. Rogers said he wished the reporters to note that what Mr. Hall said was not true.—Mr. Hall: it is true.—Mr. Rogers: It is false, and I can prove it.—After some further discussion Mr. Hall moved that Mr. Gibson be allowed to be present at the meeting, but this proposal received no seconder. Mr. Gib- son was then called in, and informed of the decisioo of the Board. He replied that he bowed to the decision of the Board, though he protested against it. THE SEWAGE Farrax.—On the report of the sanitary in- spector being read, Mr. Hall inquired as to whether the £lOO profit was going to be realised on the farm.—Mr. Dewharst said that was a doubtful matter.—Mr. Hall said he had heard such a glowing account ef what they were going to make out of the sewage farm that it really astonished him to find that they were going to make nothing. RE-APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board approving of the re-appointment of Dr. Fox as medical officer for a term of five years, the proportion of salary to be paid by the Local Board to be £22. MR. GIBSON'S APPLICATION.—The application of Mr. J. Gibson for permissiott to commence soap boiling at Massey Brook again came before the Board, the consideration of it having been adjourned from the previous meeting.—The Clerk said that as yet he had not received any report from Dr. Fox, but since the last meeting he had received more letters from residents objecting to the granting of the ap- plication. ?le then read these letters ; which were five or six in number, including ones from Mr. P. Stubs, Mrs. Croefield, Mr. Ross, and Mr. B. Brownell. There was also a petition from the Warrington Rural Sanitary Author tty—with an accompanying report from their medical officer—protesting against the granting of the application. A communication from the Town Clerk of Warrington, stating that the War- rington Corporation bad refused two applications to establish offensive trades, was likewise read, as was also a petition signed by a considerable number of farmers and other residents in Lymm and neighbourhood.—Mr. Hall next presented a bulky petition in favour of the application if it were shown that the trade would not be a nuisance and injurious to the neighbourhood.—The Chairman: How many signatures are there Mr. Hall P—Mr. Hall: Ido not know how many hundreds there are, bet if you want them you could have two or three hundreds more. Mr. Hall then in a speech of considerable length spoke in favour of the application, and criticised some of the objections to It. In conclusion, he moved "That Dr. Fox having by his ab- sence made it apparent that no nuisance would arise from the works, and that it would be a benefit to the working classes of the neighbourhood if the application be granted to Messrs. Gibson and Co. —Some discussion took place on this proposal, in the course of which Dr. Fox entered the room. In answer to the Chairman, Dr. Fox said he had inspected the works, but as yet he was in want of some in- formation necessary to a complete report.—The Chairman mentioned that he had also visited the works, and as far as he could see there was nothing offensive, but still he should like to have the doctor's report before he gave an opinien.—ln reply to Mr. Hall, Mr. Gibson, who had been again called into the room, said it was a falsehood for any ' Qua to say that if he got permission he intended to bring in labourers from the outside.—Ultimately, it was agreed to leave the matter over to allow the medical officer time to

report. AxornEß APPLICATIM—An 'application was made by Mr. D. Daniels, Booth's Hill, Lymm. for permission to pre- pare and boil tripe and cow heel.—On the motion of Mr. Rogers, seconded by Mr. Appleton, the application was granted. Thia was all the business of public interest.

THE BIREENREAD MURDER. - Robert Travis, hot./ keeper, of Sutton, and Elizabeth Platt, a woman to whom 11' was engaged to be married, were, on Wednesday, at Bickel. head, committed for trial for the murder of Mrs. M'lntyre, $ sister of the female prisoner. The deceased woman was hea to death with a pair of' tongs while she lay on a sick be't The prisoners by their own admission wore in the house!' the time, but both declared tbemselves ignorant of tbe cumstances of the assault on the woman. Travis said 13° had been drinking whisky with the two women, and aroused from a sleep by cries in the deceased's room, both he and Platt declared that they too were attacked some heavy instrument.

CADISHEAD. TEA. PAirrY.—A tea party in connection with the Total Abstainers was held on Saturday evening, followed by a temperance meeting, addressed by the Rev. D. Clegg, Con- gregational minister, Partingtoa. There was a good atten- dance. CADISHEAD WESLEYAN CHOIR.—On Tuesday a social tea meeting was held in the School-room. After tea tbe choir gave an excellent entertainment. Mr. A. Gatenby presided, and Mr. E. Aspinall was the accompanist. There was a good attendance and the programme was much appre- ciated. LimnlLL MEETING.—On Monday evening a tea party in connection with the Irlam and Cadishead Liberal Associa- tion (Eccles division) was held in the Congregational School-room, Liverpool-road, Cadishead. There was a large attendance. At the subsequent meeting Mr. Jobs A. Holmes presided, and was supported by Mr. V. K. Armitage (the Liberal candidate at the last election) and other gentlemen. —Mr. E. Clarke, Eccles, moved :—" That this meeting de- sires to express its unabated confidence in Mr. V. K. Armi- tage, and would impress upon the Council of the Eccles division the wiShes of this meeting that he be requested to become the candidate at the next election."—Mr. J. S. Brighouse, Eccles, seconded the resolution, which was carried with acclamation.—Mr. Armitage afterwards ad- dressed the meeting; and a resolution in support of the Government was adopted on the motion of Mr. John Jack- son, seconded by Mr. Bax.

WARBURTON'S BENEFIT.—On Monday even- ing a miscellaneous concert was held in the Work- men's Club, Market-place, for the benefit of Joseph Warburton, an old Warringtonian, who has been in- jured, and is unable to follow his employment. Mr. 1f homes Morris, F.G.S., presided, and commented on the fact that although the weather was inclement ' there was a large audience assembled, which, he said, evidenced the good feeling that prevailed to- wards Mr. Warburton. The programme was an ex- cellent one, and the contributors to it were all well received. It was as follows:—Selection, St. Paul's Handbell Ringers; song, "Battle Cry," Mr. Alfred Cavanagh; recitation, " Ode to the Sun," Mr. Brown; song (selected), Miss Baxter; song, "Come into the I Garden, Maud," Mr. Dell; song, "Some Day," Miss Horton; song, "Love's Request," Mr. Parr (encored); comic song, Mr. Mercer; concertina solo, " The Farm Yard," Mr. Whittaker; recitation, "Thank God for , aw these Bonny Fleawrs," Mr. Brown; selection, St. ' Paul's Handbell Ringers; recitation, " Ab-o'th-Yates' Reform Speech," Mr. Brown; song, "Within a Mile of Edinbro' Town," Miss Baxter; song, "The Maid of the Mill," Mr. Dell (encored) ; song," Golden Love," Miss Horton ; song," The Skipper," Mr. Alf. Cavanagh (encored) ; comic song, Mr. Mercer; song, "My Sweetheart when a Boy," Mr. George Parr; concer- tina solo," Blue Bells," Mr. Whittaker. Mr. George Riley was the accompanist. During the interval. the Rev. S. Wilkinson expressed his pleasure at see- ing so many present on such an unpleasant evening. Mr. Warburton well deserved the support of the Warrington public, especially those who were fond of music. He had rendered various churches much valuable aid as a singer, and had always readily given his services as a musician when desired. Mr. Warborton also said a few words in expressing his thanks for the help accorded him.
